1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 On August 15, 2021, at 15:47:12 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), a Boeing 737-800, registration N737XX, experienced a hard landing that resulted in the structural collapse of the nose landing gear (NLG) during a gusty crosswind approach to Runway 27L at Chicago O'Hare International Airport (KORD), Chicago, Illinois. The aircraft was operating as a scheduled passenger flight under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121.

1.2 The flight originated from Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (KDFW) at 13:15 Central Daylight Time (CDT) and was en route to KORD. The flight crew consisted of a captain and a second in command (SIC), along with four flight attendants and 162 passengers. The flight was conducted in accordance with the operator's approved flight operations manual and dispatch release.

1.3 Following touchdown, the aircraft sustained substantial damage to the forward fuselage, NLG assembly, lower engine cowlings, and associated flight control linkages. All occupants evacuated via the forward and overwing emergency exits without serious injury. Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting (ARFF) units arrived on scene within 2 minutes and 45 seconds of the event. The runway was closed for 4 hours and 12 minutes for wreckage recovery and surface inspection.

1.4 The accident occurred during daylight hours under visual meteorological conditions. The aircraft was configured for a normal landing with flaps set to 30 degrees, landing gear extended, and speed brakes armed. The flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) were recovered intact and transported to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for data extraction and analysis.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 The captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, certificate number 1234567, with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The captain's medical certificate was a first-class medical, issued on January 10, 2021, with no limitations. Total flight time was 14,250 hours, with 6,800 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The captain's most recent line check was completed on June 12, 2021, and the most recent recurrent simulator training was conducted on May 4, 2021. Training records indicated satisfactory performance in all required maneuvers, including crosswind landing techniques, wind shear recovery, and go-around procedures.

2.2 The SIC held an ATP certificate, certificate number 7654321, with Boeing 737 type ratings and a current first-class medical certificate issued on March 22, 2021. Total flight time was 3,450 hours, with 1,850 hours in the Boeing 737. The SIC's most recent proficiency check was completed on July 20, 2021. Training documentation confirmed that the SIC had successfully completed the operator's advanced adverse weather training module, which included simulated crosswind landings with gust factors exceeding 15 knots.

2.3 Both flight crew members were in compliance with 14 CFR 121.439 and 121.441 regarding recent flight experience and training requirements. Operator scheduling records confirmed that the captain's duty time on the day of the accident was 7 hours and 10 minutes, and the SIC's duty time was 6 hours and 15 minutes, both within the limitations prescribed by 14 CFR 117. Fatigue risk management system (FRMS) data indicated that both pilots had obtained a minimum of 8 hours of rest in the 24-hour period preceding the flight.

2.4 The flight crew's approach briefing, as documented in the operator's electronic flight bag (EFB) system, included a review of the published crosswind landing procedures, wind shear escape maneuver, and stabilized approach criteria. The briefing specifically addressed the forecasted gusty conditions and the requirement to execute a go-around if the aircraft deviated from stabilized parameters below 1,000 feet above ground level (AGL).

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 The accident aircraft was a Boeing 737-823, manufacturer serial number 34567, manufactured in 2008. At the time of the accident, the airframe had accumulated 42,150 total flight hours and 28,400 flight cycles. The aircraft was registered to a Part 121 operator and maintained under an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) in accordance with 14 CFR 121.369.

3.2 The aircraft was powered by two CFM International CFM56-7B27 turbofan engines. Engine serial numbers were 789012 (left) and 789013 (right). Maintenance logs indicated that both engines were last overhauled in accordance with CFM Service Bulletin 72-0845. The aircraft was not equipped with LEAP-1B powerplants; however, engineering documentation reviewed during the investigation noted that the operator had previously evaluated a LEAP-1B retrofit program for fleet modernization. The evaluation concluded that the retrofit was not pursued due to certification timelines and operational compatibility constraints. No modifications related to the LEAP-1B program were installed on the accident airframe.

3.3 The forward fuselage section, including the nose cone, forward pressure bulkhead, and associated stringers, was manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems. Maintenance logs indicated that the forward fuselage had undergone a detailed structural inspection on March 10, 2021, in accordance with Boeing Service Bulletin 737-53-1289. No discrepancies were noted. The aircraft was in compliance with Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2012-09-04, which mandated repetitive inspections of the fuel tank system wiring, bonding straps, and ignition source prevention measures. The most recent compliance action was documented on February 14, 2021, and was within the required 24-month interval.

3.4 The aircraft was equipped with a flight data recorder (FDR) and a cockpit voice recorder (CVR), both of which were recovered and transported to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for readout. The landing gear system was configured in accordance with the Boeing 737-800 Maintenance Planning Document (MPD). The nose landing gear assembly consisted of a dual-wheel strut, drag brace, torque link assembly, and steering actuator. Maintenance records showed the NLG had been overhauled at 24,000 cycles, with the most recent tire replacement occurring 1,200 cycles prior to the accident. The main landing gear (MLG) assemblies were last inspected on July 28, 2021, with all wear indicators within manufacturer limits.

3.5 The aircraft's weight and balance calculations were within certified limits. The takeoff weight was recorded at 158,400 pounds, and the calculated landing weight was 142,200 pounds. The center of gravity was recorded at 24.8% mean aerodynamic chord (MAC), well within the approved envelope of 15.0% to 32.0% MAC. The aircraft's fuel quantity at touchdown was 18,400 pounds, distributed across the center and wing tanks.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 At the time of the accident, the KORD Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) recorded the following conditions: wind 240° at 18 knots, gusting to 32 knots; visibility 10 statute miles; sky condition scattered at 4,500 feet and broken at 8,000 feet; temperature 28°C; dewpoint 18°C; altimeter setting 29.92 inches of mercury. The reported crosswind component for Runway 27L was approximately 24 knots, with a headwind component of 12 knots.

4.2 The Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) issued at 11:00 CDT on August 15, 2021, forecasted wind 230° at 15 knots, gusting to 28 knots, with temporary fluctuations to 35 knots between 14:00 and 18:00 CDT. The forecast accurately reflected the observed conditions at the time of the approach. The Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR) issued at 15:53 CDT confirmed sustained winds of 240° at 19 knots, gusting to 31 knots, with no significant changes in visibility or ceiling.

4.3 Pilot reports (PIREPs) from preceding arrivals indicated moderate turbulence on final approach below 3,000 feet AGL, with wind shear alerts issued by the Terminal Doppler Weather Radar (TDWR) system. The TDWR recorded a 15-knot headwind loss between 2,000 feet and 500 feet AGL on the final approach path. The flight crew acknowledged the wind shear advisory during the approach briefing. The aircraft's onboard weather radar was operational and displayed no convective activity in the immediate vicinity of the airport.

4.4 Wind tunnel data and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models for the Boeing 737-800 indicate that crosswind components exceeding 20 knots require continuous rudder and aileron inputs to maintain runway alignment. The recorded wind conditions at the time of the accident were within the aircraft's certified operational envelope but required precise control inputs to mitigate lateral drift and vertical sink rate variations.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 The aircraft touched down on Runway 27L at approximately 15:47:12 EDT. FDR data indicated a vertical acceleration of 2.8 G at initial touchdown, followed by a secondary impact of 3.4 G approximately 0.8 seconds later. The aircraft's pitch attitude at touchdown was recorded at 4.2° nose-up, with a sink rate of 1,150 feet per minute. The main landing gear (MLG) contacted the runway first, followed by a rapid descent of the nose section.

5.2 The NLG collapsed aft and downward, resulting in the forward fuselage contacting the runway surface. Scuff marks consistent with the lower forward fuselage and engine cowlings were documented along the runway centerline for approximately 1,850 feet. The aircraft came to rest 2,100 feet from the threshold, aligned with the runway heading. No post-impact fire occurred. The runway surface exhibited localized asphalt displacement and tire rubber deposits consistent with a high-energy impact.

5.3 Examination of the NLG assembly revealed that the drag brace had fractured at the lower attachment lug, and the torque link assembly exhibited plastic deformation. The NLG strut cylinder showed evidence of over-compression, with hydraulic fluid leakage observed at the upper seal. Metallurgical analysis of the fractured drag brace indicated a ductile overload failure consistent with a high-energy vertical impact. The MLG assemblies remained intact and functional throughout the landing sequence. The nose wheel tires were deflated but showed no evidence of pre-impact failure.

5.4 The forward fuselage skin sustained abrasion and localized buckling along the lower longerons. The nose radome was detached and recovered 450 feet aft of the final resting position. The left and right engine inlet cowlings exhibited impact damage from runway contact. All emergency evacuation slides deployed successfully, and the evacuation was completed within 90 seconds. The aircraft met the NTSB definition of substantial damage due to the structural failure of the NLG and the requirement for major structural repair.

5.5 The flight control system was examined post-accident. The elevator, aileron, and rudder control cables were intact, with no evidence of pre-impact failure. The flight control computer (FCC) recorded normal command inputs until the moment of NLG collapse. The autothrottle system was disengaged at 500 feet AGL, and the autopilot was disengaged at 1,000 feet AGL, consistent with standard operating procedures for manual landings in gusty conditions.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 The operator's Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for crosswind landings specified a maximum demonstrated crosswind component of 33 knots, with a recommended go-around threshold of 25 knots for gusting conditions. The SOPs required the use of a wing-low technique with opposite rudder input to maintain runway alignment. The flight crew's approach briefing documented the crosswind conditions and confirmed the selection of the appropriate landing configuration. The operator's flight operations manual referenced 14 CFR 121.189 and 121.195 regarding takeoff and landing performance limitations.

6.2 A review of operator safety reports identified three previous hard landing events involving Boeing 737-800 aircraft at KORD between 2018 and 2020. In each instance, the contributing factors included rapid wind shifts and delayed go-around decisions. The operator had subsequently issued a safety bulletin emphasizing stabilized approach criteria and mandatory go-around execution when sink rates exceeded 1,000 feet per minute below 500 feet AGL. The bulletin was distributed to all flight operations personnel and incorporated into recurrent training curricula.

6.3 The aircraft's certification basis included compliance with 14 CFR 25.783, which governs the design and testing of fuselage doors and emergency exits. The forward entry door and overwing exits were inspected post-accident and found to be fully operational, with no evidence of structural interference during deployment. The aircraft's fuel tank system was evaluated in accordance with Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 (SFAR 88), which mandates fuel tank flammability reduction and ignition source prevention. Maintenance records confirmed that all SFAR 88 requirements, including wiring separation and bonding checks, were current and compliant.

6.4 The operator contracted Island Express Helicopters to provide specialized ground handling and line maintenance support at KORD. Records indicated that the contracted personnel had completed the operator's ramp safety and aircraft servicing training within the preceding 6 months. Ground handling logs confirmed that the aircraft was marshaled to the gate following the accident without incident. No discrepancies were identified in the ground handling procedures that contributed to the accident sequence.

6.5 The investigation team reviewed the aircraft's maintenance tracking system and confirmed that all applicable airworthiness directives, including AD 2012-09-04, were complied with within the prescribed intervals. The aircraft's structural repair manual (SRM) was consulted to determine the extent of damage to the forward fuselage. The SRM indicated that the observed buckling and abrasion required major structural repair, including replacement of the lower longeron sections and forward pressure bulkhead reinforcement.

6.6 FDR and CVR data were synchronized and analyzed to reconstruct the final approach and landing sequence. The CVR captured the flight crew's callouts, including "sink rate," "flare," and "touchdown," followed by the sound of structural impact. The FDR recorded control surface deflections, engine parameters, and landing gear position throughout the event. All data parameters were within expected operational ranges until the moment of NLG collapse. The investigation remains ongoing, with additional analysis of flight control laws, pilot technique, and wind shear modeling to be documented in subsequent reports.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis conducted by the Structures and Materials Group, in coordination with the Flight Data Recorder (FDR) Group, regarding the nose landing gear (NLG) collapse and forward fuselage structural damage sustained by a Boeing 737-800, registration N738IE, operated by Island Express. The examination was initiated following a hard landing event on August 15, 2021, during a gusty crosswind approach at approximately 15:42 UTC. The aircraft sustained substantial damage to the forward pressure bulkhead, NLG attachment structure, and lower forward fuselage skin. All occupants evacuated without injury.

The scope of this examination encompassed the physical inspection, non-destructive testing (NDT), metallurgical evaluation, and mechanical testing of the NLG assembly, forward fuselage Section 41 attachment lugs, and associated structural components. Additionally, FDR and Quick Access Recorder (QAR) data were decoded, time-synchronized, and correlated with physical damage patterns to reconstruct the load sequence. The examination was conducted between August 20 and August 28, 2021, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., and the Boeing Field Salvage Facility in Seattle, Washington. Items examined included the NLG shock strut (P/N 65-43210-1, S/N 8842A), torque link assembly (P/N 65-43215-3, S/N 7719B), forward wheel well bulkhead, and the Maintenance Event Data (MED) plug interface (P/N 99-88776-001). All examinations were performed in accordance with NTSB Investigative Procedures Manual (IPM) guidelines and referenced Boeing Service Bulletins, Airworthiness Directives, and applicable ASTM/SAE standards.

2. BACKGROUND

The Boeing 737-800 NLG is a dual-wheel, oleo-pneumatic shock strut assembly designed to absorb vertical and horizontal landing loads, taxi impacts, and braking forces. The primary load path transfers vertical and lateral forces through the lower cylinder, upper cylinder, and forward/aft attachment lugs into the forward pressure bulkhead and Section 41 fuselage structure. The forward fuselage, including the NLG wheel well and primary attachment fittings, was manufactured by Spirit Aerosystems, Inc. under Boeing specification BAC5000 and drawing D6-13747. The structure is fabricated primarily from 2024-T3 aluminum alloy sheet and 7075-T73511 extrusions, with critical load-bearing lugs machined from 7050-T7451 aluminum plate.

The aircraft was certified under 14 CFR Part 25 and operated under 14 CFR Part 121. The structural design complies with the damage tolerance requirements outlined in AC 25.571-1D, which mandate that primary structure must be capable of sustaining residual strength after the initiation of fatigue cracks, with inspection intervals established to detect crack growth prior to reaching critical flaw sizes. The operator, Island Express Air Services, maintained the aircraft under an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP). At the time of the event, the airframe had accumulated 42,150 flight hours and 28,900 flight cycles. The most recent C-check was completed on March 12, 2021, with no deferred structural discrepancies.

The aircraft was equipped with a Maintenance Event Data (MED) plug, a telemetry interface module installed in the forward electronics bay that continuously monitors structural load exceedances, gear strut pressures, and FDR parameter anomalies. The MED plug records high-frequency transient events at 64 Hz and interfaces with the aircraft's central maintenance computer (CMC). The system is designed to capture load spectra exceeding 1.5G vertical or 0.8G lateral thresholds, providing post-flight engineering data for structural health monitoring. The aircraft's demonstrated crosswind limit per the Boeing 737-800 Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM) is 33 knots steady, with gust factors not to exceed 10 knots above steady state. The approach on August 15, 2021, was conducted in reported surface winds of 240° at 22 knots, gusting to 34 knots, with a calculated crosswind component of 28 knots and a peak gust crosswind of 38 knots.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

Physical examination of the recovered NLG assembly revealed catastrophic aft and inboard collapse of the shock strut. The lower cylinder was fractured at the trunnion pin interface, with the upper cylinder exhibiting permanent plastic deformation. The forward attachment lug (P/N 65-43210-2) was separated from the bulkhead, with the mating bolt holes elongated by 0.18 inches in the longitudinal axis. The torque link assembly exhibited shear failure at the upper pin (P/N 65-43215-4), with fracture surfaces oriented at 45° to the applied load axis, consistent with combined bending and torsional overload.

Non-destructive testing was performed on all primary fracture surfaces and adjacent structure. Dye penetrant inspection per ASTM E1417 revealed no pre-existing surface-breaking cracks. Magnetic particle testing per ASTM E709 on the 300M steel lower cylinder showed no subsurface discontinuities. Ultrasonic phased array scanning per ASTM E2375 of the forward bulkhead attachment zone confirmed no delaminations or hidden fatigue cracking within the 7050-T7451 aluminum plate. The absence of fatigue striations or beach marks on primary fracture surfaces indicates instantaneous failure without prior progressive crack growth.

Metallurgical analysis was conducted on representative coupons extracted from the lower cylinder and forward lug. The lower cylinder material was identified as 300M steel (AMS 6414), heat treated to a specified ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 260-280 ksi. Hardness testing per ASTM E18 yielded an average of 49.2 HRC, within the specified 48-51 HRC range. Tensile testing per ASTM E8 demonstrated a yield strength of 218 ksi and UTS of 271 ksi, with 11.2% elongation, confirming material conformance to Boeing specification BAC5621. Charpy V-notch impact testing per ASTM E23 at -40°C yielded an average absorbed energy of 28 ft-lbs, exceeding the minimum 20 ft-lbs requirement for low-temperature toughness.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the lower cylinder fracture surface revealed a ductile overload morphology characterized by microvoid coalescence and dimpled rupture. The fracture origin was located at the inner radius of the trunnion pin bore, where stress concentration is maximized. Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) confirmed the chemical composition within AMS 6414 limits: 0.42% C, 1.65% Si, 0.78% Mn, 0.81% Cr, 0.40% Mo, 1.55% Ni, balance Fe. No evidence of hydrogen embrittlement, corrosion pitting, or manufacturing defects was observed.

The forward bulkhead attachment lugs exhibited plastic deformation with localized yielding at the bolt hole edges. Hardness mapping across the lug cross-section showed a gradient from 135 HB at the surface to 128 HB in the core, consistent with 7050-T7451 temper. The MED plug was recovered intact, with no thermal or mechanical damage to the connector housing. Data extraction confirmed continuous operation through the event, with no internal memory corruption.

Photographic documentation (Photos 1-14) captures the fracture topography, dimensional measurements, and NDT results. Key measurements include: lower cylinder permanent compression of 18.7 inches (design limit 14.2 inches), forward lug bolt hole elongation of 0.18 inches, and torque link pin shear displacement of 0.31 inches. All measurements were recorded using calibrated digital calipers (±0.001 inch) and laser profilometry.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

FDR and QAR data were decoded using the Boeing 737-800 data frame specification (DFDR-737-800 Rev 14) and synchronized with the MED plug high-frequency load recordings. The FDR sampled at 1 Hz, while the MED plug provided 64 Hz transient data for strut pressure, vertical acceleration, and lateral load distribution. Time synchronization was achieved using the aircraft's UTC clock and radio altitude trigger at 500 ft AGL.

The reconstructed timeline is as follows:
- 15:42:18 UTC: 500 ft AGL, 145 KIAS, pitch attitude +2.1°, vertical acceleration 1.02G, crosswind component 28 knots, gust factor 1.3.
- 15:42:26 UTC: 200 ft AGL, 138 KIAS, pitch attitude +1.4°, sink rate 1,120 ft/min, vertical acceleration 1.08G.
- 15:42:31 UTC: 50 ft AGL, 132 KIAS, pitch attitude +0.8°, sink rate 1,850 ft/min, vertical acceleration 1.21G.
- 15:42:33 UTC: Main gear touchdown, radio altitude 0 ft, vertical acceleration 1.8G, pitch attitude -1.2°, NLG strut pressure 1,850 PSI.
- 15:42:34 UTC: NLG touchdown, vertical acceleration 3.4G, pitch attitude -4.2°, sink rate 1,420 ft/min, NLG strut pressure 3,100 PSI (design maximum).
- 15:42:35 UTC: Transient load spike recorded by MED plug: vertical acceleration 4.1G, lateral acceleration 0.92G, NLG strut pressure 4,200 PSI, pitch attitude -8.5°.
- 15:42:36 UTC: Structural failure event, vertical acceleration drops to 0.4G, pitch attitude -11.3°, NLG strut pressure 0 PSI, forward bulkhead strain gauges exceed 120% yield.

The FDR data indicates a sink rate of 1,850 ft/min at 50 ft AGL, significantly exceeding the recommended maximum of 600 ft/min for a normal landing. The vertical acceleration at NLG touchdown reached 3.4G, with a subsequent peak of 4.1G during the load spike. The calculated vertical impact load, derived from strut pressure and oleo-pneumatic compression characteristics, was approximately 142,000 lbf, exceeding the NLG design limit load of 98,000 lbf by 45%. The lateral load component, driven by the 38-knot gust crosswind and crab angle misalignment, imposed a 38,000 lbf side load on the torque link assembly, exceeding the 28,000 lbf design limit.

Comparison with normal operational parameters confirms the event exceeded both demonstrated crosswind limits and structural design envelopes. The Boeing 737-800 FCOM specifies a maximum sink rate of 600 ft/min for normal landings, with a hard landing threshold at 1.8G vertical acceleration. The recorded 4.1G peak and 1,850 ft/min sink rate at 50 ft AGL indicate an uncontrolled descent rate compounded by wind shear and delayed flare initiation. The MED plug data corroborates the FDR timeline, with high-frequency sampling capturing the 120-millisecond load transient that precipitated structural failure.

The aircraft's altitude at touchdown was 1,240 ft MSL, with field elevation at 1,180 ft MSL. The approach was conducted with flaps 30, gear down, and autobrake set to 3. The FDR shows no system malfunctions, hydraulic pressure remained nominal at 3,000 PSI, and the anti-skid system engaged normally post-touchdown. The data confirms that the NLG collapse was a direct result of dynamic overload exceeding the certified structural margins, with no evidence of system degradation or maintenance-related anomalies.

5. SUMMARY

The following technical findings are established based on physical examination, materials testing, and flight data analysis:

1. The nose landing gear shock strut (P/N 65-43210-1, S/N 8842A) failed due to instantaneous ductile overload, with fracture surfaces exhibiting microvoid coalescence and no evidence of pre-existing fatigue cracking or material degradation.
2. Metallurgical and chemical analysis confirmed the 300M steel lower cylinder conformed to AMS 6414 specifications, with hardness, tensile strength, and impact toughness within Boeing BAC5621 requirements.
3. The forward fuselage attachment lugs and torque link assembly sustained plastic deformation and shear failure consistent with combined vertical and lateral loads exceeding design limit values by 45% and 36%, respectively.
4. Non-destructive testing per ASTM E1417, E709, and E2375 revealed no hidden defects, corrosion, or fatigue initiation sites in the primary load path or adjacent bulkhead structure.
5. FDR and QAR data reconstruction documented a sink rate of 1,850 ft/min at 50 ft AGL, a vertical acceleration peak of 4.1G, and a lateral load component of 0.92G, all exceeding normal operational and design parameters.
6. The Maintenance Event Data (MED) plug recorded a 120-millisecond transient load event at 15:42:35 UTC, with strut pressure reaching 4,200 PSI, corroborating the FDR timeline and confirming instantaneous structural failure.
7. The aircraft's structural design and maintenance history complied with 14 CFR Part 121 operational requirements and applicable damage tolerance requirements, with no deferred structural discrepancies or overdue inspections.
8. The forward fuselage Section 41 structure, manufactured by Spirit Aerosystems, exhibited localized yielding at attachment points but maintained residual load path integrity, facilitating safe evacuation.
9. Environmental and operational data indicate the approach was conducted in a 38-knot peak gust crosswind, with wind shear and delayed flare initiation contributing to the excessive descent rate and impact loads.
10. All recovered components, data modules, and structural fragments were documented, measured, and preserved in accordance with NTSB chain-of-custody protocols for further engineering evaluation.

INTERVIEW OF MARCUS THORNE, GROUND OPERATIONS SUPERVISOR
Date: August 18, 2021
Time: 10:15 AM
Location: NTSB Regional Field Office, Conference Room B
Interviewer: Investigator Sarah Chen, NTSB Aviation Safety Board

Q: Mr. Thorne, thank you for making the time. For the official record, please state your full name, your current title, and your specific duties on the day of the incident.

A: Yeah, absolutely. Marcus Thorne. I’m the Ground Operations Supervisor for the main terminal ramp. On August 15th, I was working the day shift, 0600 to 1800. My job is basically... well, I coordinate all the ramp traffic, gate assignments, pushback clearances, and I make sure the ground handling crews are staged properly. I was stationed in the ramp control tower that overlooks the south approach and taxiway Bravo. So I had a direct line of sight to the runway threshold.

Q: Can you walk me through the conditions and your observations leading up to the event? Start with the weather and your initial awareness of the inbound flight.

A: Right. So, around 14:30, maybe 14:35, the wind really started picking up. We had a crosswind coming off the bay, and it was gusty. I’d say sustained around twenty knots, with gusts pushing thirty, maybe thirty-two. The ATIS was broadcasting it, obviously, but you could just see it. The windsock was whipping, and I could actually feel the tower vibrating a little. I remember looking out and thinking, "Man, the pilots are gonna have their hands full." 

I had the flight strip for the inbound 737-800. It was a scheduled arrival, operating under Part 121, so they follow the standard commercial ops protocols. I was tracking it on the radar display and also visually. I think it was about 14:52 when I first picked it up on final. Maybe three or four miles out. It was crabbing pretty hard to the left, which makes sense with that wind direction. The nose was pointed into the wind, but the fuselage was tracking straight down the centerline. Standard crosswind technique, really.

Q: Describe the approach and touchdown as you saw it. What stood out to you?

A: Okay, so... it was coming in a little fast, I thought. Not dangerously fast, but you could tell they were carrying extra speed for the gusts. At about a mile out, the wind gusted again, and the aircraft kind of... dipped. Just a slight sink rate increase. Then, maybe half a mile, they tried to correct. I saw the wings rock a bit, trying to de-crab. But the timing was off. They touched down on the main gear first, which is correct, but it was... it was a hard hit. Like, a real solid *thump*. You could hear it even from the tower. Then it bounced. Not a huge bounce, but enough to get the nose back up. 

And on the second touchdown, that’s when it went wrong. The nose came down way too fast. I saw the nose gear compress, then just... fold. It collapsed inward. There was a loud metallic screech, like grinding steel, and a puff of dust and maybe some hydraulic fluid mist. The nose dropped onto the runway, sparks flew, and it started sliding. I’d say it slid for maybe... I don’t know, two or three seconds before it came to a stop. It was just sitting there, nose down, engines still running for a few seconds before they spooled down.

Q: Did you notice any specific sounds or visual cues from the engines or airframe during the slide?

A: Yeah. The engines... they were still spooled up, I think. I heard the reverse thrust engage, but it sounded uneven. One side was louder, maybe. I’m not a mechanic, but I know enough to recognize the difference. I remember the maintenance guys later talking about how the newer MAX fleet uses those LEAP-1B engines, which are quieter and more efficient, but this was an older 737-800, so it had the CFM56s. Anyway, the sound was definitely a high-pitched whine mixed with the scraping. The aircraft yawed to the right, then corrected, and finally came to a stop maybe... I don’t know, three hundred feet past the touchdown zone. 

Q: What was your immediate response, and what did you observe next?

A: I keyed the radio to ground control and declared an emergency. We had ARFF rolling within, I’d say, forty-five seconds. I also called the ramp crew to clear the taxiway. From the tower, I watched the evacuation. The slides deployed on both sides. It was... it was chaotic but controlled. Passengers were coming down, some were moving fast, a few were hesitant. The flight attendants were directing them, shouting over the wind. I could see the crew chief doing a headcount. No one was injured, which was a huge relief. We had a few people with minor scrapes, maybe a twisted ankle, but everyone got off. 

Q: Were there any other aircraft or operators in the immediate vicinity that you coordinated with?

A: Yeah, actually. We share the south ramp with Island Express Helicopters. They had a couple of birds parked near the helipad, and their pilots were watching the whole thing. One of their guys, I think his name was Dave, actually radioed us to say he saw the nose gear go. They were pretty shaken up, honestly. I had to coordinate with their ops manager to make sure their helipad wasn’t in the way of the emergency vehicles. Also, since the airline operates under Part 121, their dispatch and maintenance control were on the line almost immediately. I was patching through comms to the airline’s ops center, giving them real-time updates.

Q: You mentioned the airline’s Part 121 operations. Did you observe any specific procedures being followed during the evacuation or post-incident phase?

A: Yeah, definitely. The crew followed the standard emergency checklist. I could see the captain doing the walk-around from the cockpit window, then shutting down the engines. The flight attendants had the passengers clear of the aircraft, and they were doing the muster count. The airline’s ground handling team arrived with the stairs and medical kits. Everything was by the book, really. I mean, you don’t want to see a gear collapse, but the response was textbook. The Part 121 training really shows in those situations. 

Q: Is there anything else you recall that might be relevant to the investigation? Any details about timing, wind shifts, or runway conditions?

A: Hmm. Let me think. The wind was definitely the main factor. It wasn’t just a steady crosswind; it was gusty, shifting. I remember checking the wind log later, and there was a microburst warning issued about twenty minutes after the landing. So, the conditions were deteriorating. Also, the runway surface... it was dry, but there was some rubber buildup near the touchdown zone. Not sure if that contributed to the bounce, but it’s worth noting. And, uh, I should mention that the aircraft’s maintenance records were pulled immediately. The mechanics were talking about the LEAP-1B engines again, but like I said, this was a classic 737-800. I think they were just comparing it to the newer fleet. Anyway, I don’t have any other details. I just hope the investigation clears up what happened with the nose gear. It’s a critical component.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Thorne. We’ll follow up if we need clarification. Do you have any questions for us?

A: No, I think that covers it. Just... glad everyone’s okay. It’s a reminder of how fast things can change out there.

FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY
REGULATORY CORRESPONDENCE
DOCKET NO. FAA-2022-0841
REFERENCE: NTSB/AAR-22/01, SAFETY RECOMMENDATION A-22-045
DATE: October 12, 2023

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This correspondence constitutes the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) formal response to National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Safety Recommendation A-22-045, issued in conjunction with the investigation of aviation accident DCA21MA089. The referenced event occurred on August 15, 2021, involving a Boeing 737-800, registration N837XX, operated by Spirit Airlines, Inc. (hereinafter “Spirit”). The aircraft sustained substantial damage following a hard landing and subsequent collapse of the nose landing gear (NLG) during a gusty crosswind approach. All occupants evacuated without serious injury. This document addresses regulatory compliance, oversight findings, and mandated corrective actions pursuant to 14 CFR Part 121, applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs), and the FAA’s statutory authority under Title 49, United States Code, Subtitle VII.

2. BACKGROUND
The operational and maintenance framework governing the subject aircraft is established under 14 CFR Part 121, specifically 14 CFR 121.344, which mandates that certificate holders maintain aircraft in accordance with approved maintenance programs and manufacturer service documentation. The Boeing 737-800 holds Type Certificate No. A16WE, with all structural and systems design criteria certified under 14 CFR Part 25. The accident investigation highlighted operational deviations during high-wind conditions, prompting a comprehensive review of crosswind approach limitations, landing gear structural integrity monitoring, and emergency evacuation procedures.

Historically, the FAA has issued multiple ADs addressing 737-series landing gear fatigue and structural reinforcement, including AD 2018-12-05 and AD 2020-09-14, which mandate enhanced eddy current inspections and bushing replacements. Concurrently, the FAA’s oversight of fuel system safety, as codified under Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88 (SFAR 88), requires continuous evaluation of fuel tank system fault tolerance, particularly following high-energy impact events. Although the subject aircraft was equipped with CFM56-7B engines, Spirit’s fleet-wide maintenance program incorporates cross-platform engine monitoring protocols that interface with airframe vibration and landing gear load tracking. This integration necessitates alignment with manufacturer service bulletins and FAA-approved Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) provisions, particularly when evaluating predictive maintenance architectures that span multiple engine types, including the LEAP-1B engine utilized in newer fleet acquisitions.

The NTSB’s preliminary findings indicated that the First Officer, acting as Pilot Flying, initiated a stabilized approach that subsequently encountered unforecasted wind shear and gusting crosswind components exceeding 25 knots. The resulting vertical load factor exceeded the design limit load for the NLG, precipitating structural failure. Post-impact evacuation procedures were executed in accordance with Section 25.783, which governs fuselage door design, operation, and emergency egress requirements. The FAA’s Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) and Flight Standards Service (AFS) have jointly reviewed the operator’s compliance posture, training curricula, and maintenance tracking systems to determine regulatory adequacy.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive audit of Spirit’s maintenance and operational records, conducted by the Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) and Principal Operations Inspector (POI), confirms baseline compliance with 14 CFR Part 121.344 and 14 CFR 121.351. The operator’s approved maintenance program incorporated all applicable ADs, and the subject aircraft’s landing gear had undergone the most recent heavy inspection within the prescribed interval. However, the investigation revealed systemic gaps in the operator’s crosswind training syllabus and real-time wind shear mitigation protocols. Specifically, the First Officer’s decision to continue the approach beyond the stabilized approach gate, despite deteriorating meteorological conditions, contravened Spirit’s Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and FAA Advisory Circular 120-71A.

Regulatory oversight actions included the issuance of a Letter of Investigation (LOI) to Spirit’s Director of Maintenance and Chief Pilot, followed by a targeted ramp inspection under 14 CFR 121.542. The FAA identified deficiencies in the operator’s Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) program, which failed to flag recurrent exceedance events for high vertical descent rates during crosswind approaches. Furthermore, while the operator’s MMEL authorized dispatch with certain non-critical system inoperative, the integration of engine health monitoring data—particularly concerning vibration signatures that may correlate with airframe stress—lacked standardized cross-referencing protocols. Although the LEAP-1B engine is not installed on the 737-800, Spirit’s fleet-wide predictive maintenance framework utilizes shared data architecture that requires harmonization across engine types to ensure comprehensive structural load analysis.

The FAA’s analysis also examined the applicability of SFAR 88 requirements to post-impact fuel system integrity. The investigation confirmed that the fuel tank system remained intact and that no ignition sources were present, consistent with SFAR 88 fault tolerance objectives. However, the structural deformation of the forward fuselage, as evaluated against Section 25.783, demonstrated that emergency door operation was marginally impeded by localized airframe distortion. This finding underscores the necessity of revising evacuation drill parameters to account for asymmetric structural deformation scenarios.

A critical regulatory gap was identified in the current certification basis for crosswind landing performance. Existing 14 CFR Part 25 requirements do not mandate real-time gust load factor monitoring or automated go-around triggers for wind shear conditions exceeding demonstrated crosswind limits. The FAA acknowledges that operator discretion, while necessary, must be constrained by enhanced procedural safeguards and mandatory training modules addressing high-energy landing dynamics.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
Pursuant to the findings outlined herein, the FAA mandates the following corrective actions and compliance timelines:

1. Revised Crosswind Training and SOP Enforcement: Spirit shall implement an enhanced crosswind and wind shear training curriculum, incorporating full-flight simulator scenarios that replicate gusting conditions exceeding 20 knots. The curriculum must be submitted to the POI for approval within 90 days of this correspondence. All line pilots, including the First Officer involved in the subject event, shall complete recurrent training within 180 days.

2. Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) Program Enhancement: The operator shall modify its FDM algorithms to automatically flag vertical descent rate exceedances and crosswind component deviations during final approach. A quarterly compliance report shall be submitted to the FAA’s Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) for a period of 24 months.

3. Landing Gear Inspection Protocol Revision: In coordination with Boeing and the FAA’s Aircraft Certification Service, Spirit shall adopt an accelerated eddy current inspection interval for the NLG trunnion and drag brace assemblies. This modification shall be incorporated into the operator’s Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program (CAMP) within 120 days, with full fleet compliance required within 365 days.

4. Evacuation Procedure Validation: The operator shall conduct full-scale emergency evacuation drills simulating asymmetric fuselage deformation, in accordance with Section 25.783 and SFAR 88 post-impact evaluation criteria. Results shall be documented and submitted to the FAA within 150 days.

5. Cross-Fleet Maintenance Data Harmonization: Spirit shall establish a unified predictive maintenance protocol that integrates engine health monitoring data across all fleet types, including CFM56-7B and LEAP-1B platforms, to ensure comprehensive structural load correlation. A compliance plan shall be submitted to the PMI within 60 days.

The FAA will conduct a follow-up audit of Spirit’s compliance posture no later than 180 days from the issuance of this document. Failure to meet the stipulated timelines may result in enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR 13.19 and potential suspension of operating authority under 14 CFR 121.542. This response is issued under the authority of the Administrator and shall be maintained in the official regulatory docket (FAA-2022-0841) for public and interagency review.

Respectfully submitted,

Director, Flight Standards Service
Federal Aviation Administration
Washington, D.C. 20591

All 162 Evacuate Safely After Boeing 737 Nose Gear Collapses in Gusty Crosswind Landing

Elena Rostova, The National Chronicle
CHICAGO, Ill. — A Boeing 737-800 carrying 156 passengers and six crew members suffered a hard landing and collapsed its nose landing gear on Sunday, Aug. 15, 2021, at O’Hare International Airport. Despite the violent touchdown and substantial airframe damage, emergency crews successfully evacuated everyone aboard without serious injury.

The incident occurred during a turbulent approach marked by sudden, gusty crosswinds that pushed the aircraft off its intended glide path. As the jet touched down, the forward landing gear buckled under the impact, sending the nose slamming onto the runway. The aircraft skidded several hundred feet before coming to a halt, triggering an immediate emergency response. Runway closures caused cascading delays across the Midwest, but the swift evacuation prevented what could have been a far more severe outcome.

“Our preliminary assessment indicates the aircraft experienced a high-energy touchdown in challenging meteorological conditions,” said National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigator-in-charge David Chen during a Monday press briefing. “The nose gear collapse is consistent with excessive vertical and forward loads, but we are examining all data before drawing conclusions.” Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) officials confirmed the aircraft met all maintenance requirements prior to departure. “The operator followed standard protocols, and the crew executed the evacuation checklist flawlessly,” FAA regional director Maria Gonzalez stated. “We are fully cooperating with the NTSB to determine the exact sequence of events.” Airline spokesperson Thomas Vance praised the flight crew’s training. “Our pilots and cabin crew are rigorously prepared for abnormal situations. Their quick actions ensured every passenger reached safety within 90 seconds of the aircraft coming to rest.”

The aircraft, operated by a major domestic carrier, was completing a routine domestic route from Denver to Chicago. The Boeing 737-800, a workhorse of commercial aviation, has been in service for over two decades and is widely recognized for its reliability. The specific airframe involved was manufactured in 2014 and had accumulated approximately 38,000 flight hours. Maintenance records show the jet underwent a routine heavy inspection just four months prior, with no outstanding discrepancies reported.

Aviation safety analysts note that crosswind landings require precise control inputs, particularly when wind shear or sudden gusts disrupt the aircraft’s alignment. “When a plane hits the runway too hard, especially with a strong crosswind component, the landing gear can experience forces beyond its design limits,” explained Dr. Alan Mercer, a former commercial pilot and aerospace engineering professor at Purdue University. “The nose gear is particularly vulnerable if the aircraft pitches forward or if the main gear touches down unevenly.” Investigators are also reviewing the aircraft’s structural components, including parts sourced from Spirit AeroSystems, a primary manufacturer of fuselage and landing gear support structures for Boeing. While no immediate link has been established, the NTSB will examine whether any manufacturing or maintenance factors contributed to the failure. Additionally, regulators are reviewing compliance with Airworthiness Directive 2012-09-04, a longstanding FAA mandate that requires enhanced inspections of certain structural fittings and plug installations on 737 models. The directive specifically addresses the integrity of the Main Equipment Deck (MED) plug, a reinforced access panel located near the forward fuselage that houses critical avionics and environmental control systems. Though the MED plug is not part of the landing gear assembly, investigators routinely verify that all mandated structural modifications remain intact following high-stress landings. Compliance with AD 2012-09-04 and related maintenance logs from the Wichita-based supplier will be cross-referenced with the aircraft’s service history.

For those on board, the moments after touchdown were chaotic but ultimately survivable. “We hit the ground so hard I thought the plane was going to break in half,” said passenger Marcus Lin, 34, who was traveling for a family wedding. “The nose dropped, there was a loud metallic crunch, and then the emergency slides deployed. It was terrifying, but the flight attendants kept us calm and moving.” Lin’s wife, Sarah, who was waiting at the gate, described the agonizing wait for information. “When the airport screens went red and the emergency vehicles started rolling, my heart stopped. I just kept praying they were all okay. Hearing that everyone made it out was the greatest relief of my life.”

Hard landings resulting in gear collapse are rare but not unprecedented in commercial aviation. The 737-800 has an extensive safety record, with millions of successful flights logged worldwide. However, similar incidents have occurred during severe weather events, including a 2018 landing in Istanbul where a 737-800 overran a runway after a hard touchdown in heavy rain, and a 2019 incident in Florida where crosswinds contributed to a nose gear failure. In each case, investigators cited a combination of pilot technique, weather conditions, and maintenance history as contributing factors. The aviation industry has continuously refined training programs and aircraft design to mitigate such risks, but extreme weather remains a persistent challenge.

The NTSB has dispatched a “go-team” to Chicago to recover the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, both of which were retrieved intact on Monday morning. Investigators are currently downloading and analyzing the data, which will provide precise information on airspeed, descent rate, control inputs, and wind conditions during the final approach. The damaged aircraft remains secured on a remote taxiway, where engineers will conduct a detailed structural examination. The FAA has not issued any new operational restrictions for the 737-800 fleet pending the investigation’s findings. “We will follow the data wherever it leads,” Chen emphasized. “This process takes time, but our priority is ensuring the traveling public understands exactly what happened and how to prevent it in the future.”

1. INTRODUCTION

Spirit AeroSystems, Inc. (hereinafter referred to as Spirit or the Company) submits this technical analysis in support of the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigative hearing regarding the August 15, 2021, hard landing and subsequent nose landing gear (NLG) collapse involving a Boeing 737-800. As the original equipment manufacturer responsible for the forward fuselage section, NLG trunnion attachment structure, and associated lower fuselage access assemblies, Spirit has conducted a comprehensive engineering review of the incident. This submission is authored by the undersigned Lead Structural Integrity & Landing Gear Integration Engineer, representing Spirit’s technical position before the Board.

The scope of this document encompasses a detailed examination of the structural load paths, certification compliance, maintenance history, and operational parameters that contributed to the event. Our analysis draws upon flight data recorder (FDR) telemetry, quick access recorder (QAR) parameters, metallurgical examination reports, and maintenance documentation entered into the public docket. While the incident resulted in substantial airframe damage, the successful evacuation of all occupants underscores the inherent structural redundancy and crashworthiness of the design. Spirit’s position, supported by engineering data and regulatory compliance records, is that the NLG collapse was the direct result of an operational exceedance of certified structural limits during a high-energy, gusty crosswind touchdown. No evidence of manufacturing defect, material degradation, or maintenance non-compliance has been identified. This submission outlines the technical basis for that conclusion and provides actionable safety recommendations to mitigate similar events across the fleet.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On August 15, 2021, the subject Boeing 737-800 was conducting a scheduled passenger flight under instrument meteorological conditions. The approach phase was characterized by a reported crosswind component of 28 knots, with gusts exceeding 35 knots and intermittent wind shear alerts. According to FDR data (Docket Exhibit FDR-04A), the aircraft experienced a rapid descent rate during final approach, culminating in a touchdown with a vertical sink rate of approximately 1,100 feet per minute. The QAR data (Docket Exhibit QAR-07B) indicates significant lateral drift correction inputs during the flare, with asymmetric main gear touchdown followed by a high-energy nose gear contact. The resulting impact forces exceeded the design limit loads for the NLG attachment structure, leading to immediate collapse of the forward strut and substantial damage to the lower forward fuselage.

Maintenance records reviewed by Spirit confirm that the aircraft was fully compliant with all applicable airworthiness directives and service bulletins. Notably, the forward fuselage and NLG bay had undergone the most recent heavy maintenance check 14 months prior to the incident, with all structural inspections completed in accordance with Airworthiness Directive 2012-09-04. The 2012 structural inspection mandate specifically addresses high-cycle fatigue zones in the 737 Next Generation forward fuselage, including the NLG trunnion fittings and surrounding skin panels. All eddy current and ultrasonic inspections documented in the maintenance logbook (Docket Exhibit MAINT-12C) returned nominal results, with no indications of crack initiation, fastener elongation, or corrosion.

The forward lower fuselage incorporates a Main Equipment Deck access plug (commonly referenced in engineering drawings as the MED plug), which provides maintenance access to avionics bays and interfaces structurally with the NLG bay bulkhead. Post-incident examination of the MED plug assembly revealed no deformation, fastener failure, or load-path disruption. The plug’s titanium fastener pattern remained within design tolerances, and the surrounding doublers showed only impact-related scuffing consistent with ground contact following the collapse.

While the incident aircraft is powered by CFM56-7B engines, Spirit’s structural analysis methodology leverages load-path validation frameworks originally developed during the CFM LEAP-1B engine program integration effort. The LEAP-1B integration effort required extensive finite element modeling (FEM) of forward fuselage load redistribution under asymmetric thrust and high-gust conditions. These validated models have been adapted to assess the 737-800’s structural response during the August 15 event, providing a robust analytical baseline for evaluating the NLG attachment behavior under extreme off-nominal loading.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The technical assessment of the August 15, 2021, incident centers on three interrelated domains: structural load exceedance, certification compliance, and operational dynamics. Each domain is evaluated against docket evidence, industry standards, and Spirit’s proprietary engineering databases.

Structural Load Exceedance and Failure Mode
Metallurgical analysis of the recovered NLG trunnion fittings and forward bulkhead structure (Docket Exhibit MET-09A) reveals classic ductile overload fracture surfaces. The fracture morphology exhibits significant plastic deformation, shear lip formation, and microvoid coalescence, with no evidence of fatigue striations, stress corrosion cracking, or pre-existing material defects. This confirms that the structural failure was instantaneous and load-driven, rather than progressive or degradation-related.

Finite element reconstruction of the touchdown event, utilizing FDR-derived vertical acceleration (peak ~3.8g) and lateral drift vectors, demonstrates that the combined load path through the NLG trunnion exceeded 1.5 times the certified limit load. The 737-800 NLG is designed to withstand vertical, lateral, and torsional loads within a defined envelope per 14 CFR 25.571. However, the simultaneous application of high vertical impact energy, asymmetric lateral shear, and rapid pitch-down moment created a triaxial stress state that surpassed the ultimate load threshold. The forward fuselage structure, including the MED plug interface, performed as designed by absorbing and redistributing secondary loads, preventing catastrophic fuselage rupture and enabling safe evacuation.

Certification and Regulatory Compliance
The forward fuselage and NLG attachment structure were originally certified under Part 25.571, which mandates rigorous damage-tolerance and fatigue evaluation of primary structure. Spirit’s compliance documentation, submitted to the FAA during type certification and subsequent supplemental type certificates, demonstrates that all critical load paths were evaluated for crack growth, residual strength, and inspection interval optimization. The structural design incorporates multiple load-sharing elements, including reinforced trunnion lugs, doubler plates, and fail-safe bulkhead configurations.

While SFAR 88 (Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88) specifically addresses fuel tank system fault tolerance, the engineering philosophy and hazard analysis methodologies established under the fuel tank safety directive have been systematically integrated into Spirit’s broader structural criticality assessments. The fault-tolerance validation protocols, including failure mode effects analysis (FMEA) and redundancy mapping, were adapted to evaluate NLG attachment zones, ensuring that single-point failures do not compromise overall airframe integrity. This cross-disciplinary safety management approach is reflected in the aircraft’s ability to maintain structural continuity despite the NLG collapse.

Maintenance and Inspection Compliance
All maintenance actions documented in the aircraft’s technical logbook align with manufacturer recommendations and regulatory mandates. The 2012 structural inspection directive required enhanced eddy current and ultrasonic scanning of the forward fuselage skin, NLG trunnion fittings, and adjacent fastener rows. Spirit’s review of the inspection reports confirms 100% compliance, with all measurements falling within acceptable tolerance bands. No deferred maintenance items, repeat discrepancies, or structural repair station (SRS) modifications were identified in the vicinity of the NLG bay.

Operational Dynamics and Crosswind Landing Factors
The QAR and FDR data indicate that the approach was conducted in rapidly changing wind conditions, with crosswind components fluctuating between 22 and 35 knots. The flight crew executed a crab-to-sideslip transition during the flare, resulting in a brief period of lateral drift before touchdown. The main gear contacted the runway with a slight lateral offset, followed by a rapid nose-down pitch and high-energy NLG impact. This sequence is consistent with known aerodynamic challenges in gusty crosswind conditions, where wind shear and delayed drift correction can produce asymmetric touchdown loads.

Industry best practices, as outlined in FAA Advisory Circular 25.571-1D and IATA Landing Safety Guidelines, emphasize the importance of stabilized approach criteria, timely go-around decision-making, and drift correction techniques. The data suggests that the aircraft’s flight control laws and NLG steering geometry responded within design parameters, but the combined operational inputs and environmental conditions exceeded the certified structural envelope. This is not indicative of a design deficiency, but rather a manifestation of the inherent limitations of any transport category aircraft when subjected to extreme, off-nominal landing conditions.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on a comprehensive review of flight data, metallurgical evidence, maintenance records, and structural load modeling, Spirit’s technical position is that the August 15, 2021, NLG collapse was the direct result of an operational exceedance of certified structural limits during a high-energy, gusty crosswind landing. The failure mode is consistent with instantaneous ductile overload, with no evidence of manufacturing defect, material degradation, fatigue crack propagation, or maintenance non-compliance. The forward fuselage structure, including the Main Equipment Deck access plug and NLG trunnion attachment zones, performed within its certified design envelope and successfully maintained airframe integrity to facilitate a safe evacuation.

The incident underscores the complex interaction between environmental conditions, pilot technique, and structural load limits. While the aircraft’s design complies fully with 14 CFR 25.571 and all applicable airworthiness directives, the event highlights the need for enhanced operational guidance and real-time monitoring to prevent similar exceedances. Spirit recommends the following safety improvements:

1. Enhanced Crosswind Landing Training: Operators should implement scenario-based training modules focusing on drift correction timing, wind shear recognition, and go-around decision thresholds in gusty conditions. Emphasis should be placed on maintaining stabilized approach parameters and avoiding late flare corrections that increase lateral and vertical impact loads.

2. Real-Time Structural Load Monitoring: Integration of flight data monitoring (FDM) systems with real-time sink rate and lateral load alerting can provide crews with immediate feedback during high-energy approaches. Threshold-based warnings, calibrated to certified limit loads, can support timely go-around decisions.

3. Updated Operator Guidance for Gusty Conditions: Airlines should revise standard operating procedures (SOPs) to include specific crosswind and gust factor limitations, with clear escalation protocols for wind shear alerts and unstable approach parameters.

4. Industry-Wide Data Sharing: Establishment of a centralized database for high-energy landing events, including FDR/QAR parameters, structural inspection results, and maintenance actions, will enable predictive trend analysis and proactive safety interventions.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In response to the August 15, 2021, incident, Spirit has initiated several immediate and long-term corrective actions to support fleet safety and enhance structural monitoring capabilities.

Actions Already Taken
- Service Information Letter (SIL) Issuance: Spirit has distributed a comprehensive SIL to all 737-800 operators, detailing enhanced post-high-energy landing inspection protocols for the NLG trunnion zone, forward bulkhead, and MED plug assembly. The SIL includes updated torque verification procedures, eddy current scanning parameters, and visual inspection criteria for impact-related deformation.
- FDM Threshold Calibration: In collaboration with Boeing and major operators, Spirit has contributed engineering data to recalibrate flight data monitoring alert thresholds for vertical acceleration and lateral drift during landing. The updated parameters are designed to flag approaches that approach 80% of certified limit loads, enabling proactive maintenance and training interventions.
- Metallurgical and Load Path Review: Spirit’s engineering team has completed a full review of the recovered structural components, confirming that the failure mode aligns with predicted overload behavior. The findings have been shared with the FAA and the NTSB to support ongoing investigation efforts.

Proposed Future Improvements
- Predictive Structural Health Monitoring (SHM): Spirit is developing a next-generation SHM module that integrates strain gauge telemetry, acoustic emission sensors, and machine learning algorithms to monitor NLG attachment loads in real time. The system will provide operators with predictive maintenance alerts and structural fatigue tracking, reducing reliance on scheduled inspections alone.
- Enhanced EFB Integration: Spirit proposes the integration of real-time crosswind and gust advisory data into electronic flight bag (EFB) applications, with dynamic landing performance calculations that account for wind shear, runway friction, and aircraft weight. This will support more informed go-around decisions and reduce the likelihood of high-energy touchdowns.
- Joint Industry Working Group: Spirit recommends the formation of a multi-stakeholder working group comprising manufacturers, operators, regulators, and pilot unions to develop standardized high-energy landing mitigation strategies. The group will focus on training curriculum updates, FDM data standardization, and regulatory guidance for crosswind operations.
- Continued Regulatory Collaboration: Spirit remains committed to supporting the FAA and NTSB in the development of updated certification guidance for landing gear structural limits, particularly in the context of increasingly variable weather patterns and advanced flight control systems.

Spirit AeroSystems reaffirms its unwavering commitment to aviation safety, engineering excellence, and transparent collaboration with regulatory authorities. The August 15, 2021, incident, while resulting in substantial airframe damage, did not compromise the fundamental safety of the aircraft or its occupants. The structural design, maintenance compliance, and operational response all functioned within their intended parameters. By implementing the recommended safety improvements and continuing to advance predictive monitoring technologies, the industry can further reduce the risk of similar events and enhance the overall resilience of commercial aviation operations.

TO: All Maintenance Technicians, Quality Assurance Inspectors, Fleet Engineering, and Line Maintenance Supervisors
FROM: Director of Maintenance & Quality Assurance, Pacific Coast MRO Division
DATE: September 12, 2021
SUBJECT: QUALITY ALERT 2021-089 – Post-Incident Nose Landing Gear Structural & Torque Verification Protocol
REF: QA-2021-089, WO-7742-88A, AMM Rev 44, NTSB Docket Entry #2021-08-15-004

PURPOSE:
Issue immediate directive for enhanced inspection, torque verification, and documentation procedures for Boeing 737-800 nose landing gear (NLG) assemblies following the August 15, 2021, hard landing event. Mandate compliance with updated structural assessment protocols and maintenance tracking requirements across all active work orders.

BACKGROUND:
On 15 August 2021, an Island Express B737-800 (Reg. N738IE) experienced a hard landing during a gusty crosswind approach. The vertical and lateral impact forces exceeded certified design limits, resulting in complete collapse of the nose landing gear and substantial airframe damage. All passengers and crew evacuated safely. Preliminary NTSB data indicates potential discrepancies in recent NLG attachment bolt torque values and shock strut servicing records. While the aircraft was operated by Island Express Air, our facility maintains identical fleet configurations and shares common maintenance tracking infrastructure.

This alert aligns with our obligations under 14 CFR 121.344, which requires continuous airworthiness maintenance programs and strict adherence to manufacturer-recommended inspection intervals. Historical compliance with AD 2012-09-04 (fuel tank system inspections) and SFAR 88 (fuel system safety evaluations) has established baseline documentation standards that must now be extended to landing gear structural interfaces. Note that Spirit AeroSystems supplied the forward fuselage and NLG support structure for this airframe series; their service bulletins (SB-737-32-1142) must be cross-referenced during all structural assessments.

DETAILS:
Post-incident teardown and metallurgical review identified three primary areas of concern:
1. Torque Verification Gaps: Three of four primary NLG trunnion bolts showed torque values 8–12% below AMM-specified limits. Documentation in WO-7742-88A lacked secondary inspector sign-off.
2. Corrosion & Fatigue Indicators: Micro-fracturing observed at the NLG support beam interface. This region interfaces directly with the Spirit forward fuselage assembly. Standard visual checks are insufficient; eddy current testing (ECT) is now mandatory.
3. Documentation & Cross-System Tracking: Maintenance logs did not reflect recent updates to the mid-exit door plug (MDP) retention hardware, which shares common fastener specifications with NLG attachment points. Inconsistent part tracking across our CMMS (SAP PM Module) has created audit vulnerabilities.

While the CFM LEAP-1B powerplants on our MAX-series fleet are not directly implicated, the same torque verification and documentation protocols will be applied to engine pylon attachment points to ensure fleet-wide consistency. All work orders involving landing gear, pylon, or fuselage structural interfaces must now include dual-signature verification and photographic evidence of torque stripe application.

Updated procedural requirements:
- All NLG removal/installation tasks must reference AMM Chapter 32-11-00, Rev 44, with mandatory use of calibrated digital torque wrenches (PN: TQ-9942-LE).
- Eddy current inspection of NLG support beams and adjacent fuselage frames is required per SB-737-32-1142.
- All fasteners ≥ 3/8” diameter in structural zones require secondary torque verification within 24 hours of initial installation.
- CMMS entries must include part lot numbers, torque values, inspector IDs, and timestamped photos.

ACTION REQUIRED:
Effective immediately, the following actions are mandatory:

1. Fleet-Wide Inspection (Deadline: 14 Days from Issue Date)
   - Line Maintenance: Complete visual and torque verification on all B737-800/900 NLG trunnion bolts.
   - Heavy Maintenance: Schedule ECT on NLG support beams for all aircraft with >15,000 flight cycles.
   - Responsible: Shift Supervisors, QA Inspectors

2. Documentation & CMMS Update (Deadline: 7 Days)
   - Update all open work orders to include dual-signature fields and photo upload requirements.
   - QA Engineering to issue revised checklist PKG-2021-089-NLG.
   - Responsible: Maintenance Control, IT/CMMS Admin

3. Training & Competency Verification (Deadline: 30 Days)
   - All Level II/III technicians must complete refresher module TRN-2021-044 (Landing Gear Structural Interfaces & Torque Protocols).
   - Practical evaluation required before signing off on NLG-related tasks.
   - Responsible: Training Department, QA Compliance

4. Regulatory & Audit Alignment
   - Ensure all actions comply with §121.344 maintenance program requirements.
   - Cross-reference Airworthiness Directive 2012-09-04 and Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88 documentation standards for fuel-adjacent structural zones.
   - QA to submit compliance report to FAA Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) by 10/15/2021.

Non-compliance with this alert will result in immediate work stoppage and mandatory retraining. All findings, discrepancies, and corrective actions must be logged in the Quality Management System (QMS) under Incident Code QA-2021-089. Direct technical questions to Fleet Engineering (Ext. 4410) or QA Compliance (Ext. 4422).

Distribution: Maintenance Control, Quality Assurance, Fleet Engineering, Training, Line & Base Maintenance, Records & Compliance
Classification: INTERNAL – OPERATIONAL SENSITIVE
Retention: Permanent (NTSB Docket Reference: 2021-08-15-004)

SYNOPSIS
On August 15, 2021, at approximately 1432 local time, a Boeing 737-800, operated under 14 CFR Part 121, experienced a hard landing that resulted in the collapse of the nose landing gear during a scheduled passenger flight. Initial information indicates the aircraft was conducting an approach to the active runway under gusty crosswind conditions when the forward gear assembly failed upon touchdown. All passengers and crew members evacuated the aircraft without serious injury, and the airframe sustained substantial damage to the forward fuselage and nose gear structure.

INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information gathered during the initial site survey and preliminary interviews suggests the flight crew was conducting a visual approach to the designated runway. Initial witness accounts from ground operations personnel and air traffic control indicate the aircraft encountered fluctuating wind conditions during the final approach phase, with reported crosswind components approaching the upper limits of the aircraft’s demonstrated capabilities. The flight crew, including the Second in Command (SIC), reported a firm touchdown followed by a pronounced forward pitch and subsequent collapse of the nose landing gear strut. Preliminary examination of the wreckage site revealed that the nose gear assembly separated from the forward fuselage structure, with associated damage extending to the lower forward pressure bulkhead and adjacent avionics bays.

Weather data obtained from the airport’s automated surface observing system (ASOS) and nearby meteorological stations indicate sustained winds of 18 knots, gusting to 28 knots, with a crosswind component of approximately 22 knots at the time of the event. Visibility was reported as unrestricted, and ceiling conditions were above published minimums. Initial information indicates that the flight crew was operating in accordance with standard approach procedures, though a comprehensive review of flight data, crew resource management practices, and operational decision-making remains pending.

Damage assessment conducted by the NTSB Structures and Systems groups indicates substantial deformation to the nose landing gear trunnion and forward fuselage skin panels. Preliminary examination of the forward fuselage components, including those manufactured by Spirit Aerosystems, revealed localized buckling and fastener shear consistent with high-energy vertical and longitudinal loading. The main equipment door (MED) plug was observed in the stowed position, and initial inspection suggests it remained intact and properly secured during the impact sequence. Maintenance records reviewed to date indicate the aircraft was current on all required inspections and airworthiness directives, with no outstanding deferred maintenance items related to the landing gear or flight control systems. Compliance with 14 CFR Part 121, specifically regarding operator maintenance and operational control programs, is currently under review to verify that all applicable service bulletins and manufacturer recommendations were properly incorporated. Additionally, adherence to 14 CFR 121.344, pertaining to the maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations program, is being evaluated to confirm that all required inspections and component replacements were documented and executed in accordance with regulatory standards.

INVESTIGATION STATUS
The National Transportation Safety Board has activated the following investigative groups: Operations, Structures, Systems, Human Performance, Weather, and Air Traffic Control. The investigation is being conducted in accordance with established NTSB protocols, with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) serving as a participating party. Additional parties to the investigation include the aircraft operator, the airframe manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, and the landing gear component manufacturer. Representatives from Spirit Aerosystems (SAI) have been designated as technical advisors for the forward fuselage and structural components.

All available evidence has been secured, cataloged, and placed under strict chain-of-custody protocols. The flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) have been recovered and transported to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for data extraction and validation. Maintenance logs, crew training records, dispatch documentation, and weight-and-balance calculations have been obtained and are undergoing preliminary review. The wreckage has been stabilized, and a detailed photographic and dimensional survey of the impact site has been completed. The collapsed nose landing gear assembly, along with associated structural fragments, has been removed from the site and transported to a secure examination facility for metallurgical and mechanical analysis.

Initial examinations of the flight control system and hydraulic lines indicate no evidence of pre-impact failure or fluid leakage. However, these observations are strictly preliminary and subject to change upon completion of laboratory testing and component teardown. The investigation team has initiated interviews with the flight crew, cabin crew, air traffic controllers, and maintenance personnel. All interviews are being conducted in accordance with standard NTSB procedures, with appropriate legal and union representation present as required. The SIC and captain have been interviewed separately, and their statements are being cross-referenced with available operational data.

NEXT STEPS
Planned investigative activities over the coming weeks include the complete download and validation of FDR and CVR data, followed by a detailed timeline reconstruction of the approach, flare, and touchdown sequence. The Systems group will conduct a teardown and functional examination of the nose landing gear components, including the shock strut, drag brace, steering mechanism, and associated hydraulic actuators. The Structures group will perform non-destructive testing and metallurgical analysis on the forward fuselage attachment points to determine the sequence and magnitude of structural loading, with particular attention to components supplied by SAI.

The Operations and Human Performance groups will conduct a comprehensive review of the operator’s crosswind landing procedures, crew training records, and simulator performance data. A full-scale operational evaluation will be coordinated with the aircraft manufacturer to assess aircraft handling characteristics under simulated gusty crosswind conditions. Additionally, the investigation team will review the applicability and incorporation of relevant manufacturer service information, with particular attention to maintenance requirements outlined in Part 121 and the specific provisions of Section 121.344. The MED plug and surrounding door frame will undergo detailed dimensional inspection to verify proper installation and structural integrity prior to the event.

A preliminary factual report is anticipated within 30 days of the accident date, pending the completion of initial data downloads and component examinations. Subsequent updates will be issued as laboratory results become available and as additional witness interviews are concluded. All findings documented in this preliminary report are subject to revision as the investigation progresses. The NTSB will not issue a determination of probable cause until all investigative phases have been completed, all evidence has been thoroughly analyzed, and the final report has been reviewed and approved by the Board.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On August 15, 2021, at 1432 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), a Boeing 737-800, registration N738IE, experienced a hard landing event resulting in the collapse of the nose landing gear (NLG) during the landing roll. The accident occurred on Runway 27L at Coastal Regional Airport (KCRG), Jacksonville, Florida. The aircraft was operating under instrument flight rules (IFR) on a scheduled passenger service.
