The local time of the event corresponded to 1832 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). The accident site was located at latitude 30.3321° N, longitude 81.5144° W, with an airport elevation of 30 feet mean sea level (MSL).

1.2 Aircraft and Operator Identification
The aircraft was manufactured by The Boeing Company, model 737-8H4, serial number 38452. The registered operator at the time of the accident was Island Express Airlines, a certificated air carrier. The aircraft was configured for 189 passenger seats in a single-class layout, with a maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) of 174,200 pounds. The flight was designated as Island Express Flight 442, operating from Orlando International Airport (KMCO) to Coastal Regional Airport (KCRG). The aircraft was dispatched with a calculated landing weight of 142,850 pounds, with a center of gravity (CG) position at 24.1% mean aerodynamic chord (MAC).

1.3 Flight Operations Classification
The flight was conducted under the provisions of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121, specifically as a scheduled domestic passenger operation. The operator held an Air Carrier Certificate and Operations Specifications authorizing Boeing 737-800 operations. The flight was dispatched in accordance with standard Part 121 dispatch and flight release procedures, including fuel planning, alternate airport selection, and weight and balance verification. The flight plan was filed via the FAA’s National Airspace System (NAS) with a filed altitude of Flight Level 350, transitioning to a standard instrument approach procedure (SIAP) for Runway 27L.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Records
The captain, age 48, held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, certificate number 2145893, with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The captain’s medical certificate was a first-class medical, issued on March 12, 2021, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 14,250 hours, with 6,840 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The captain was employed by the operator since 2014 and had completed all required recurrent training and proficiency checks within the preceding 12 months. The captain’s training file indicated satisfactory performance in all line checks, simulator evaluations, and emergency procedure drills.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Records
The first officer, age 34, held a commercial pilot certificate with multi-engine land and instrument ratings, and was working toward an ATP certificate under restricted privileges. The first officer’s medical certificate was a first-class medical, issued on May 5, 2021. Total flight time was 3,120 hours, with 1,450 hours in the Boeing 737-800. The first officer was hired by the operator in 2019 and had successfully completed all line-oriented flight training (LOFT) and checkride requirements per the operator’s approved training program. The first officer’s records indicated no prior incidents, accidents, or enforcement actions.

2.3 Recent Flight Experience and Training Records
Both flight crewmembers were current and qualified for the flight. The captain had flown 82 hours in the preceding 30 days and 14 hours in the preceding 7 days. The first officer had flown 76 hours in the preceding 30 days and 12 hours in the preceding 7 days. Both crewmembers had completed the operator’s annual wind shear and crosswind landing training module on June 10, 2021. Training records indicated satisfactory performance in simulator-based gusty crosswind scenarios, with emphasis on stabilized approach criteria, wind correction techniques, and go-around decision points. The operator’s training syllabus required a minimum of 100 hours of line flying between recurrent simulator sessions, which both crewmembers had satisfied.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Aircraft Data
The accident aircraft, N738IE, was delivered to the operator on November 18, 2012. At the time of the accident, the aircraft had accumulated 42,115 total flight hours and 28,940 total flight cycles. The aircraft was equipped with CFM International CFM56-7B26 engines, serial numbers 784521 and 784522, each rated at 26,300 pounds of thrust. The aircraft was maintained under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) approved by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The aircraft’s avionics suite included dual flight management computers (FMC), a weather radar system, and a ground proximity warning system (GPWS) compliant with TSO-C151b.

3.2 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
The most recent heavy maintenance visit (C-check) was completed on May 22, 2021, at 41,890 flight hours. All scheduled inspections were documented as complete. The aircraft was in compliance with all applicable airworthiness directives (ADs) at the time of the accident. Specifically, compliance with AD 2012-09-04 was verified through maintenance logbook entries dated October 14, 2012, and subsequent recurring inspections documented in the aircraft maintenance tracking system. The AD required repetitive inspections of the forward fuselage skin lap splices and associated fastener holes for cracking. No discrepancies were noted during the most recent inspection cycle. The operator’s maintenance control center (MCC) confirmed that all deferred maintenance items were within the minimum equipment list (MEL) time limits.

3.3 Landing Gear and Structural Systems
The main landing gear (MLG) and nose landing gear (NLG) assemblies were manufactured by Goodrich Corporation. The NLG, part number 65-12345-1, had accumulated 18,450 flight cycles since overhaul. The NLG shock strut was serviced with MIL-PRF-5606 hydraulic fluid and nitrogen to a pressure of 1,850 psi at 70°F, per the Component Maintenance Manual (CMM). The NLG steering system and retraction actuators were inspected during the May 2021 C-check and found within manufacturer tolerances. The aircraft’s structural design incorporated fail-safe principles consistent with Section 25.571 of the Federal Aviation Regulations, which addresses damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation of structure. The primary load paths for the NLG were routed through the forward fuselage bulkhead and reinforced longerons, designed to withstand vertical and lateral loads up to 2.5g limit load factor.

3.4 Fuselage and Door Plug Configuration
The fuselage was manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems, which supplied the forward and mid-fuselage sections to Boeing for final assembly. The aircraft was equipped with a mid-exit door plug installed at station 1016, replacing a standard Type III emergency exit to accommodate a higher-density seating configuration. The door plug assembly was installed per Boeing Service Bulletin 737-53-1234 and FAA-approved supplemental type certificate (STC) data. The installation included reinforced frame doublers and modified latch mechanisms. The plug was inspected during the May 2021 maintenance visit, with all fasteners torqued to specification and sealant integrity verified. The mid-exit door plug was designed to maintain cabin pressurization integrity and emergency egress functionality under normal and abnormal flight conditions.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Weather Overview
On August 15, 2021, a stationary frontal boundary extended across northern Florida, with a low-pressure system situated over the Gulf of Mexico. The synoptic pattern produced scattered to broken cumulonimbus development, with localized convective activity and gusty surface winds. The National Weather Service (NWS) issued a convective outlook indicating a moderate risk of severe weather, including wind gusts exceeding 30 knots, across the Jacksonville terminal area. The atmospheric instability index (CAPE) was recorded at 1,850 J/kg, with a lifted index of -4, indicating a high potential for convective turbulence and rapid wind shifts.

4.2 Airport Weather Observations (METAR/TAF)
The routine aviation weather observation (METAR) for KCRG at 1400 EDT was: KCRG 151400Z 24018G32KT 10SM FEW035 SCT050 BKN080 31/22 A2992 RMK AO2 PK WND 25035/1355 SLP128 T03110222. The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) issued at 1130 EDT predicted: KCRG 151130Z 1512/1612 23015G25KT P6SM SCT040 BKN080 TEMPO 1514/1518 24020G35KT 4SM TSRA BKN030CB. The observed wind direction and speed at the time of the accident were consistent with the forecasted gusty conditions. The runway condition report (RCR) indicated dry pavement with a friction coefficient of 0.52, measured by a continuous friction measuring equipment (CFME) vehicle at 1345 EDT.

4.3 Pilot Weather Reports and Wind Data
A pilot report (PIREP) filed at 1415 EDT by a preceding aircraft reported moderate turbulence on final approach to Runway 27L, with wind shear alerts from the Terminal Doppler Weather Radar (TDWR). The airport’s automated surface observing system (ASOS) recorded a peak wind gust of 34 knots from 245° at 1428 EDT. The crosswind component for Runway 27L (magnetic heading 273°) was calculated at approximately 22 knots, with a headwind component of 18 knots. The operator’s crosswind limitation for the Boeing 737-800 under dry runway conditions was 33 knots, with a maximum demonstrated crosswind of 35 knots. The low-level wind shear alert system (LLWAS) recorded a 12-knot wind speed differential between the runway threshold and midpoint sensors at 1430 EDT.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Impact Site and Wreckage Distribution
The initial touchdown point was located 1,850 feet from the Runway 27L threshold, as indicated by tire marks on the runway surface. The aircraft contacted the runway with a vertical descent rate estimated at 1,200 feet per minute, based on flight data recorder (FDR) parameters. The primary impact sequence involved the main landing gear contacting the runway first, followed by a rapid pitch-down motion that resulted in the nose landing gear striking the pavement at a high vertical load. The aircraft continued along the runway centerline for approximately 2,100 feet before coming to rest. The wreckage distribution was confined to the runway and adjacent taxiway shoulder, with no debris field extending beyond the paved surface. The aircraft’s final heading was 271° magnetic.

5.2 Nose Landing Gear Examination
The nose landing gear assembly was recovered and transported to the NTSB Materials Laboratory for detailed examination. The NLG strut exhibited catastrophic compression failure, with the outer cylinder fractured at the lower bearing housing. The fracture surface displayed characteristics consistent with overload, including ductile tearing and shear lip formation. The NLG drag brace was bent aft, and the steering torque tube was fractured at the universal joint. The NLG retraction actuator was found in the extended position, with hydraulic fluid leakage noted at the rod seal. The NLG wheel and tire assembly remained attached to the axle, with the tire exhibiting circumferential tread separation and sidewall abrasion marks. Metallurgical analysis confirmed that the failure mode was consistent with a single-event overload exceeding the design limit load.

5.3 Fuselage and Lower Lobe Damage
The forward fuselage sustained substantial damage due to the NLG collapse. The lower lobe skin between stations 400 and 600 exhibited buckling, tearing, and localized puncture. The forward cargo door was deformed but remained latched. The mid-exit door plug assembly was inspected and found to be structurally intact, with no evidence of fastener failure, sealant degradation, or frame distortion. The plug’s retention latches were in the locked position, and the surrounding skin showed no stress cracking. The damage was consistent with localized ground contact and did not propagate to the pressurized cabin structure. The forward pressure bulkhead and avionics bay floor beams exhibited minor deformation but remained within structural tolerance limits.

5.4 Systems and Component Recovery
The flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) were recovered and downloaded. The FDR recorded 25 hours of data, with the final 30 minutes capturing the approach and landing sequence. Parameters indicated a stabilized approach until 500 feet above ground level (AGL), at which point the aircraft experienced a 15-knot airspeed fluctuation and a 3° pitch oscillation. The CVR captured standard crew communications, including callouts for wind shear and crosswind correction inputs. The engine fire detection system, hydraulic system A and B, and electrical buses were examined and found to be within operational limits prior to impact. The emergency evacuation slides deployed automatically upon NLG collapse, and all 178 passengers and 6 crewmembers evacuated via the forward and overwing exits.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Operator Policies and Procedures
Island Express maintained a comprehensive Flight Operations Manual (FOM) and Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) document, approved by the FAA. The FOM specified crosswind landing techniques, including the use of wing-low and crab methods, with a mandatory go-around if the aircraft became unstabilized below 500 feet AGL. The operator’s policy required flight crews to monitor real-time wind data and adhere to published crosswind limitations. The SOP also mandated that any hard landing exceeding 1.5g vertical acceleration be reported immediately and followed by a mandatory maintenance inspection. The operator’s safety management system (SMS) included a voluntary reporting program for wind shear and crosswind events, with quarterly trend analysis conducted by the safety department.

6.2 Regulatory Framework and Compliance
The aircraft’s design and certification were conducted in accordance with 14 CFR Part 25, Airworthiness Standards: Transport Category Airplanes. Specifically, Section 25.571 established the damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation requirements for primary structure, ensuring that the airframe could withstand expected operational loads without catastrophic failure. The fuselage door plug installation complied with 14 CFR 25.783, which governs fuselage doors and emergency exits, including requirements for structural integrity, sealing, and retention mechanisms under pressurization and flight loads. The operator’s maintenance program adhered to Section 121.344, which mandates the establishment of a continuous airworthiness maintenance program, including scheduled inspections, defect reporting, and compliance with airworthiness directives. All maintenance actions were documented in accordance with FAA Advisory Circular 120-78A.

6.3 Historical Incident Data
A review of the NTSB and FAA databases identified 14 similar hard landing events involving Boeing 737-800 aircraft between 2010 and 2020, with 3 resulting in NLG collapse. The majority of these events occurred during gusty crosswind conditions, with reported vertical descent rates exceeding 900 feet per minute. In each case, the NLG failure mode was consistent with overload beyond the design limit load factor of 2.5g. The operator’s internal safety database recorded 2 hard landing reports for the Boeing 737-800 fleet in the preceding 24 months, both of which were investigated and resulted in procedural updates regarding stabilized approach criteria and wind shear recovery techniques. The manufacturer’s service difficulty reports (SDRs) indicated that NLG structural failures in the 737-800 series are rare, with a fleet-wide occurrence rate of 0.0004 per 100,000 flight hours.

6.4 Evacuation and Emergency Response
The emergency evacuation was initiated at 1433 EDT, approximately 45 seconds after the aircraft came to rest. The cabin crew deployed the forward and overwing evacuation slides, and passengers were directed to exit via the nearest available doors. The airport rescue and firefighting (ARFF) units arrived on scene at 1435 EDT, with three crash trucks and two ambulances. No injuries were reported among passengers or crew. The evacuation was completed at 1438 EDT, with all occupants accounted for and transported to the terminal for medical screening. The operator’s emergency response plan was activated in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121 requirements, and coordination with local emergency services proceeded without delay. The aircraft was subsequently towed to a secure maintenance hangar for further examination and data preservation. All emergency equipment functioned as designed, and the evacuation timeline met the regulatory requirement of 90 seconds for full egress.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis conducted by the Structures and Materials Group in support of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigation into the August 15, 2021, hard landing event involving a Boeing 737-800, registration N737IE. The scope of this examination encompasses the forward fuselage structure, nose landing gear (NLG) assembly, associated attachment fittings, and the forward fuselage DOOR PLUG assembly. The investigation was initiated following a high-energy touchdown during a gusty crosswind approach that resulted in NLG collapse and substantial airframe damage.

The physical examination of the recovered components was conducted between August 20 and August 28, 2021, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., and at the Boeing Field Salvage Yard in Seattle, Washington. Items examined included the NLG shock strut (Part Number 65-43210-001, Serial Number NLG-88421), upper and lower drag brace assemblies, trunnion attachment lugs, forward fuselage skin panels (Station 240 to 360), and the DOOR PLUG assembly (Part Number 65-43210-12, Serial Number DP-99104). Flight Data Recorder (FDR) and Quick Access Recorder (QAR) data were downloaded, synchronized, and analyzed to correlate recorded flight parameters with observed structural deformation and failure modes. All examinations were conducted in accordance with NTSB Investigative Procedures Manual (IPM) Chapter 4, Section 4.2, and referenced applicable Boeing Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) and Structural Repair Manual (SRM) documentation.

2. BACKGROUND

The Boeing 737-800 is a twin-engine, narrow-body transport category aircraft certified under 14 CFR Part 25. The nose landing gear system is a dual-wheel, oleo-pneumatic shock-absorbing assembly designed to absorb vertical and horizontal landing loads, provide steering capability, and retract into the forward fuselage wheel well. The primary load path during landing consists of the shock strut cylinder, piston, drag brace, side brace, and trunnion fittings, which transfer loads into the forward fuselage bulkhead at Station 280. The design ultimate load factor for the NLG is +2.5g vertical and ±1.5g lateral, with a certified maximum sink rate of 600 feet per minute (fpm) at maximum landing weight.

The forward fuselage section, including the wheel well structure and the DOOR PLUG assembly, was manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems, Inc. (SAS) under Boeing specification BAC5000. The DOOR PLUG is a structurally integrated access panel installed at Station 310, left side, designed to provide maintenance access to the forward avionics bay and NLG retraction mechanism. The plug is secured via 24 Hi-Lok fasteners (Part Number HL10V-6-4) and incorporates a dual-latch mechanism compliant with 14 CFR 25.783, which governs fuselage door and plug design, load distribution, and fail-safe requirements. The certification basis for the plug assembly includes static load testing to 1.5 times limit load, fatigue testing to 3 design service goals (DSG), and damage tolerance analysis per AC 25.571-1D.

The subject aircraft, operated by Island Express Air Services, was delivered in March 2014 and had accumulated 42,118 flight hours and 28,542 flight cycles at the time of the event. Maintenance records indicate compliance with all Airworthiness Directives (ADs) and Boeing Service Bulletins (SBs) applicable to the NLG and forward fuselage. The most recent heavy maintenance visit (C-Check) was completed on June 12, 2021, which included NLG oleo servicing, drag brace bushing replacement, and eddy current inspection of the trunnion lugs per AMM 32-11-00. No deferred maintenance items or structural repair orders (SROs) were recorded for the forward fuselage or NLG attachment points. The DOOR PLUG assembly had been installed at the time of delivery and had not been removed or modified.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

Physical examination of the recovered NLG assembly revealed catastrophic failure of the lower drag brace at the mid-span clevis joint. The fracture surface exhibited 100% ductile overload characteristics, with pronounced necking, shear lips, and dimpled rupture morphology consistent with rapid tensile and bending failure. No evidence of fatigue striations, corrosion pitting, or manufacturing defects was observed. The upper drag brace exhibited plastic buckling at the mid-section, with a permanent lateral deflection of 0.312 inches measured from the original centerline. The shock strut cylinder showed localized crushing at the lower bearing housing, with a measured compression of 0.185 inches beyond the fully extended position. The trunnion attachment lugs on the forward bulkhead remained intact, though the surrounding skin panels exhibited out-of-plane deformation ranging from 0.042 to 0.128 inches.

The DOOR PLUG assembly was recovered with 18 of 24 Hi-Lok fasteners sheared at the shank-to-head transition. The remaining six fasteners exhibited elongated holes and bearing deformation. The plug frame showed localized yielding at the lower latch interface, with a measured gap of 0.065 inches between the plug and the surrounding skin. The latch mechanism was found in the unlocked position, with the primary cam follower sheared and the secondary latch spring fractured. Metallurgical analysis of the fastener material (AMS 5731, 15-5PH stainless steel) confirmed compliance with specification, with a measured ultimate tensile strength of 195 ksi and hardness of 38 HRC. Chemical composition analysis via optical emission spectroscopy (OES) matched the certified mill test report within ±0.05% for all major alloying elements.

Material testing was conducted on extracted coupons from the forward fuselage skin (2024-T3 aluminum alloy) and the drag brace (7075-T6 aluminum alloy). Tensile testing per ASTM E8 yielded an average yield strength of 48.2 ksi and ultimate strength of 68.5 ksi for the 2024-T3 skin, and 72.1 ksi yield and 81.4 ksi ultimate for the 7075-T6 drag brace. Hardness mapping across the fracture zones showed uniform values within the specified range (Rockwell B 85-92 for 2024-T3, Rockwell C 42-46 for 7075-T6). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) confirmed the absence of intergranular corrosion, exfoliation, or hydrogen embrittlement. All material properties were within Boeing BAC5000 and AMS 4079/AMS 4075 specifications.

Non-destructive testing (NDT) was performed on the remaining forward fuselage structure using phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) and eddy current per Boeing NDT Manual 650-001. No subsurface cracking, delamination, or hidden corrosion was detected within the inspected volume (Station 240 to 380, Stringer 12 to 24). The DOOR PLUG seal compression was measured at 0.018 inches, below the minimum design requirement of 0.025 inches, indicating loss of structural preload during the impact sequence. Fastener torque verification on the remaining intact fasteners showed values between 180 and 210 in-lbs, consistent with the specified installation torque of 195 ± 15 in-lbs.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

FDR and QAR data were extracted from the aircraft's solid-state recorder and processed using NTSB-standard decoding software (v4.2.1). The data stream was sampled at 128 Hz and synchronized with the Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) using a common time reference. Key parameters analyzed included radio altitude (RA), vertical acceleration (Gz), pitch attitude, indicated airspeed (IAS), crosswind component, NLG oleo pressure, and main gear wheel speed.

The approach phase data indicated a stabilized descent until 500 feet above ground level (AGL), at which point the aircraft encountered a sustained crosswind of 24 knots with gusts to 32 knots. At 200 feet AGL, the crosswind component increased to 28 knots, gusting to 35 knots, exceeding the demonstrated crosswind limit of 33 knots published in the Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM). The pilot initiated a flare maneuver at 30 feet RA, but the aircraft experienced a rapid sink rate increase from 450 fpm to 1,250 fpm over a 1.8-second interval. The pitch attitude at touchdown was 2.1 degrees nose-up, below the recommended 3.0 to 4.0 degree flare attitude.

At touchdown (T+0.00s), the FDR recorded a peak vertical acceleration of +3.8g, significantly exceeding the design limit load of +2.5g. The NLG oleo pressure spiked from 1,850 PSI to 3,420 PSI within 0.12 seconds, indicating rapid compression beyond the designed stroke. The drag brace load sensors (derived from strain gauge telemetry) registered a peak bending moment of 14,200 ft-lbs, approximately 1.6 times the ultimate design limit. The lateral load component, derived from the yaw rate and crosswind vector, reached 1.8g, contributing to asymmetric loading on the NLG assembly.

The DOOR PLUG structural response was inferred from fuselage strain gauge data and FDR-derived airframe flexure parameters. At T+0.08s, the forward fuselage experienced a localized bending moment of 8,900 ft-lbs, causing the DOOR PLUG frame to deflect 0.072 inches relative to the surrounding skin. This deflection exceeded the fastener shear capacity, resulting in progressive fastener failure. The latch mechanism disengaged at T+0.14s, coinciding with a 0.4g lateral acceleration spike. The DOOR PLUG remained attached via the secondary retention straps, preventing complete separation.

Comparison with normal operational parameters confirms that the event exceeded multiple design envelopes. The certified maximum sink rate of 600 fpm was exceeded by 108%. The vertical acceleration limit of +2.5g was exceeded by 52%. The crosswind component exceeded the demonstrated limit by 6%. The combined vertical and lateral loading created a resultant load vector of approximately 4.1g at a 22-degree angle from vertical, which aligns with the observed drag brace fracture and DOOR PLUG fastener shear patterns. No pre-impact anomalies were detected in the FDR data. All system parameters, including hydraulic pressure, flight control surface positions, and engine thrust, remained within normal operating ranges until touchdown.

5. SUMMARY

The physical examination, material testing, and flight data analysis confirm that the nose landing gear collapse and forward fuselage structural deformation resulted from a high-energy touchdown that exceeded the aircraft's certified design load limits. The NLG lower drag brace failed in ductile overload due to a combined vertical and lateral load vector of approximately 4.1g, with a peak vertical acceleration of +3.8g and a sink rate of 1,250 fpm. The upper drag brace exhibited plastic buckling consistent with the same overload event. The shock strut cylinder experienced localized crushing, and the trunnion attachment lugs remained structurally intact.

The DOOR PLUG assembly sustained fastener shear and frame yielding due to localized fuselage flexure during the impact sequence. Eighteen of 24 Hi-Lok fasteners failed in shear, and the primary latch mechanism disengaged. Material analysis of the 2024-T3 skin, 7075-T6 drag brace, and 15-5PH fasteners confirmed compliance with all applicable AMS and Boeing specifications. No evidence of fatigue, corrosion, manufacturing defects, or improper maintenance was identified. Non-destructive testing of the surrounding structure revealed no hidden damage or subsurface cracking.

Flight data analysis confirms that the aircraft encountered a crosswind component of 28 knots, gusting to 35 knots, during the final approach phase. The sink rate increased rapidly during the flare, resulting in a touchdown energy that exceeded the design ultimate load by 52%. The DOOR PLUG assembly, manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems, Inc., performed within its certified load path until the fuselage flexure exceeded the fastener shear capacity. The structural response aligns with the requirements of 14 CFR 25.783, which mandates fail-safe retention and load distribution for fuselage plugs. The operator, Island Express Air Services, maintained the aircraft in accordance with all applicable maintenance programs, and no pre-existing structural deficiencies were identified. All findings are factual and based on direct examination, testing, and recorded data.

INTERVIEW OF MARCUS THORNE, LEAD LINE MAINTENANCE TECHNICIAN
Date: August 17, 2021
Time: 14:30 Local
Location: Airport Operations Conference Room B, Terminal 3
Interviewer: Investigator Sarah Chen, NTSB Office of Aviation Safety
Witness: Marcus Thorne, Lead Line Maintenance Technician, SkyPort Ground Services

Q: Mr. Thorne, thank you for making yourself available. For the official record, please state your full name, your current title, and your role relative to the incident on August 15th.

A: Yeah, sure. Marcus Thorne. I’m the lead line maintenance technician for SkyPort Ground Services. Basically, I run the day-shift ramp crew, handle heavy troubleshooting, and act as the liaison between the airline’s engineering desk and our on-site mechanics. On the 15th, I was working the south apron, covering the heavy jet gates. I was actually out on the tarmac when the aircraft came in.

Q: Can you walk me through your location and what you were doing in the minutes leading up to the landing?

A: Right. So, it was… I want to say around 16:45, maybe 16:48 local time. We were just finishing up a fueling op on a regional turboprop, and the wind was really picking up. You could feel it through your jacket. It wasn’t just steady, it was gusting hard, shifting direction every few seconds. The tower had already issued a wind shear advisory. I was standing near our maintenance van, scrolling through a deferred defect log on my tablet, when I heard the approach. You know, after a while you can just tell when a heavy jet is fighting the air. The engine spool-up was… uneven. Choppy. Like it was hunting for thrust.

Q: What did you observe as the aircraft descended toward the runway?

A: Well, I was looking up, obviously. It was a 737-800, I recognized the blended winglets and the general profile. It was on final, but it was crabbing pretty aggressively. The nose was pointed maybe ten, twelve degrees off the runway heading. And then, just before the flare, it… it dropped. Fast. I mean, it wasn’t a smooth transition. It was like the pilot lost the cushion, or the wind just shoved it down. I heard the main gear hit first—thud, thud—but then, almost immediately, there was this… this metallic crunch. Like a car hitting a concrete barrier at speed, but way louder. The nose just… it didn’t roll out. It slammed. I saw the nose strut buckle inward, and the forward fuselage scraped the pavement. Sparks flew, actually. A lot of them.

Q: What happened immediately after the aircraft came to a stop?

A: It slid for… I don’t know, maybe a hundred and fifty, two hundred feet? The engines were still running, but you could hear the compressors surging, kind of a rhythmic whooshing. The aircraft came to a rest, nose-down, basically resting on the forward belly. Then the engines spooled down. Within, I’d say, thirty seconds, the evacuation slides deployed. Both forward doors, the overwing exits, aft doors. I saw passengers coming out, moving quick but not panicking. The cabin crew was directing them, pointing away from the wings. I grabbed my radio and called it in to the tower and our ops center. “Aircraft down, nose gear collapsed, slides deployed, requesting ARFF.”

Q: Did you approach the aircraft after the evacuation was underway?

A: Yeah, but not right away. Fire trucks were rolling in, and we had to wait for the all-clear from the incident commander. Once the ARFF guys gave the thumbs up, I walked over with two of my techs. The smell… it was jet fuel, hot brakes, and that distinct ozone smell from the electrical systems. The nose was buried in the concrete. The forward pressure bulkhead looked stressed, but the fuselage skin was holding. I remember looking at the left side, near the forward entry door, and I noticed the MED plug area. You know, the maintenance access plug for the forward avionics bay. It was… it was slightly misaligned. Not popped, but the seal was compromised. Probably from the impact load.

Q: You mentioned the MED plug. Can you elaborate on what you observed there and how it factored into your initial assessment?

A: Sure. The MED plug is… it’s a structural access panel, basically. On these airframes, it’s critical for maintaining pressure integrity and routing wiring. I’ve worked on dozens of these, and I know how they’re supposed to sit. This one had shifted maybe a quarter-inch. The latches were still engaged, but the gasket was pinched. I didn’t touch it, obviously. Just documented it with photos and flagged it in the log. Later, when the airline’s engineering team came out, they referenced the structural repair manual and, uh, 14 CFR 25.783. That’s the regulation for fuselage doors, hatches, and access panels, right? They were checking if the impact had compromised the pressure boundary or if the plug had exceeded its load limits. From what I could see, the plug itself was intact, but the surrounding frame had some minor deformation. Nothing catastrophic.

Q: Were you involved in the post-incident inspection or securing of the aircraft?

A: Yeah, after the passengers were bussed out and the NTSB team arrived, we were tasked with securing the site. We had to chock the mains, install the tow bar, and make sure the fuel lines were isolated. I was also coordinating with the OEM reps. Spirit AeroSystems had a field service engineer on site by the next morning. They were looking at the forward fuselage structure, specifically the nose section. They mentioned that the hard landing loads exceeded the design limits for the nose gear attachment points. I mean, I’m not a stress engineer, but I’ve seen what happens when a 737 comes down like that. The gear doesn’t just fold—it shears.

Q: Did Spirit AeroSystems provide any specific guidance during the initial response, and how did they approach the structural assessment?

A: Not immediately. They were on a conference call with the airline’s maintenance control. But when their guy got here, he brought out the structural damage assessment checklist. He was focused on the forward pressure bulkhead and the nose gear well. He also asked about the engine mounts. We had CFM56s on this bird, but he was cross-referencing it with the newer LEAP engine installation procedures, just to see if there were any common hard-landing stress points across the 737 family. I think he was just being thorough. The LEAP-1Bs are heavier, different pylon design, but the forward fuselage loads are similar. Anyway, he walked the perimeter with me, pointed out the scrape marks, and told us not to move anything until the investigators finished their documentation.

Q: Let’s go back to the timeline. Approximately what time did the aircraft come to a complete stop, and when was the evacuation complete?

A: Touchdown was around 16:52. It stopped sliding by 16:53, maybe 16:53:30. The slides deployed almost instantly. Evacuation… I’d say it took about four minutes total. The last passenger was off by 16:57. The cabin crew did a sweep, came out the aft stairs, and the captain was the last one off. I saw him talking to the ARFF commander. Everyone was accounted for. No serious injuries, just a few bumps and bruises.

Q: Did you notice anything unusual about the aircraft’s configuration or systems before or during the approach?

A: Not from the ground. I couldn’t see the cockpit, obviously. But the flaps were extended, gear was down. I heard the gear warning horn for a split second before touchdown, which is normal. The only thing that stood out was the… the way it bounced. It hit the mains, bounced maybe two feet, then came down hard on the nose. That’s when the strut failed. I’ve seen crosswind landings before, but this was… it was like the wind just dropped out from under it. A microburst, maybe? Or just a severe shear. The tower later said the wind shifted from 270 at 25 to 310 at 38 in a matter of seconds.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add that we haven’t covered?

A: Just… I want to make sure the record shows that the crew handled it well. Once it was down, they got everyone out fast. And from a maintenance standpoint, the airframe held together. The forward fuselage didn’t rupture, the MED plug stayed seated, and the pressure boundary wasn’t breached. That’s… that’s a testament to the design. I know 14 CFR 25.783 has strict requirements for door and hatch integrity under emergency loads, and this aircraft met them. Even with the nose gear gone, the structure did its job. I’ve been doing this for twelve years, and I’ve seen worse. But yeah, it was a hard landing. No doubt about it.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Thorne. We’ll follow up if we need clarification.

A: Yeah, no problem. I’ll be around.

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION
FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
FLIGHT STANDARDS SERVICE
WASHINGTON, D.C. 20591

MEMORANDUM

DATE: October 14, 2023
TO: National Transportation Safety Board, Office of Aviation Safety
FROM: Federal Aviation Administration, Aircraft Certification Service & Flight Standards District Office
SUBJECT: Regulatory Response to NTSB Safety Recommendation A-22-045
DOCKET NO.: FAA-2022-0891; NTSB ACCIDENT NO.: DCA21MA142
REFERENCE: 14 CFR Part 121, Section 121.344; AD 2022-14-08

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This correspondence constitutes the Federal Aviation Administration’s formal regulatory response to National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Safety Recommendation A-22-045, issued following the investigation of the August 15, 2021, runway excursion and structural failure event involving a Boeing 737-800, registration N738SP, operated by Spirit Airlines. The incident, cataloged under NTSB Accident Number DCA21MA142, involved a hard landing with subsequent collapse of the nose landing gear assembly during a gusty crosswind approach at Orlando International Airport (KMCO). The aircraft sustained substantial damage to the forward fuselage and primary landing gear structure; however, all passengers and flight crew evacuated safely without serious injury. This document addresses regulatory compliance, oversight actions, and mandated corrective measures pertaining to Section 121.344, Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2022-14-08, and associated operational and maintenance protocols.

2. BACKGROUND
The regulatory framework governing the operation, maintenance, and airworthiness of transport category aircraft is established under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR), specifically Parts 21, 25, 121, and 145. The subject aircraft, certified under Type Certificate No. A16WE, was operating under a Part 121 certificate at the time of the occurrence. The powerplant configuration, comprising CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, was installed pursuant to Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) ST03456NY, which mandates specific structural load monitoring, vibration analysis, and maintenance interval adjustments to accommodate altered thrust-to-weight ratios and aerodynamic loading profiles.

Historically, the Federal Aviation Administration has issued multiple Airworthiness Directives addressing landing gear structural integrity and crosswind operational limitations for the 737-800 series, including AD 2018-11-05 and AD 2020-09-12. These directives established mandatory inspection intervals for the nose gear trunnion, drag brace assemblies, and shock strut seals. Furthermore, 14 CFR § 121.344 prescribes the duties and responsibilities of the Second in Command (SIC), including the requirement to monitor flight parameters, cross-verify approach speeds, and execute go-around procedures when stabilized approach criteria are not met.

Following the August 15, 2021, event, the NTSB identified deficiencies in the operator’s adherence to stabilized approach protocols and the timely reporting of exceedance events. The investigation highlighted that the flight crew, specifically the SIC, did not initiate a mandatory go-around despite recorded wind shear alerts and vertical acceleration exceedances surpassing 2.1 G. Additionally, maintenance records indicated that the Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) deferral for the associated flight data monitoring system had expired, compromising post-flight data retrieval and hindering the operator’s ability to conduct a timely engineering review.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive review of Spirit Airlines’ operational and maintenance records, conducted by the Atlanta Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) in coordination with the Aircraft Certification Service (AIR), reveals partial compliance with applicable regulatory mandates. While the operator maintained a valid Part 121 operating certificate and adhered to the prescribed AD compliance schedules for the primary landing gear structure, several regulatory gaps were identified.

First, regarding Section 121.344, the investigation determined that the SIC failed to execute the required cross-check of approach parameters and did not formally challenge the Pilot Flying’s decision to continue the approach below the stabilized approach gate. The operator’s Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) lacked explicit, enforceable language mandating SIC intervention during unstabilized approaches in adverse meteorological conditions. This deficiency contravenes the intent of § 121.344, which requires the SIC to actively participate in flight deck resource management and safety-critical decision-making.

Second, the maintenance tracking system utilized by the operator’s approved repair station did not adequately correlate flight data exceedance events with mandatory structural inspections. Although the LEAP-1B powerplant installation under STC ST03456NY requires enhanced vibration and load monitoring, the operator’s engineering department failed to integrate these parameters into the continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP). Consequently, the cumulative stress on the nose landing gear assembly was not accurately modeled, delaying the identification of fatigue precursors and compromising the airworthiness limitations section (ALS) compliance.

Third, regulatory oversight actions taken by the FAA included the issuance of a Letter of Investigation (LOI) and a subsequent Notice of Proposed Certificate Action (NPCA) for violations of 14 CFR § 121.344 and § 121.363 (Maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations). The FAA’s Principal Operations Inspector (POI) and Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) conducted an unannounced surveillance audit, which confirmed that the operator’s MMEL deferral tracking system contained systemic discrepancies. The audit further revealed that the operator’s training curriculum did not adequately address gusty crosswind recovery techniques or hard landing reporting thresholds.

The regulatory framework currently lacks a unified, real-time data-sharing mechanism between flight operations quality assurance (FOQA) programs and maintenance engineering departments. This gap impedes the proactive identification of structural degradation trends and limits the FAA’s ability to mandate timely corrective actions prior to catastrophic failure.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
In response to the identified deficiencies and in accordance with NTSB Safety Recommendation A-22-045, the Federal Aviation Administration mandates the following corrective actions and compliance timelines:

a. Operational Procedure Revisions: Spirit Airlines shall revise its Part 121 General Operations Manual (GOM) to explicitly codify SIC authority and mandatory intervention protocols during unstabilized approaches. The revised procedures must align with Section 121.344 and incorporate mandatory callouts for wind shear alerts, vertical acceleration exceedances, and crosswind component limitations. Compliance is required within 90 days of this memorandum’s issuance.

b. Training and Qualification Updates: The operator shall implement a revised recurrent training program for all flight crewmembers, with specific emphasis on crosswind landing techniques, hard landing recognition, and go-around decision-making. The curriculum must include simulator-based scenarios replicating gusty crosswind conditions and exceedance thresholds. Initial training rollout shall be completed within 120 days, with full fleet compliance achieved within 180 days.

c. Maintenance and Engineering Integration: The operator’s CAMP shall be amended to integrate flight data exceedance parameters with structural inspection intervals. Specifically, the maintenance program must incorporate automated alerts for vertical acceleration events exceeding 1.8 G, triggering immediate nose landing gear trunnion and drag brace inspections per AD 2022-14-08. The FAA’s PMI will conduct a compliance verification audit within 60 days of CAMP submission.

d. MMEL and FOQA System Overhaul: The operator shall rectify all MMEL deferral tracking discrepancies and implement a real-time data synchronization protocol between the FOQA system and the maintenance engineering database. This system must ensure that exceedance events are automatically routed to the Director of Maintenance for engineering review. Full implementation is required within 150 days.

e. Regulatory Oversight Schedule: The FAA will conduct quarterly surveillance audits of the operator’s compliance with the aforementioned corrective actions. The first audit is scheduled for January 15, 2024. Continued non-compliance will result in enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR § 13.19 and may necessitate the suspension of the operator’s Part 121 certificate.

The Federal Aviation Administration acknowledges the NTSB’s investigative findings and remains committed to enhancing the regulatory oversight framework governing transport category aircraft operations. All referenced documentation, including revised GOM sections, training syllabi, and CAMP amendments, shall be submitted to the Atlanta FSDO for formal approval prior to implementation.

Respectfully submitted,
