Island Express Jet Collapses Nose Gear in Gusty Crosswind Landing; All 142 Aboard Evacuate Safely

By Elena Rostova, Global Aviation News
PORTLAND, Maine — An Island Express Boeing 737-800 sustained substantial damage and collapsed its nose landing gear during a turbulent approach on Sunday, August 15, 2021, but all passengers and crew members escaped without serious injury. The aircraft touched down hard at Portland International Jetport amid severe crosswinds, prompting an emergency evacuation that unfolded within minutes.

The incident occurred as the flight battled shifting wind gusts exceeding 30 knots during its final descent. The force of the firm touchdown buckled the forward landing gear, causing the aircraft’s nose to drop onto the runway surface. Emergency response teams quickly deployed evacuation slides, and all 142 passengers and six crew members exited the plane safely. While the airframe suffered significant structural damage to the forward fuselage and nose section, officials confirmed there were no fatalities or life-threatening injuries.

“The evacuation was executed flawlessly by the flight crew and ground responders,” said National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigator-in-charge David Chen. “Our priority right now is securing the wreckage and downloading the flight data and cockpit voice recorders to understand exactly what happened during those final seconds.” Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) officials echoed the sentiment, noting that the airline’s emergency protocols functioned as designed. “We are working closely with the NTSB and the operator to ensure a thorough investigation,” said FAA regional administrator Maria Gonzalez. Island Express spokesperson Thomas Vance added, “Our hearts go out to everyone on board Flight 412. We are providing full support to our passengers and crew, and we are cooperating completely with federal investigators.”

The aircraft, a 12-year-old Boeing 737-800 operated by Island Express, was completing a routine domestic route from Chicago O’Hare International Airport. The 737-800 is one of the most widely flown commercial jets in the world, known for its reliability and short-to-medium range capabilities. The specific aircraft involved is equipped with CFM International LEAP-1B engines, a modern powerplant series recently integrated into the carrier’s fleet during a scheduled mid-life upgrade program aimed at improving fuel efficiency and reducing emissions. The flight’s second in command (SIC), First Officer Marcus Lin, was at the controls during the approach, while Captain Sarah Jenkins monitored the landing parameters and weather conditions.

Aviation safety analysts suggest the combination of high crosswinds and a firm touchdown likely overwhelmed the nose gear’s structural limits. “When you have a strong crosswind, pilots must use a technique called a crab or sideslip to keep the aircraft aligned with the runway centerline,” said Dr. Alan Reeves, a former commercial pilot and aviation safety professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. “If the aircraft isn’t perfectly aligned at the moment of touchdown, or if the vertical descent rate is too high, the lateral and downward forces can exceed what the landing gear is designed to handle. It’s a known operational risk, but one that rigorous training and strict weather minimums are meant to mitigate.”

For those on board, the moments following touchdown were chaotic but ultimately survivable. “We hit the runway so hard that my coffee cup flew out of my hand,” said passenger David Chen, who was traveling with his family. “The nose dropped, there was a loud metallic screech, and then the captain calmly told us to brace. The slides deployed, and we were out in under two minutes. I’m just grateful everyone is okay.” Family members waiting at the terminal described a scene of anxious relief. “I saw the news alerts and immediately called my daughter,” said Margaret Hayes, whose son was on the flight. “When she finally texted back that she was safe, I just broke down. You never expect something like this to happen on a routine trip.”

Hard landings resulting in gear collapse are rare but not unprecedented in commercial aviation. The 737-800 has a strong safety record, though several similar incidents have occurred globally over the past two decades, often linked to adverse weather, pilot technique, or runway conditions. Industry safety standards have evolved significantly since the late 1990s, particularly following the implementation of Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88, which mandated rigorous fuel system safety reviews, enhanced wiring inspections, and stricter maintenance protocols across commercial fleets. While SFAR 88 primarily targeted fuel tank ignition prevention, its broader impact on maintenance culture and component inspection routines has contributed to the overall resilience of modern aircraft systems. Island Express has maintained a clean safety record for over a decade, with no prior hull-loss incidents.

The NTSB has dispatched a specialized “go team” to the scene, and investigators are currently examining the runway for skid marks, debris, and meteorological data. The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered and are being transported to NTSB laboratories in Washington, D.C., for detailed analysis. Weather reports indicate wind gusts reached 35 knots with rapid directional shifts during the approach window. The FAA has temporarily grounded the specific aircraft for inspection, while Island Express continues to operate its remaining fleet under standard safety protocols. Investigators expect preliminary findings within 30 days, though a final report could take up to a year. “We will leave no stone unturned,” Chen said. “Every piece of data, every maintenance log, and every crew interview will be scrutinized to ensure this doesn’t happen again.”

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Chief Flight Operations Engineer and Director of Flight Safety & Engineering on behalf of Island Express (hereinafter referred to as IEA, the Operator, or Island Express Air). As the certificate holder and operator of the accident aircraft, IEA has participated fully in the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigative process, providing access to flight data, maintenance records, crew training files, and internal safety management system (SMS) documentation. The purpose of this document is to present the Operator’s technical position regarding the August 15, 2021, hard landing and subsequent nose landing gear (NLG) collapse involving a Boeing 737-800. 

The scope of this analysis encompasses meteorological conditions, aircraft structural and systems performance, crew operational decision-making, and regulatory compliance. Our position, grounded in engineering data, operational records, and human factors analysis, is that the event was precipitated by a rapidly evolving microburst and crosswind environment that exceeded stabilized approach parameters, compounded by a delayed initiation of a missed approach. The aircraft’s design, maintenance status, and propulsion response performed within certified limits. This submission synthesizes docket evidence, engineering assessments, and industry best practices to clarify the causal chain and outline the Operator’s commitment to continuous safety enhancement.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On August 15, 2021, at approximately 14:32 local time, the subject Boeing 737-800 was conducting an instrument approach to Runway 27L under visual meteorological conditions that rapidly deteriorated during final approach. The flight crew reported encountering moderate turbulence and variable wind conditions beginning at approximately 1,500 feet AGL. According to the Flight Data Recorder (FDR) readout (Docket Item 14), the aircraft crossed the runway threshold at 148 knots indicated airspeed with a calculated crosswind component of 28 knots and a developing 6-knot tailwind. The FDR recorded a peak vertical acceleration of 3.2g upon initial touchdown, followed by a secondary impact that resulted in the collapse of the NLG. All 142 passengers and 6 crew members evacuated without serious injury.

Meteorological data (Docket Item 22) from the Low-Level Wind Shear Alert System (LLWAS) and terminal Doppler weather radar indicate a sudden wind shift of 45 degrees and a 22-knot increase in headwind-to-tailwind gradient within a 12-second window at 800 feet AGL. The crew’s Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) transcript (Docket Item 18) confirms that the pilot monitoring called “wind shear” at approximately 500 feet, but the pilot flying elected to continue the approach, citing visual contact with the runway environment and a desire to avoid a diversion.

Maintenance records (Docket Item 31) demonstrate that the aircraft was in full compliance with all airworthiness directives, service bulletins, and scheduled inspections. The NLG assembly had undergone a detailed structural inspection 142 flight cycles prior to the event, with no discrepancies noted. The landing gear retraction and extension mechanisms were verified as compliant with 14 CFR 121.344, and all associated hydraulic, electrical, and mechanical linkages were within manufacturer tolerances. No deferred maintenance items or open work orders existed for the landing gear system.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The Operator’s engineering and flight safety teams have conducted a multi-disciplinary review of the event, integrating FDR/CVR data, structural load modeling, meteorological reconstruction, and operational procedure analysis. The findings are organized below.

Environmental and Aerodynamic Factors
The meteorological reconstruction confirms the presence of a localized microburst that generated a rapid wind gradient exceeding the aircraft’s certified crosswind and tailwind limits for a stabilized approach. The FDR indicates that the aircraft’s groundspeed increased by 14 knots in the final 10 seconds before touchdown due to the sudden loss of headwind component. This energy state, combined with a 28-knot crosswind, required significant lateral control input and increased sink rate to maintain the glidepath. Industry guidance, including FAA Advisory Circular 120-71A and Boeing’s Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM), establishes that approaches should be stabilized by 1,000 feet AGL in instrument conditions and 500 feet AGL in visual conditions. The FDR shows that the aircraft was not fully stabilized at 500 feet, with airspeed fluctuations of ±8 knots and a descent rate exceeding 1,200 feet per minute.

Structural and Landing Gear Performance
The NLG collapse was a direct consequence of vertical and lateral load factors exceeding the design limit loads specified in 14 CFR Part 25.723 and the certification basis for the 737-800. Finite element modeling and post-impact metallurgical analysis (Docket Item 27) indicate that the primary failure initiated at the NLG drag brace attachment lug, where combined bending and shear stresses surpassed the ultimate load threshold. The landing gear system, including the shock strut, torque links, and retraction mechanism, was maintained in strict accordance with Part 121.344 and the manufacturer’s Maintenance Planning Document. There is no evidence of fatigue cracking, corrosion, or improper lubrication that would have contributed to premature failure. The collapse mechanism is consistent with a high-energy, off-axis impact rather than a systemic or maintenance-related deficiency.

Propulsion and Thrust Response Characteristics
A critical element of the investigation has been the evaluation of engine response during the wind shear encounter. The accident aircraft was equipped with CFM56-7B engines. To ensure a comprehensive understanding of thrust spool dynamics across the Operator’s mixed fleet, our engineering team conducted a comparative analysis of engine acceleration profiles, including data from the newer CFM LEAP-1B powerplants. The analysis confirms that both engine families exhibit similar spool-up characteristics under rapid thrust demand, with the CFM56-7B achieving 90% N1 within 3.2 seconds from idle. The FDR shows that the crew advanced thrust levers to go-around power at 2.1 seconds after touchdown, which is within normal operational response times. The LEAP-1B comparative data further validates that propulsion response did not delay the initiation of the missed approach or contribute to the energy state at touchdown.

Human Factors and Operational Decision-Making
The CVR and FDR data, when analyzed through a human factors lens, reveal a classic scenario of continuation bias under time pressure and environmental uncertainty. The pilot flying acknowledged the wind shear call but prioritized runway acquisition over executing a go-around. This decision was influenced by several factors: recent successful landings in similar conditions, a desire to maintain schedule, and an underestimation of the rapidly shifting wind vector. The Operator’s Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) mandate a go-around if the approach is not stabilized by 500 feet AGL or if wind shear is detected. While the crew verbally acknowledged the wind shear, the procedural trigger was not actioned until after touchdown. This highlights a gap between procedural knowledge and real-time execution under high workload, a well-documented phenomenon in aviation safety literature.

Regulatory and Industry Benchmarking
The Operator’s crosswind training program, dispatch weather minimums, and stabilized approach criteria align with FAA regulations, IATA IOSA standards, and manufacturer recommendations. The event does not indicate a systemic regulatory deficiency but rather underscores the limitations of predictive weather modeling in rapidly evolving convective environments. The Operator’s SMS has since classified this event as a high-severity, low-probability occurrence driven by environmental unpredictability and operational decision latency.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the comprehensive review of flight data, structural analysis, maintenance records, and operational procedures, the Operator concludes that the August 15, 2021, hard landing and NLG collapse were not attributable to aircraft design flaws, maintenance deficiencies, or propulsion system anomalies. The primary contributing factors were:

1. A sudden, unforecasted microburst that generated a crosswind and tailwind gradient exceeding the aircraft’s stabilized approach parameters.
2. A delayed go-around decision despite explicit wind shear alerts and failure to meet stabilized approach criteria at 500 feet AGL.
3. High-energy, off-axis touchdown loads that exceeded the certified structural limits of the NLG assembly, resulting in a predictable mechanical failure mode.

The aircraft’s landing gear system, including all components governed by 14 CFR 121.344, was fully airworthy and maintained to manufacturer specifications. The propulsion response, validated through comparative analysis with both legacy and next-generation powerplants including the LEAP-1B, performed within certified parameters and did not impede the crew’s ability to execute a timely missed approach. The Operator acknowledges the complexity of real-time decision-making in deteriorating weather and recognizes that procedural compliance must be reinforced through enhanced training, technological aids, and cultural emphasis on go-around authority.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In response to this event, Island Express has implemented immediate and long-term corrective actions to mitigate recurrence and strengthen operational resilience.

Actions Already Taken
- Issued Fleet Safety Bulletin 2021-08-15, mandating strict adherence to stabilized approach gates and reinforcing the “go-around first” philosophy for all flight crews.
- Updated the Operator’s FCOM and Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) to include explicit crosswind and wind shear decision matrices, with mandatory callouts at 1,000 and 500 feet AGL.
- Integrated a dedicated microburst and wind shear recovery module into the full-flight simulator curriculum, requiring recurrent training for all 737-800 and 737 MAX pilots.
- Enhanced dispatch weather minimums for Runway 27L and similar high-gust environments, incorporating real-time LLWAS and terminal Doppler data into pre-flight risk assessments.
- Conducted a fleet-wide inspection of NLG attachment points and drag brace assemblies, confirming 100% compliance with Part 121.344 and manufacturer service life limits.

Proposed Future Improvements
- Implementation of an Electronic Flight Bag (EFB) application that provides real-time crosswind component calculation and automated stabilized approach alerts, reducing pilot workload during high-stress phases of flight.
- Development of a predictive wind shear alerting system that integrates ground-based radar, aircraft-derived meteorological data, and machine learning algorithms to provide earlier, more accurate hazard warnings.
- Expansion of the Operator’s SMS data-sharing initiative to include anonymized hard landing and go-around metrics across the industry, fostering collaborative safety research.
- Standardization of crosswind and wind shear training across the entire fleet, ensuring that crews transitioning between CFM56-7B and LEAP-1B equipped aircraft receive consistent procedural and performance guidance.
- Advocacy for regulatory updates to 14 CFR 121.344 and related landing gear maintenance standards to incorporate advanced non-destructive testing (NDT) intervals for high-cycle operators, ensuring continued structural integrity under extreme operational loads.

The Operator remains fully committed to transparency, continuous improvement, and collaboration with the NTSB, manufacturers, and regulatory bodies. The lessons learned from this event have been institutionalized into our safety management framework, and we are confident that the implemented and proposed measures will significantly reduce the likelihood of similar occurrences in the future.

TO: Fleet Maintenance Engineering, Line Maintenance Supervisors, Quality Assurance Division, Technical Records, MRO Planning
FROM: Director of Airworthiness & Structural Integrity, Engineering & Maintenance
DATE: 24 August 2021
SUBJECT: QUALITY ALERT 2021-08-04: Post-Hard-Landing Structural & Systems Inspection Protocol – 737-800 & Cross-Fleet Applicability
REF: QA-2021-08-04, AMM 32-00-00 Rev 14, SB-737-32-1182, NTSB Docket Entry 2021-08-15-001, WO-2021-HL-01

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert establishes mandatory post-hard-landing inspection procedures for all Boeing 737-800 aircraft in our fleet, with cross-fleet applicability to 737 MAX and A320neo platforms. The directive is issued following the 15 August 2021 incident involving substantial structural damage and nose landing gear (NLG) collapse during a gusty crosswind approach. Immediate compliance is required to ensure continued airworthiness, standardize maintenance response, and align with internal damage tolerance requirements (DTRs).

BACKGROUND:
On 15 August 2021, aircraft N737IE (operated under lease by Island Express) experienced a hard landing at approximately 1,850 fpm vertical descent rate with a 28-knot crosswind component. The event resulted in NLG collapse, forward fuselage skin buckling, and secondary damage to the lower lobe avionics bay. All passengers and crew evacuated safely without injury. Preliminary data from the Quick Access Recorder (QAR) and Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) systems confirm exceedance of the 1.5g hard-landing threshold.

Post-incident teardown and NDI (Non-Destructive Inspection) revealed micro-fractures in the NLG trunnion fitting and localized stress concentrations in the forward pressure bulkhead. These findings align with known load-path vulnerabilities in Spirit AeroSystems (SAS)-supplied Section 41 assemblies. While the affected aircraft is a 737-800, our engineering review indicates that similar load transfer characteristics exist across the 737 family, including the mid-exit door plug (MEDP) retention structure on MAX variants. Additionally, our mixed-fleet maintenance program requires harmonized inspection criteria for high-impact events. This alert supersedes previous guidance in QA-2019-03-11 and incorporates updated torque and NDI thresholds.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, all maintenance personnel shall implement the following inspection and documentation protocols for any aircraft reporting a hard landing, gear collapse, or severe turbulence encounter:

1. Initial Assessment & Data Retrieval
   • Download and archive QAR/FDM data within 2 hours of aircraft arrival.
   • Cross-reference exceedance thresholds against AMM 32-00-00 and internal Work Order WO-2021-HL-01.
   • Notify Engineering & Quality Assurance via the Airworthiness Reporting Portal (ARP) before releasing the aircraft for further service.

2. Structural & Landing Gear Inspection
   • Perform detailed visual and eddy-current inspection of the NLG trunnion, drag brace, and forward fuselage attachment points per SB-737-32-1182.
   • Inspect all SAS Section 41 fasteners (P/N 737-41-001 through 737-41-089) for elongation, fretting, or torque loss. Replace any fastener showing >0.005” elongation.
   • Verify mid-exit door plug retention hardware torque values against current AMM 52-40-00 specifications. Document all readings in the Aircraft Technical Log (ATL).

3. Engine & Pylon Load-Path Verification
   • For aircraft equipped with LEAP engine installations (A320neo/737 MAX), conduct borescope and ultrasonic inspection of the forward pylon attach fittings and thrust reverser actuator mounts.
   • Confirm that all engine mount shear bolts meet OEM torque and stretch specifications. Any deviation requires immediate grounding and Engineering disposition.

4. Regulatory & Documentation Compliance
   • All inspections must satisfy FAA 14 CFR §25.571 damage tolerance requirements, specifically regarding crack propagation limits and residual strength margins.
   • Complete Form QA-2021-HL-02 (Post-Hard-Landing Structural Assessment) and attach all NDI reports, torque logs, and QAR data extracts.
   • Submit completed documentation to Technical Records within 48 hours of inspection completion.

5. Island Express (IEX) Fleet Coordination
   • Coordinate with IEX maintenance control to verify historical hard-landing events for aircraft N737IE and sister tail numbers.
   • Cross-check maintenance records for any deferred structural repairs or recurring NLG vibration reports. Flag discrepancies for immediate Engineering review.

ACTION REQUIRED:
• Line Maintenance Supervisors: Ensure all incoming aircraft are screened for hard-landing exceedances. Halt release of any aircraft pending completion of WO-2021-HL-01. Deadline: Immediate.
• NDI Technicians: Prioritize all pending structural inspections. Calibrate eddy-current and ultrasonic equipment per QA-CAL-2021-08. Report anomalies directly to Structural Engineering. Deadline: 48 hours from aircraft grounding.
• Quality Assurance Division: Audit 100% of completed WO-2021-HL-01 packages for compliance. Issue nonconformance reports (NCRs) for any missing torque logs, incomplete NDI, or unreported exceedances. Deadline: 72 hours post-inspection.
• Engineering & Airworthiness: Review all submitted QA-2021-HL-02 forms. Issue fleet-wide Service Bulletin (SB) or Airworthiness Directive (AD) compliance guidance if systemic trends are identified. Deadline: 10 September 2021.
• Technical Records: Archive all documentation in the digital maintenance tracking system (MRO-Track v4.2). Ensure cross-referencing with NTSB docket materials and internal incident logs. Deadline: 5 September 2021.

Failure to comply with this Quality Alert constitutes a violation of internal airworthiness procedures and may result in immediate grounding of affected aircraft. All personnel are required to acknowledge receipt via the company intranet portal by 26 August 2021.

For technical questions, contact the Structural Integrity Desk at ext. 4410 or email structural.eng@company.com.

1. SYNOPSIS
On August 15, 2021, at approximately 1432 local time, a Boeing 737-800, operated by a commercial passenger carrier, experienced a hard landing that resulted in the collapse of the nose landing gear during a gusty crosswind approach at a regional international airport. The aircraft sustained substantial damage to the forward fuselage and lower airframe structures, though all passengers and crew successfully evacuated without serious injury. This preliminary report summarizes initial factual data, establishes the investigative scope, and documents early procedural determinations. All information contained herein is subject to revision as the investigation progresses and does not represent a final determination of probable cause.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary information indicates that the flight was conducting a scheduled revenue service when it encountered a dynamic wind environment during the final approach phase. Initial witness accounts from air traffic control personnel and ground observers suggest the aircraft exhibited a pronounced descent rate and lateral drift prior to touchdown. The First Officer (FO), who was serving as the pilot flying at the time of the event, has provided an initial statement indicating that wind shear alerts were activated and that control inputs were applied to maintain runway centerline alignment. These accounts remain uncorroborated and are subject to further validation through flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) analysis.

Meteorological data obtained from the airport’s automated weather observing system (AWOS) and adjacent radar installations indicate surface winds were variable between 240 and 290 degrees at 18 to 25 knots, with gusts reported up to 32 knots. Crosswind components during the approach phase appear to have approached or exceeded the aircraft’s demonstrated crosswind limits, though precise values will require correlation with recorded flight parameters and pilot technique evaluation.

Preliminary damage assessment conducted by on-scene investigators reveals substantial deformation to the nose landing gear assembly, forward pressure bulkhead, and lower fuselage skin. The main landing gear remained intact, and no evidence of in-flight structural failure, fire, or post-impact fuel leakage has been identified. As part of the initial configuration verification process, investigators are reviewing maintenance documentation, airworthiness directives, and parts tracking records to confirm the installed components and their compliance with applicable regulatory frameworks. This review includes an examination of structural modifications and component sourcing, with particular attention to assemblies manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems (SAS). Additionally, investigators are cross-referencing the aircraft’s maintenance history against fuel system safety requirements outlined in Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88 (SFAR 88) and door structural integrity standards referenced in Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations Part 25.783 (14 CFR 25.783) to ensure no latent compliance issues contributed to the event.

It should be noted that while certain preliminary inspections have referenced components such as the DOOR PLUG assembly and propulsion systems including the LEAP-1B turbofan, these references are part of a standardized configuration verification protocol and do not imply direct relevance to the current accident sequence. The aircraft in question is a 737-800 variant, and investigators are actively reconciling maintenance logs, parts tracking databases, and manufacturer service bulletins to confirm the exact installed configuration. All preliminary observations remain subject to revision as additional data is recovered, analyzed, and peer-reviewed.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The National Transportation Safety Board has activated multiple investigative groups to address the technical, operational, and human factors aspects of this event. The Operations, Structures, Systems, and Human Performance groups have been formally established and are currently conducting on-site and remote data collection. The Operations Group is focusing on flight crew training records, dispatch documentation, and air traffic control communications. The Structures Group is overseeing the detailed examination of the collapsed nose gear, forward fuselage, and surrounding airframe components. The Systems Group is tasked with the recovery and initial readout of the flight data and cockpit voice recorders, as well as the evaluation of flight control, hydraulic, and landing gear systems. The Human Performance Group is coordinating with the flight crew and cabin personnel to gather preliminary statements and assess operational workload and environmental stressors.

Parties to the investigation have been designated in accordance with NTSB procedures. Representatives from the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, the operator, the flight crew union, and relevant regulatory authorities have been invited to participate under the supervision of NTSB group chairs. All party participation is strictly governed by established protocols to ensure the integrity, transparency, and independence of the investigative process.

Critical evidence has been secured at the accident site. The FDR and CVR have been recovered and transported to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for initial data extraction. The collapsed nose landing gear assembly has been stabilized, tagged, and is scheduled for transport to a secure examination facility. Photogrammetric documentation, debris field mapping, and runway surface condition assessments have been completed. Preliminary metallurgical and non-destructive testing of the landing gear components is planned to identify any pre-existing anomalies, corrosion, or fatigue indicators. All examinations will be conducted under controlled conditions, and findings will be documented in accordance with standard investigative procedures.

4. NEXT STEPS
The immediate priority for the investigative teams is the complete download, validation, and synchronization of flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder information. This data will be correlated with air traffic control transcripts, weather radar imagery, and maintenance records to establish a preliminary timeline of events. The Structures Group will conduct a detailed teardown and dimensional analysis of the nose landing gear and forward fuselage structures to assess load paths, stress concentrations, and potential failure modes. The Systems Group will evaluate the functionality of the flight control and hydraulic systems, with particular attention to any anomalies that may have influenced the aircraft’s handling characteristics during the approach and flare phases.

Additional investigative activities will include interviews with maintenance personnel, review of operator standard operating procedures for crosswind and gusty wind conditions, and an assessment of pilot training records related to adverse weather operations. The Human Performance Group will continue to evaluate crew resource management, decision-making processes, and environmental factors that may have influenced the flight crew’s actions. All data collection and analysis will be conducted with the understanding that initial observations are subject to change as the investigation progresses and as new evidence is integrated into the analytical framework.

A factual update will be issued within 30 days, pending the completion of recorder data analysis and initial structural examinations. Subsequent updates will be provided as significant findings are validated and as the investigation transitions from the preliminary phase to the detailed analysis stage. The NTSB emphasizes that all information contained in this document is preliminary, has not been peer-reviewed, and does not represent a determination of probable cause. The investigation remains ongoing, and all conclusions will be deferred until a comprehensive review of all available evidence is complete.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On August 15, 2021, at 14:32 Pacific Daylight Time (PDT), a Boeing 737-800, registration N737XK, experienced a hard landing with subsequent collapse of the nose landing gear (NLG) during a visual approach to Runway 27L at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (KSEA), Washington. The accident occurred at coordinates 47°26′58″N, 122°18′32″W, at an elevation of 433 feet mean sea level (MSL). The local time of the event corresponded to 21:32 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).

1.2 Aircraft and Operator
The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737-800, serial number 34567, manufactured in 2008. The aircraft was registered to a commercial air carrier operating under 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 121. The operator maintained a principal base of operations at KSEA and held an active Air Carrier Certificate and Operations Specifications authorizing scheduled domestic passenger service. Maintenance and line support services were contracted through multiple approved vendors, including Island Express Helicopters (IEH), which provided contracted ground handling, ramp coordination, and specialized simulator facility access for recurrent training modules. The helicopter operator, operating under 14 CFR Part 135, maintained a separate certificate but provided ancillary aviation support services under a service-level agreement with the Part 121 operator.

1.3 Nature of Flight
The flight was a scheduled domestic passenger service, designated as Flight 442, operating from San Francisco International Airport (KSFO) to Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (KSEA). The flight was conducted under instrument flight rules (IFR) transitioning to visual flight rules (VFR) for the final approach segment. The flight carried 156 passengers and 6 crewmembers. The flight departed KSFO at 12:48 PDT and was en route for approximately 1 hour and 44 minutes prior to the accident sequence. The flight was conducted in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121 operating requirements.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain
The captain, age 48, held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The captain possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on March 12, 2021, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 8,742 hours, with 3,418 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The captain completed the most recent line check on May 18, 2021, and the most recent recurrent simulator training on June 22, 2021. Training records indicated satisfactory performance in all evaluated maneuvers, including crosswind landing techniques, rejected landing procedures, and wind shear recovery. The captain was designated as a check airman and had completed instructor qualification training on February 10, 2020.

2.2 First Officer
The first officer, age 34, held an ATP certificate with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The first officer possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on April 5, 2021, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 2,185 hours, with 892 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The first officer completed the most recent line check on July 14, 2021, and the most recent recurrent simulator training on August 2, 2021. Training records indicated satisfactory completion of all required modules, including adverse weather operations and manual flight control techniques. The first officer was assigned as the pilot flying (PF) for the accident flight.

2.3 Duty and Rest Periods
Both flight crewmembers were on a 4-day trip pairing that commenced on August 12, 2021. The captain reported for duty at 09:15 PDT on August 15, 2021, and the first officer reported at 09:30 PDT. Both crewmembers had a minimum of 10 hours of uninterrupted rest prior to reporting, in compliance with 14 CFR 117.25. Duty time at the time of the accident was 5 hours and 17 minutes. Fatigue risk management system (FRMS) data indicated no reported fatigue-related concerns in the preceding 72 hours. Both crewmembers were medically fit for duty and had consumed no alcohol or medications within the 8-hour window preceding the flight, per 14 CFR 121.575.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Data
The accident aircraft was a Boeing 737-800, equipped with two CFM International CFM56-7B26 turbofan engines. The aircraft was configured for 160 passengers in a two-class layout. Total airframe time at the time of the accident was 42,158 flight hours, with 28,914 flight cycles. The aircraft was equipped with a digital flight data recorder (DFDR) and a cockpit voice recorder (CVR), both of which were recovered and downloaded. The aircraft was maintained under an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) in accordance with 14 CFR 121.369.

3.2 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
Maintenance records indicated compliance with all applicable airworthiness directives (ADs) and service bulletins. The aircraft was subject to a supplemental type certificate (STC) that modified the cabin configuration to include a mid-exit door plug in lieu of a standard Type III emergency exit. The mid-exit door plug was installed per STC ST00123SE and was inspected during the most recent C-check on June 10, 2021. Inspection records documented torque verification, seal integrity checks, and structural fastener inspections. All findings were within manufacturer-specified limits. The aircraft was also subject to structural maintenance programs aligned with damage tolerance requirements as mandated by 14 CFR 25.571. Fatigue crack propagation monitoring, corrosion prevention, and structural repair manual (SRM) compliance were documented in the operator’s maintenance tracking system. No deferred maintenance items related to the landing gear, flight controls, or fuselage structure were recorded in the 30 days preceding the accident.

3.3 Landing Gear and Structural Systems
The Boeing 737-800 is equipped with a retractable tricycle landing gear configuration. The nose landing gear assembly consists of a shock strut, torque links, drag brace, steering actuator, and dual-wheel axle. The main landing gear assemblies are mounted to the wing center section and feature a dual-wheel configuration with anti-skid braking systems. The aircraft’s primary structure, including fuselage sections 41 through 48, was manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems. Original equipment manufacturer (OEM) documentation and structural repair records were maintained in accordance with Boeing Service Bulletin 737-53A1234. The landing gear was last overhauled at 38,200 flight hours, with subsequent inspections performed at 500-hour intervals. The most recent landing gear functional test was conducted on July 28, 2021, with all parameters within operational limits.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Surface Observations
The KSEA automated weather observing system (AWOS) recorded the following conditions at 14:30 PDT: wind 270° at 22 knots, gusting to 35 knots; visibility 10 statute miles; scattered clouds at 3,500 feet MSL; temperature 24°C; dewpoint 12°C; altimeter setting 29.92 inches of mercury. The reported crosswind component for Runway 27L was calculated at 21 knots, with a headwind component of 7 knots. The gust factor was 13 knots, indicating rapidly fluctuating wind velocities.

4.2 Terminal Aerodrome Forecasts and Pilot Reports
The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) for KSEA, valid from 12:00 to 18:00 PDT, predicted wind 260° at 18 knots, gusting to 30 knots, with temporary conditions of wind 280° at 25 knots, gusting to 38 knots between 13:00 and 15:00 PDT. Pilot reports (PIREPs) received between 13:45 and 14:15 PDT indicated moderate turbulence on final approach to Runway 27L, with wind shear alerts reported by two preceding aircraft. The Boeing 737-800 flight crew received an automated wind shear warning from the airport’s low-level wind shear alert system (LLWAS) at 14:28 PDT, approximately 4 nautical miles from the runway threshold.

4.3 Wind Component Analysis
The demonstrated crosswind limit for the Boeing 737-800, as published in the Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM), is 33 knots. The operator’s standard operating procedures (SOPs) established a maximum crosswind limit of 30 knots for dry runway conditions and 25 knots for wet or contaminated runways. At the time of touchdown, the calculated crosswind component was 21 knots, with peak gusts reaching 35 knots. The gust-to-mean wind ratio exceeded 1.5, indicating highly variable wind conditions. The aircraft’s flight data recorder recorded a peak lateral acceleration of 0.42g during the final 10 seconds of approach, consistent with rapid wind direction and velocity fluctuations.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Impact Sequence and Wreckage Distribution
The aircraft touched down on Runway 27L at 14:32:08 PDT, approximately 1,200 feet beyond the displaced threshold. The initial touchdown was recorded at a vertical descent rate of 1,150 feet per minute, with a pitch attitude of -2.1 degrees. The main landing gear contacted the runway surface first, followed by a secondary impact of the nose landing gear 0.8 seconds later. The NLG collapsed aft and downward, resulting in forward fuselage contact with the runway surface. The aircraft slid approximately 1,850 feet before coming to rest on the runway centerline. Wreckage distribution was confined to the runway surface, with no debris field extending beyond the paved area. The aircraft sustained substantial damage as defined by 49 CFR 830.2, including NLG structural failure, forward fuselage skin abrasion, and lower lobe structural deformation.

5.2 Nose Landing Gear Examination
The collapsed NLG assembly was recovered and transported to the NTSB Materials Laboratory for detailed examination. The shock strut exhibited plastic deformation consistent with overload failure. The torque link upper and lower lugs showed evidence of tensile fracture, with fracture surfaces displaying ductile dimpling and no indications of fatigue cracking. The drag brace attachment pins were sheared, and the steering actuator housing was fractured at the mounting flange. Metallurgical analysis confirmed that the failure mode was consistent with a single-event overload exceeding the design ultimate load limit. No pre-existing cracks, corrosion, or manufacturing defects were identified. The NLG retraction actuator and position sensors were intact and showed no evidence of electrical or hydraulic anomalies prior to impact.

5.3 Fuselage and Cabin Systems
The forward fuselage section, including the nose cone and avionics bay, sustained abrasion and localized buckling. The mid-exit door plug remained secured, with no evidence of structural compromise or seal failure. The cabin floor beams in the forward section exhibited minor deformation, but the primary load path remained intact. Emergency evacuation slides deployed automatically upon NLG collapse, with all 162 occupants evacuating via the forward and overwing exits. The evacuation was completed in 82 seconds, with no serious injuries reported. The aircraft’s fire suppression system was not activated, and no post-impact fire occurred. The CVR and DFDR were recovered undamaged, and data extraction was completed within 48 hours of the accident.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Operator Policies and Training Programs
The operator’s Flight Operations Manual (FOM) and Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) required flight crews to execute a go-around if the aircraft exceeded a stabilized approach criteria at 1,000 feet above ground level (AGL) or if wind conditions exceeded published limits. Crosswind landing training was conducted in full-flight simulators, with emphasis on manual flight control techniques, rudder input timing, and wind gust compensation. The operator contracted recurrent simulator training modules through Island Express Helicopters (IEH), which maintained FAA-approved training devices under 14 CFR Part 142. Training records indicated that both flight crewmembers completed crosswind and wind shear recovery scenarios within the preceding 12 months. The operator’s safety management system (SMS) tracked wind-related approach deviations, with 14 reported events in the preceding 24 months, none of which resulted in structural damage.

6.2 Previous Similar Events
A review of NTSB and FAA databases identified 11 similar hard landing events involving Boeing 737-800 aircraft in crosswind conditions between 2015 and 2020. In 7 of these events, the NLG sustained structural damage, with 3 resulting in gear collapse. Common contributing factors included rapid wind direction shifts, delayed go-around decisions, and excessive vertical descent rates during flare. The FAA issued Safety Alert for Operators (SAFO) 18004 in 2018, emphasizing the importance of adhering to stabilized approach criteria and executing timely go-arounds in gusty crosswind conditions. The operator incorporated SAFO 18004 guidance into its training curriculum and revised its wind limit policy in 2019.

6.3 Regulatory Framework and Guidance
The accident aircraft was certified under 14 CFR Part 25, with structural design and maintenance requirements governed by 14 CFR 25.571, which establishes damage tolerance requirements for transport category airplanes. The operator’s maintenance program complied with 14 CFR 121.369 and 121.373, requiring continuous monitoring of structural integrity and fatigue-critical components. The Boeing 737-800 Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM) provided guidance for crosswind landings, recommending a crab-to-sideslip technique, increased approach speed by 5 to 10 knots in gusty conditions, and immediate go-around execution if the aircraft was not stabilized at 500 feet AGL. The operator’s operations specifications authorized operations in crosswind conditions up to 30 knots, with additional restrictions for wet or contaminated runways. All applicable airworthiness directives, service bulletins, and manufacturer recommendations were documented in the aircraft’s maintenance records. The investigation team reviewed all regulatory compliance documentation, training records, and operational data to establish the factual basis for the event sequence.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis conducted by the Structures and Materials Group, in coordination with the Flight Data Recorder (FDR) Group, regarding the nose landing gear (NLG) collapse and forward fuselage structural damage sustained by a Boeing 737-800, registration N738XX, during a hard landing event on August 15, 2021. The scope of this examination encompasses the physical and metallurgical evaluation of the NLG assembly, forward fuselage load-bearing structure, and associated hydraulic components, alongside the extraction, validation, and engineering interpretation of recorded flight data.

The physical examination of the recovered components was conducted between August 20 and August 27, 2021, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., and the Boeing Field Structural Test Facility in Seattle, Washington. The FDR and Quick Access Recorder (QAR) data were downloaded and analyzed at the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory on August 22, 2021. All examinations were performed in accordance with NTSB Investigative Procedures Manual (IPM) guidelines, ASTM E2375-18 (Ultrasonic Testing), AMS 2644 (Penetrant Inspection), and Boeing Document D6-17487 (Structural Repair Manual). The investigation was coordinated with engineering data provided by Spirit AeroSystems, the original equipment manufacturer for the forward fuselage and NLG bay structure.

2. BACKGROUND

The subject aircraft is a Boeing 737-800, serial number 34512, equipped with CFM56-7B26 engines and a standard 737NG landing gear configuration. The NLG assembly, Boeing Part Number 65-43210-1, Serial Number 88421, is a dual-wheel, trailing-link design featuring a 300M steel shock strut, 7075-T6 aluminum alloy torque links, and a Ti-6Al-4V titanium trunnion assembly. The trunnion interfaces with the forward fuselage structure at Station 240, transferring vertical, lateral, and drag loads into the primary longerons and bulkhead web. The forward fuselage, manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems, incorporates reinforced door cutouts and load-distribution doublers designed to comply with 14 CFR Part 25 certification requirements, including Section 25.783, which governs structural integrity, load path continuity, and fail-safe design criteria for fuselage doors and adjacent pressure bulkhead regions.

The aircraft accumulated 42,150 flight hours and 28,900 flight cycles at the time of the event. Maintenance records indicate the NLG was last overhauled at 38,200 cycles, with a subsequent eddy current inspection of the trunnion lugs and forward fuselage attachment points performed by Island Express Helicopters, a contracted non-destructive inspection (NDI) and structural repair facility, on March 12, 2019. The inspection was documented as compliant with Boeing Service Bulletin 737-32-1284 and Airworthiness Directive 2012-09-04, which mandates enhanced inspection intervals for NLG trunnion fatigue-prone zones and FDR data retention verification.

The FDR system is an L3Harris FA2100 solid-state recorder, certified under TSO-C124a, configured to record 88 parameters at 1 Hz and 16 high-rate parameters at 8 Hz. The system interfaces with the aircraft's data acquisition unit via a dedicated Maintenance Event Data (MED) plug, which provides direct access to raw PCM-encoded telemetry for post-flight analysis. The aircraft was operating under 14 CFR Part 121 at the time of the incident.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

The NLG assembly was recovered in a fully collapsed configuration, with the strut compressed to 18.2 inches (design maximum extension: 14.5 inches; design maximum compression: 12.0 inches). The left trunnion lug exhibited a complete transverse fracture, while the right lug remained partially attached with a 42° oblique crack propagation path. The forward fuselage NLG bay structure displayed localized buckling of the Station 240 bulkhead web, with permanent deformation measuring 14.3 mm aft and 8.7 mm left of the centerline. The torque link upper and lower bearings showed evidence of plastic deformation, with measured clearances exceeding the 0.005-inch service limit by 0.018 inches.

Fracture surface analysis of the left trunnion lug was conducted using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). The fracture morphology revealed a distinct fatigue initiation zone measuring 12.4 mm in length, located at the inner radius of the lug bore. Beach marks and fatigue striations were clearly visible, indicating progressive crack growth over an estimated 1,200 to 1,500 flight cycles. The final fracture zone, occupying 89.6 mm of the cross-section, exhibited ductile dimple rupture consistent with rapid overload. EDS analysis confirmed the base material as 300M steel (AMS 6415), with a measured hardness of 48.5 HRC (specification: 47-51 HRC). No evidence of hydrogen embrittlement, intergranular corrosion, or manufacturing defects was identified.

Ultrasonic thickness mapping of the forward fuselage longerons and bulkhead doublers revealed no subsurface cracking or delamination. Dye penetrant inspection (AMS 2644, Type II, Method C) of the NLG bay attachment fittings showed no additional crack indications beyond the primary trunnion failure site. Tensile coupon testing of recovered 7075-T6 aluminum torque link material yielded an ultimate tensile strength of 78.4 ksi and a yield strength of 68.1 ksi, both within Boeing D6-17487 allowable ranges.

Hydraulic system B pressure lines connected to the NLG steering and shimmy damper circuits were severed during the collapse. Residual fluid analysis indicated no contamination or degradation. The MED plug interface was utilized to extract raw telemetry from the FDR and cross-reference it with the aircraft's central maintenance computer (CMC) fault logs. All recorded parameters were validated against the Boeing FDR Parameter Mapping Document (PMD-737-800-REV14). Compliance with Airworthiness Directive 2012-09-04 was verified through maintenance log review, confirming that all required structural inspections and FDR data retention protocols were current at the time of the event.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

FDR and QAR data were synchronized using GPS timecode and radio altitude (RA) triggers. The data stream was decoded using NTSB-standard PCM demodulation software, with parameters filtered to remove high-frequency noise using a 4th-order Butterworth low-pass filter (cutoff: 10 Hz). The following key parameters were analyzed for the final approach and touchdown sequence:

- Radio Altitude (RA): 500 ft to 0 ft
- Indicated Airspeed (IAS): 148 KIAS to 132 KIAS
- Vertical Acceleration (Gz): 1.0g to 9.4g
- Pitch Attitude: +2.1° to -4.8°
- Roll Attitude: +1.2° to -6.4°
- NLG Strut Pressure: 1,850 PSI to 4,850 PSI
- Hydraulic System B Pressure: 3,000 PSI to 1,200 PSI
- Control Column Position: +4° to -12°
- Rudder Pedal Position: 0° to 18° left

At 500 ft RA, the aircraft was established on a 3.0° glidepath with a 12-knot steady crosswind from 280° and gusts to 38 knots. The SIC, who was the pilot flying, maintained a crab angle of approximately 8° to compensate for drift. At 50 ft RA, the aircraft transitioned to a wing-low sideslip configuration, with 14° of left aileron and 18° of left rudder applied. The touchdown occurred at 134 KIAS, with the main landing gear (MLG) contacting the runway first at 1.4g. The NLG contacted the runway 0.6 seconds later, at which point the vertical acceleration (Gz) registered 3.8g.

Within 0.8 seconds of NLG touchdown, Gz increased to 6.2g, coinciding with a rapid forward control column input of 12° by the SIC. The NLG strut pressure spiked to 4,850 PSI, exceeding the design limit of 3,200 PSI by 51.6%. At 1.4 seconds post-NLG touchdown, Gz peaked at 9.4g, and the FDR recorded a sudden loss of NLG strut pressure to 0 PSI, indicating structural failure. The aircraft's pitch attitude dropped to -4.8°, and the nose contacted the runway surface, resulting in forward fuselage scraping and NLG bay deformation.

The recorded data was compared against Boeing 737-800 Normal Operations Manual (NOM) parameters, which specify a maximum demonstrated crosswind component of 33 knots and a recommended touchdown Gz envelope of 1.2g to 1.6g. The 38-knot gust component, combined with the forward control input and elevated sink rate (calculated at 1,150 ft/min at 50 ft RA), generated vertical and lateral loads that exceeded the NLG trunnion's ultimate design strength. The FDR data correlates directly with the metallurgical findings: the fatigue-initiated crack in the left trunnion lug propagated rapidly under the 9.4g overload, resulting in catastrophic separation.

The MED plug extraction confirmed no FDR parameter dropouts or data corruption during the event sequence. All 88 recorded parameters maintained synchronization within ±0.05 seconds. The QAR data, sampled at 1 Hz, corroborated the high-rate FDR parameters, with minor deviations attributable to sampling rate differences. The SIC's control inputs, while within the physical limits of the control column travel, contributed to the rapid load transfer into the NLG structure during the post-touchdown phase.

5. SUMMARY

The specialist examination of the Boeing 737-800 nose landing gear and forward fuselage structure, in conjunction with FDR/QAR data analysis, yielded the following factual findings:

1. The left NLG trunnion lug failed due to fatigue crack propagation originating at the inner bore radius, with an estimated initiation period of 1,200 to 1,500 flight cycles. The final fracture occurred under a rapid overload condition.
2. Metallurgical analysis confirmed the trunnion material as 300M steel (AMS 6415) with mechanical properties and hardness values within manufacturer specifications. No evidence of corrosion, hydrogen embrittlement, or manufacturing anomalies was identified.
3. The forward fuselage NLG bay structure sustained localized buckling and permanent deformation consistent with a 9.4g vertical load event. The Station 240 bulkhead web and adjacent longerons remained structurally intact, with no secondary crack propagation detected.
4. FDR data indicates the aircraft touched down with a vertical acceleration of 3.8g, which rapidly increased to 9.4g within 1.4 seconds. The NLG strut pressure peaked at 4,850 PSI, exceeding the design limit of 3,200 PSI.
5. The recorded crosswind component reached 38 knots, exceeding the aircraft's demonstrated limit of 33 knots. The SIC applied 12° of forward control column and 18° of left rudder during the touchdown sequence, contributing to rapid load transfer into the NLG assembly.
6. All maintenance records, including inspections performed by Island Express Helicopters, were current and compliant with Airworthiness Directive 2012-09-04. The FDR system, accessed via the MED plug, functioned within certification parameters, with no data loss or parameter corruption.
7. The structural design of the forward fuselage and NLG attachment points complies with 14 CFR Part 25 requirements, including Section 25.783, with load path continuity and fail-safe design criteria met under normal operational conditions.

The physical, metallurgical, and recorded data findings are consistent with a structural overload event initiated by a hard landing in gusty crosswind conditions, resulting in fatigue-accelerated failure of the NLG trunnion assembly.

INTERVIEW OF MARCUS THORNE, LEAD MAINTENANCE INSPECTOR
Date: August 18, 2021
Time: 14:15 Local
Location: NTSB Field Office, Conference Room B, Regional Maintenance Base
Interviewer: Investigator Sarah Chen, NTSB Aviation Safety Board

Q: Please state your full name, current title, and your role relative to the incident on August 15th.

A: Yeah, sure. Marcus Thorne. I’m the Lead Maintenance Inspector for the line maintenance division here at the base. I’ve been with the airline for about eleven years now, mostly heavy checks and structural inspections. On the fifteenth, I was actually out on the ramp doing a routine fluid check on a different aircraft when Flight 442 came in. So I was an eyewitness to the arrival, and then I got pulled into the initial damage assessment team once the aircraft was secured and towed to the hangar.

Q: Walk me through what you observed from the moment you first noticed the aircraft on final approach.

A: Right. It was late afternoon. I’d say around 16:45, maybe 16:50. The wind was really picking up. We’d had gusts reported all day, crosswind component was hovering around twenty-five knots, maybe pushing thirty at times. I was over by the fuel farm, checking a refueler, when I heard the engines spooling up for final. You know how a 737 sounds on approach—steady, predictable, that low hum. But this one… it was different. The pitch was higher, like they were fighting it. I looked up and saw the aircraft, it was a -800, obviously, and it was crabbed pretty hard. The wings were dipping, just… rocking side to side. I remember thinking, “They’re gonna go around.” But they didn’t.

Q: Describe the touchdown and what happened immediately after.

A: Yeah. It hit the runway hard. I mean, really hard. You could hear it from where I was standing—maybe three hundred yards out. It wasn’t a normal thud. It was a sharp, metallic crack, followed by this… this grinding, tearing sound. The nose came down way too fast. I saw the nose gear just… fold. It didn’t bounce, it just collapsed inward. The nose dropped, sparks flew everywhere, and the whole airframe shuddered. It slid for a bit, maybe fifty, sixty feet, before it stopped. Then the engines spooled down. I grabbed my radio, called out “Mayday, aircraft down on runway two-seven,” or whatever the tower frequency was. I was running toward it with a couple of other line techs.

Q: What did you see once you reached the aircraft?

A: Smoke, mostly. Not fire, just… hydraulic fluid vaporizing on hot metal, I think. The nose was resting on the concrete. The forward fuselage was scuffed, obviously, but the main gear held. The evacuation slides deployed on the left side. I could hear the PA system crackling, then the flight attendants shouting, “Heads down, stay down,” and then “Evacuate, evacuate.” Passengers were coming out fast, but orderly. No panic, really. The crew did a good job. I helped direct a few folks away from the wing, just in case. Fire trucks were there in under two minutes. They sprayed the nose area as a precaution.

Q: You mentioned being pulled into the damage assessment. What was your role in that phase?

A: Right. Once the aircraft was cleared and towed to the maintenance bay—this was around 19:00, I think—we started the initial survey. My job was to document structural damage, check for hidden stress fractures, and verify the maintenance logs for any prior discrepancies. We had to follow the manufacturer’s hard landing checklist, obviously, but we also had to cross-reference a bunch of regulatory stuff. You know, with the 737 fleet, there’s always extra scrutiny.

Q: Can you elaborate on the regulatory and maintenance documentation you reviewed?

A: Yeah, sure. So, first thing, we pulled the aircraft’s maintenance records. We had to verify compliance with the latest airworthiness directives. Specifically, we checked AD 2012-09-04, which covers the fuel tank system inspections. I know it’s a bit older, but it’s still active, and we had to make sure the fuel tank wiring and venting were up to spec before we even thought about moving the aircraft. That ties into SFAR 88, the Special Federal Aviation Regulation for fuel tank safety. We’ve been running those checks religiously since it came out. I mean, back when I was at Island Express Helicopters, we didn’t deal with jet fuel tanks like this, but the principles are the same—containment, ignition prevention, all that.

Q: You mentioned SFAR 88 and AD 2012-09-04. Were there any other regulatory frameworks that guided your inspection?

A: Definitely. We’re a Part 121 operator, so everything we do has to align with those operational and maintenance standards. The hard landing triggered a mandatory structural review. We had to look at the forward fuselage, the door plug area, the bulkheads. I spent a good chunk of time inspecting the DOOR PLUG installation. You know, the one on the forward left side. It’s a critical pressure boundary. We checked the fasteners, the sealant, the alignment. Everything looked intact, but we still had to document it per the damage tolerance requirements. That’s… that’s a big one. The FAA’s really strict on that now. You can’t just eyeball it. You have to run the fatigue analysis, check the crack propagation limits, make sure the structure can handle the stress cycles.

Q: How does 14 CFR 25.783 factor into your assessment?

A: Oh, right. That’s the fuselage door regulation. It covers the design, installation, and inspection of doors and plugs. We had to verify that the DOOR PLUG met the load-bearing and sealing criteria under 14 CFR 25.783. Even though the hard landing was primarily a gear issue, the impact loads travel through the airframe. We had to make sure the door plug didn’t shift, that the latches weren’t compromised. I used a borescope to check the internal structure, and we ran a torque check on all the perimeter bolts. It was all within limits, but we still had to sign off on it. You know, in this business, if it’s not documented, it didn’t happen.

Q: Were there any discrepancies or concerns that stood out during your inspection?

A: Not really with the door or the fuel systems. The main issue was the nose gear. The strut was completely sheared, the torque links were bent, and there was some minor buckling on the forward pressure bulkhead. But structurally, the airframe held together. The crew’s handling of the crosswind was… well, it was tough. I’ve seen worse, but that gust was brutal. I talked to the captain later, briefly. He said the wind shear warning went off at about two hundred feet, and they tried to correct, but the downdraft just… it pushed them down. They didn’t have time to flare properly.

Q: Did you coordinate with any external organizations or contractors during the assessment?

A: Yeah, we brought in a structural engineering team from the OEM, and we also had a third-party NDT crew come in for ultrasonic testing. We also had to notify the FAA’s local FSDO, obviously. And, uh, we actually contracted a few of the ramp handling procedures to a local ground services company, but the maintenance side was all in-house. I did reach out to a former colleague at Island Express Helicopters, actually. They’ve got a great composite repair shop, and I just wanted to bounce some ideas off them about the forward fuselage skin. But ultimately, we handled it here.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add about the incident or your observations?

A: Just that… it was a tough day, but the system worked. The aircraft did what it was designed to do. The gear collapsed to absorb the energy, the fuselage stayed intact, the evacuation was clean. We followed the checklists, we referenced the regs, we documented everything. I mean, you can’t control the weather, but you can control how you respond. And honestly, the crew did everything right. The maintenance side, we just had to make sure the paperwork and the inspections were airtight. That’s the job.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Thorne. We’ll follow up if we need clarification.

A: Yeah, no problem. I’ll be around.

FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY
AIRCRAFT CERTIFICATION SERVICE
TRANSPORT STANDARDS BRANCH

DATE: October 14, 2023
TO: National Transportation Safety Board, Office of Aviation Safety
FROM: Federal Aviation Administration, Aircraft Certification Service, Transport Standards Branch
SUBJECT: RESPONSE TO NTSB SAFETY RECOMMENDATION A-22-045 AND COMPLIANCE ASSESSMENT REGARDING POST-ACCIDENT AIRWORTHINESS DIRECTIVE IMPLEMENTATION
REFERENCE: NTSB Accident Number DCA21MA087; Docket No. FAA-2022-0891; AD 2022-14-08

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This correspondence constitutes the Federal Aviation Administration’s formal response to National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Safety Recommendation A-22-045, issued in conjunction with the investigation of the August 15, 2021, accident involving a Boeing 737-800, registration N738IE, operated by Island Express. The referenced event, designated under NTSB Accident Number DCA21MA087, involved a hard landing during a gusty crosswind approach that resulted in the collapse of the nose landing gear (NLG) and substantial airframe damage. All occupants evacuated without injury. This document addresses compliance with Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2022-14-08, applicable to Boeing 737-600/700/800/900 series aircraft, and evaluates the operator’s adherence to 14 CFR Part 121 maintenance and operational requirements, with specific reference to structural integrity mandates, fuel system safety protocols under Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88, and the installation and inspection criteria for the Main Equipment Deck (MED) Plug assembly.

2. BACKGROUND
The regulatory framework governing the continued airworthiness of transport category aircraft is established under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR), specifically Parts 21, 25, 43, and 121. The Boeing 737-800 type certificate (TC) holder is required to maintain compliance with 14 CFR 25.571, which mandates damage tolerance requirements for principal structural elements, including landing gear attachment points, fuselage pressure bulkheads, and primary load-bearing longerons. Following the August 15, 2021, event, the FAA initiated a comprehensive review of the operator’s maintenance program, flight operations manual, and compliance history.

Historically, the 737-800 fleet has been subject to multiple ADs addressing fatigue cracking in the NLG trunnion and forward fuselage structure. AD 2018-12-09 previously mandated repetitive eddy current inspections of the NLG forward trunnion fitting. Concurrently, Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 (SFAR 88) established mandatory fuel tank system review and modification requirements to mitigate ignition sources, which intersects with structural routing and equipment bay configurations, including the MED Plug installation. The MED Plug, a structural and environmental sealing component manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems, is installed in accordance with Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) SA03891SE and is subject to specific inspection intervals under the operator’s approved Maintenance Review Board Report (MRBR) and Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) provisions.

Island Express, as a Part 121 certificate holder, is obligated under 14 CFR 121.368 and 14 CFR 121.373 to maintain an FAA-approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) and ensure all personnel are trained in accordance with 14 CFR 121.401. The operator’s CAMP must incorporate all applicable ADs, service bulletins, and manufacturer-recommended structural inspection programs. Prior to the subject accident, the FAA had issued Safety Recommendation A-19-012, which highlighted deficiencies in crosswind landing technique training and NLG load monitoring for high-cycle 737-800 aircraft. The current investigation expands upon those findings, particularly regarding the interaction between operational exceedances, structural fatigue accumulation, and the adequacy of existing damage tolerance requirements.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive audit of Island Express’s maintenance records, flight data monitoring (FDM) parameters, and engineering evaluations reveals partial compliance with applicable regulatory mandates. The operator’s CAMP incorporated AD 2018-12-09; however, the inspection interval for the NLG forward trunnion was extended beyond the manufacturer’s recommended threshold without an approved alternative method of compliance (AMOC) from the Aircraft Certification Service (AIR-100). This deviation contravenes 14 CFR 121.373(a)(2), which requires strict adherence to AD compliance timelines unless explicitly authorized.

Structural analysis of the recovered NLG components indicates that the collapse was precipitated by a combination of excessive vertical and lateral load factors during the gusty crosswind touchdown, compounded by undetected fatigue cracking at the trunnion lug interface. The damage tolerance requirements outlined in 14 CFR 25.571 were not fully satisfied due to the operator’s failure to implement enhanced inspection protocols for high-cycle airframes operating in high-wind environments. Furthermore, the MED Plug assembly, which interfaces with the forward equipment bay and adjacent structural longerons, exhibited minor fastener elongation consistent with repeated high-G loading events. While the plug itself did not fail, its installation documentation revealed discrepancies in torque verification records, raising concerns regarding compliance with 14 CFR 43.13(a) and the manufacturer’s structural repair manual (SRM) specifications.

Regulatory oversight actions included a targeted surveillance audit conducted by the FAA Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) and Principal Operations Inspector (POI) under 14 CFR 121.9. The audit identified systemic gaps in the operator’s risk assessment methodology for adverse weather operations and inadequate integration of FDM exceedance data into the CAMP. Additionally, the FAA determined that the operator’s MMEL deferral practices for NLG-related discrepancies lacked sufficient engineering justification, potentially compromising the airworthiness baseline.

A critical gap in the current regulatory framework pertains to the harmonization of operational exceedance reporting with structural inspection scheduling. While 14 CFR 121.703 requires operators to report certain mechanical irregularities, there is no explicit mandate requiring automatic recalibration of damage tolerance inspection intervals following documented hard landing events exceeding manufacturer-defined load limits. This regulatory deficiency was further exacerbated by the absence of a unified tracking mechanism for Spirit AeroSystems-manufactured structural components, which are subject to varying service life limitations depending on the specific STC or TC configuration.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
In response to the identified deficiencies and in accordance with NTSB Safety Recommendation A-22-045, the FAA mandates the following corrective actions and compliance timelines:

a. Immediate Structural Inspection and AMOC Implementation: Island Express shall conduct a one-time detailed inspection of all Boeing 737-800 NLG forward trunnion fittings and associated attachment lugs in accordance with Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 737-32A1456, Revision 2. This inspection must be completed within 60 calendar days of this memorandum’s issuance. Any findings of cracking or deformation exceeding 0.010 inches shall require immediate grounding and repair per 14 CFR 121.373 and the applicable SRM. An AMOC request for extended inspection intervals must be submitted to AIR-100 with supporting fatigue analysis data.

b. MED Plug Verification and Documentation Compliance: All aircraft within the operator’s fleet shall undergo a torque verification and fastener integrity inspection of the MED Plug assembly, manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems, in accordance with STC SA03891SE maintenance instructions. Discrepancies shall be rectified within 30 days. The operator shall revise its CAMP to include mandatory photographic documentation and dual-signature verification for all structural fastener installations, ensuring compliance with 14 CFR 43.13(a) and 14 CFR 121.368.

c. Operational and Training Enhancements: Island Express shall implement a revised crosswind and gusty wind landing training module, incorporating simulator-based exceedance scenarios and mandatory FDM review protocols. The operator shall establish a formalized process to automatically trigger enhanced structural inspections following any recorded vertical acceleration exceeding 2.1G or lateral load factor exceeding 0.8G during landing. This process shall be integrated into the CAMP within 90 days and submitted to the FAA for approval under 14 CFR 121.373.

d. Regulatory Framework Review and SFAR 88 Alignment: The FAA will initiate a rulemaking action to amend 14 CFR Part 121 to require mandatory post-exceedance structural assessment protocols for transport category aircraft. Concurrently, the agency will evaluate the intersection of damage tolerance requirements and fuel system safety mandates under Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 to ensure that equipment bay modifications, including MED Plug installations, do not compromise structural load paths or ignition source mitigation measures. A preliminary regulatory impact analysis will be published in the Federal Register within 180 days.

e. Compliance Verification and Follow-Up Schedule: The FAA Principal Maintenance Inspector shall conduct a follow-up audit within 120 days to verify implementation of all corrective actions. Subsequent surveillance will occur at 6-month intervals until three consecutive audit cycles demonstrate sustained compliance. The operator shall submit quarterly compliance reports to the FAA Aircraft Certification Service, detailing inspection results, training completion rates, and FDM exceedance trends.

This memorandum constitutes the FAA’s formal response to the referenced NTSB safety recommendation and establishes the regulatory compliance baseline for continued operation of the affected fleet. Failure to adhere to the prescribed timelines and corrective measures may result in enforcement action pursuant to 14 CFR 13.19 and potential suspension of the operator’s Part 121 certificate under 14 CFR 121.5.

Respectfully submitted,

Director, Transport Standards Branch
Aircraft Certification Service
