1. SYNOPSIS
On August 15, 2021, at approximately 1432 local time, a Boeing 737-800, registered as NXXXXX, experienced a hard landing that resulted in the collapse of the nose landing gear during a gusty crosswind approach at a regional commercial airport. The aircraft, operated under Part 121 air carrier regulations, sustained substantial damage to the forward fuselage and lower airframe structure, though all passengers and crew members successfully evacuated without serious injury. This preliminary procedural document summarizes initial factual data, establishes the investigative scope, and outlines early procedural determinations. All information contained herein is subject to revision as technical examinations progress and additional data are validated.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary information indicates that the flight was conducting a scheduled passenger operation when it encountered a dynamic wind environment during the final approach phase. Initial data retrieved from the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) suggest that the aircraft descended at a vertical rate exceeding standard touchdown parameters, with lateral drift correction inputs recorded in the seconds preceding ground contact. The second in command (SIC), who was occupying the right seat, reported to investigators that the approach remained stabilized until approximately 500 feet above ground level, at which point wind shear alerts were activated and manual control inputs were increased to maintain runway alignment.

Weather observations recorded at the time of the event indicate surface winds from 270 degrees at 18 knots, gusting to 28 knots, with a crosswind component that approached the operational limits documented in the aircraft flight manual. Initial witness accounts from air traffic control personnel and ground observers describe a firm touchdown followed by a pronounced forward pitch and a scraping sound consistent with forward fuselage contact. The aircraft subsequently came to rest on the runway centerline, approximately 2,400 feet beyond the threshold.

A preliminary damage assessment conducted by NTSB structural specialists revealed substantial deformation to the nose landing gear assembly, forward pressure bulkhead, and lower forward fuselage skin. The main landing gear remained extended and appeared structurally intact. Emergency evacuation slides were deployed, and cabin crew initiated standard egress procedures. Initial examination of the cabin emergency systems, including the MED plug (Medical Evacuation Door plug) and associated deployment mechanisms, indicates that the equipment functioned as designed, though a detailed functional analysis is required to confirm full compliance with 14 CFR 121.344. Maintenance records and operational logs are currently being reviewed to assess compliance with Part 121 requirements and to evaluate the applicability of structural certification standards, including 14 CFR 25.571 (Damage-Tolerance and Fatigue Evaluation of Structure) and 14 CFR 25.783 (Fuselage Doors), to the observed damage patterns.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The National Transportation Safety Board has activated multiple investigative groups to address the technical and operational aspects of this event. The Operations, Structures, Systems, and Human Performance groups have been formally established and are currently conducting initial data collection, documentation, and interviews. The Operations group is focusing on flight crew training records, dispatch documentation, and approach procedures, while the Structures group is conducting a detailed survey of the airframe, with particular attention to the nose gear attachment points and forward fuselage load paths. The Systems group is tasked with the readout of the FDR and CVR, as well as the examination of flight control and landing gear extension systems.

Parties to the investigation include representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration, the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, the operator, and the pilot union. Island Express Helicopters (hereinafter referred to as IEH) has been identified as a contracted ground support and maintenance coordination entity for the operator’s regional facilities and has been included in the investigative party structure to provide relevant operational context and facility records. All parties have been briefed on the preliminary scope and are operating under the established NTSB party system protocols.

Evidence secured to date includes the flight data and cockpit voice recorders, which have been transported to the NTSB laboratory for readout and analysis. The aircraft wreckage has been secured in place, and a comprehensive photographic and laser scan survey has been completed to document the final resting position and damage distribution. Maintenance logs, crew duty records, and weather data packages have been collected and are undergoing preliminary review. Planned examinations include a teardown of the collapsed nose landing gear assembly, metallurgical analysis of fractured components, and a functional evaluation of the flight control surfaces and hydraulic systems. The investigation team will also conduct a detailed review of the operator’s crosswind landing procedures and training curricula to determine alignment with current regulatory guidance.

4. NEXT STEPS
The investigative groups will continue to process and analyze the secured evidence over the coming weeks. The Systems group anticipates completing the initial FDR and CVR data extraction within 14 days, after which a preliminary data summary will be distributed to the party representatives. The Structures group will coordinate with the manufacturer to develop a teardown plan for the nose landing gear and forward fuselage components, with metallurgical testing scheduled to commence upon completion of the non-destructive examinations. The Operations group will conduct follow-up interviews with flight crew, cabin crew, and air traffic control personnel to clarify the sequence of events during the approach and landing phases.

A procedural review will be conducted to ensure that all investigative activities remain aligned with the established scope and that regulatory compliance assessments, particularly those pertaining to 14 CFR 25.571, 14 CFR 25.783, and Part 121 operational standards, are thoroughly documented. The investigation team will also evaluate the need for additional specialized testing, including wind tunnel simulations or flight simulator reconstructions, to better understand the aerodynamic and control dynamics present during the final approach.

All findings documented in this preliminary report are subject to revision as additional data becomes available and technical examinations progress. No conclusions regarding operational performance, maintenance practices, or probable cause have been reached at this stage. The NTSB will issue subsequent updates as the investigation advances, with a comprehensive factual report anticipated within 12 to 18 months, pending the completion of all technical analyses and party reviews.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On August 15, 2021, at 1432:18 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), a Boeing 737-800, registration N738IE, experienced a hard landing that resulted in the collapse of the nose landing gear during the landing roll. The accident occurred on Runway 27L at Coastal Regional Airport (KCRG), located at latitude 30.3321° N, longitude 81.5144° W, elevation 30 feet mean sea level (MSL). The aircraft was operating under instrument flight rules (IFR) on a scheduled domestic passenger service. The flight originated from Orlando International Airport (KMCO) and was en route to KCRG.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator Identification
The aircraft was owned and operated by Island Express, a certificated air carrier conducting scheduled domestic operations under FAA oversight. The operator’s certificate number was IEX-121-044. The aircraft was configured for 189 passengers in a single-class layout, with a maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) of 174,200 pounds. At the time of the accident, the aircraft was operating at a landing weight of 142,850 pounds, with a center of gravity (CG) position of 24.1 percent mean aerodynamic chord (MAC).

1.3 Flight Operations Classification
The flight was conducted in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121, specifically under the provisions governing scheduled domestic passenger operations. All operational, maintenance, and training activities were subject to the regulatory oversight of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) under the applicable sections of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations. The operator’s operations specifications (OpSpecs) authorized the use of Boeing 737-800 aircraft for domestic route structures, with specific limitations regarding crosswind components, runway surface conditions, and minimum equipment list (MEL) deferrals.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Experience
The captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, certificate number 1234567, with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The captain possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on May 10, 2021, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 8,450 hours, with 3,210 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The captain had completed the required recurrent training and proficiency check on June 12, 2021, in accordance with 14 CFR 121.433. The captain’s duty time on the day of the accident was 6 hours and 14 minutes, well within the limitations prescribed by 14 CFR 117.

2.2 Second in Command (SIC) Qualifications and Experience
The SIC held a commercial pilot certificate with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings, along with an instrument rating. The SIC’s certificate number was 7654321, and a first-class medical certificate was issued on April 22, 2021. Total flight time was 2,890 hours, with 1,140 hours in the Boeing 737-800. The second-in-command had successfully completed the operator’s line-oriented flight training (LOFT) and simulator evaluation on July 5, 2021. The SIC’s logbook reflected 42 landings in the preceding 90 days, meeting the recency requirements of 14 CFR 121.439.

2.3 Recent Training and Proficiency Records
Both flight crewmembers were current and qualified for the flight. Training records indicated that the captain and SIC had completed a crosswind landing module during their most recent simulator session, which included gusty wind conditions up to 25 knots with 15-knot gusts. The operator’s training manual specified that all flight crewmembers must demonstrate proficiency in manual landings under adverse wind conditions at least once per training cycle. The simulator evaluation included scenarios involving wind shear alerts, delayed flare initiation, and manual thrust management. No discrepancies were noted in the crew’s recent flight experience or duty time records. The SIC’s performance during the evaluation was documented as satisfactory, with specific emphasis on rudder coordination and aileron input during crosswind approaches.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Aircraft Data
The accident aircraft was a Boeing 737-800, manufacturer serial number 34567, manufactured on March 14, 2012. The aircraft was equipped with two CFM International CFM56-7B26 turbofan engines, each rated at 26,300 pounds of thrust. At the time of the accident, the airframe had accumulated 41,230 total flight hours and 28,910 total flight cycles. The aircraft was registered to Island Express and operated under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) approved by the FAA. The aircraft’s weight and balance records were current, and the load sheet indicated compliance with all structural and operational limitations.

3.2 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
The aircraft’s maintenance records were reviewed and found to be current. The most recent heavy maintenance check (C-check) was completed on May 20, 2021, at 40,890 flight hours. All applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) were complied with, including AD 2018-12-05 regarding main landing gear trunnion inspections and AD 2020-04-11 concerning engine pylon fastener torque verification. The aircraft was in compliance with SFAR 88, which addresses fuel tank system fault tolerance evaluation and ignition source prevention. Documentation confirmed that the fuel tank flammability reduction system (FTFRS) was operational and had been inspected per the manufacturer’s service bulletin. The operator’s maintenance tracking system indicated zero open deferred items at the time of departure.

3.3 Landing Gear and Structural Systems
The Boeing 737-800 is equipped with a retractable tricycle landing gear configuration. The nose landing gear (NLG) consists of a dual-wheel assembly, shock strut, steering actuator, and retraction mechanism. Maintenance logs indicated that the NLG shock strut was serviced on July 10, 2021, with nitrogen pressure and hydraulic fluid levels verified within manufacturer specifications. The main landing gear (MLG) had undergone a detailed inspection on June 15, 2021, with no anomalies reported. The aircraft’s structural design complies with 14 CFR 25.571, which establishes damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation requirements for transport category airplanes. The landing gear attachment points were inspected during the C-check, and all fasteners were torqued to specification.

3.4 Fuselage and Door Plug Configuration
The fuselage was manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems and delivered to Boeing for final assembly. The aircraft was equipped with a mid-exit door plug installed at station 1015, which was configured in accordance with the operator’s cabin layout requirements. The door plug assembly was inspected during the most recent C-check, and all fasteners, latches, and sealing mechanisms were verified to be within tolerance. No discrepancies were noted in the door plug maintenance records. The plug was not involved in the accident sequence and remained secured throughout the event. The fuselage manufacturer’s structural analysis confirmed that the mid-exit door plug met all static and fatigue load requirements under 14 CFR Part 25.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Weather Overview
On August 15, 2021, a stationary frontal boundary extended across the southeastern United States, contributing to unstable atmospheric conditions. A low-pressure system located approximately 150 nautical miles west of the accident site generated convective activity and enhanced low-level wind shear. Surface observations indicated a temperature of 31°C (88°F) with a dew point of 24°C (75°F), resulting in a relative humidity of 72%. The density altitude at the time of the approach was calculated at 1,850 feet, which marginally reduced aircraft performance margins during the flare and touchdown phases.

4.2 Airport Weather Observations (METAR/TAF)
The automated weather observing system (AWOS) at KCRG recorded the following METAR at 1425 EDT: KCRG 151425Z 24018G28KT 10SM FEW035 SCT050 BKN080 31/24 A2992. The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) issued at 1100 EDT predicted winds from 230° at 15 knots, gusting to 25 knots, with temporary conditions of 240° at 20 knots, gusting to 30 knots, between 1300 and 1600 EDT. The crosswind component for Runway 27L was calculated at approximately 16 knots, with a headwind component of 12 knots. The runway surface was dry, and braking action was reported as good by preceding traffic.

4.3 Pilot Weather Reports and Wind Shear Alerts
A pilot report (PIREP) received at 1410 EDT from a preceding aircraft indicated moderate turbulence on final approach and a 10-knot wind shift at 500 feet above ground level (AGL). The airport’s low-level wind shear alert system (LLWAS) recorded a 12-knot wind speed differential between the runway threshold and midfield sensors at 1428 EDT. The flight crew acknowledged the LLWAS alert and the preceding PIREP during the approach briefing. The aircraft’s flight data recorder (FDR) indicated that the indicated airspeed fluctuated between 138 and 145 knots during the final approach segment, consistent with the reported gusty conditions. The vertical speed indicator recorded a descent rate of 850 feet per minute at 50 feet AGL, increasing to 1,120 feet per minute at 10 feet AGL.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Impact Site and Wreckage Distribution
The aircraft touched down on Runway 27L at 1432:18 EDT, approximately 1,200 feet beyond the threshold. The initial touchdown was recorded on the main landing gear, followed by a rapid descent of the nose section. The nose landing gear collapsed upon initial contact with the runway surface, resulting in the forward fuselage impacting the pavement. The aircraft continued to slide for approximately 850 feet before coming to rest aligned with the runway centerline. Wreckage distribution was confined to a linear path measuring 1,200 feet in length and 45 feet in width. No debris was scattered beyond the runway boundaries. Tire marks on the runway surface indicated a 14-degree crab angle at touchdown, with subsequent yaw correction inputs recorded by the FDR.

5.2 Nose Landing Gear Examination
Post-accident examination of the nose landing gear revealed that the shock strut had fully compressed, and the upper cylinder had fractured at the trunnion attachment point. The fracture surface exhibited characteristics consistent with an overload failure, with no evidence of pre-existing fatigue cracks or corrosion. The steering actuator was sheared from its mounting bracket, and the retraction linkages were bent beyond serviceable limits. The dual-wheel assembly remained attached to the axle, with both tires deflated due to impact forces. The NLG collapse sequence was consistent with a high vertical descent rate combined with a forward pitching moment during touchdown. Metallurgical analysis of the fractured trunnion pin confirmed that the material properties met original equipment manufacturer (OEM) specifications.

5.3 Fuselage and Systems Damage Assessment
The forward fuselage sustained substantial damage, including buckling of the lower skin panels, deformation of the avionics bay structure, and separation of the nose radome. The mid-exit door plug remained intact and showed no signs of structural compromise or seal failure. The main landing gear assemblies were inspected and found to be within manufacturer specifications, with no evidence of structural failure or abnormal wear. The engine pylons, wing spars, and empennage structures were examined and determined to be undamaged. Fuel system components were inspected for leaks, and no fuel spillage was observed. The aircraft’s emergency locator transmitter (ELT) activated automatically upon impact and transmitted a signal to the Cospas-Sarsat satellite network. Hydraulic system A and B reservoirs were intact, with no evidence of fluid loss prior to impact.

5.4 Evacuation and Emergency Response
The flight crew initiated an emergency evacuation at 1433:45 EDT. All 178 passengers and 6 crewmembers evacuated via the forward and aft passenger doors, as well as the overwing exits. The evacuation was completed in 4 minutes and 12 seconds, with no serious injuries reported. Airport rescue and firefighting (ARFF) personnel arrived on scene within 2 minutes of the initial impact. Fire suppression foam was applied to the forward fuselage as a precautionary measure. The operator’s emergency response plan was activated in accordance with 14 CFR 121.344, which requires operators to establish and maintain procedures for emergency evacuation and passenger safety. Post-evacuation medical screening identified 14 passengers with minor abrasions and 2 crewmembers with sprained wrists, all of whom were treated on site and released.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Operator Policies and Crosswind Limitations
Island Express’s operations specifications (OpSpecs) and flight operations manual (FOM) established a maximum demonstrated crosswind component of 33 knots for the Boeing 737-800. The operator’s policy required flight crews to consider wind gusts, runway conditions, and aircraft weight when determining landing feasibility. The FOM specified that if the crosswind component exceeded 25 knots with gusts greater than 10 knots above the steady-state value, a go-around or diversion to an alternate airport was recommended. The flight crew’s approach briefing documented the wind conditions, and the captain elected to continue the approach based on the aircraft’s weight and runway length available. The operator’s standard operating procedures (SOPs) emphasized the use of a wing-low technique, with aileron input into the wind and opposite rudder to maintain runway alignment.

6.2 Regulatory Framework and Compliance
The accident aircraft and operator were subject to the requirements of 14 CFR Part 121, which governs the certification and operation of domestic, flag, and supplemental air carriers. Compliance with 14 CFR 121.344 was verified through the operator’s emergency procedures manual and training records. The aircraft’s structural design and maintenance program adhered to 14 CFR 25.571, which mandates damage tolerance evaluations and fatigue testing for primary structures. Additionally, the operator’s fuel tank safety program was developed in accordance with SFAR 88, ensuring that ignition source prevention measures were implemented and maintained. The mid-exit door plug configuration was certified under the original type design and met all applicable airworthiness standards. The operator’s quality assurance program conducted quarterly audits of maintenance and flight operations, with all findings documented and closed within regulatory timeframes.

6.3 Historical Incident Data and Safety Recommendations
A review of NTSB and FAA databases identified 14 similar hard landing events involving Boeing 737-800 aircraft between 2010 and 2020, with 6 resulting in nose landing gear collapse. Common contributing factors included gusty crosswind conditions, high vertical descent rates, and delayed flare initiation. The manufacturer issued a service bulletin in 2019 recommending enhanced pilot training for manual landings in turbulent conditions and revised crosswind landing techniques. The operator had incorporated these recommendations into its training curriculum. No outstanding safety recommendations were applicable to this specific event. The FAA issued an advisory circular in 2020 emphasizing the importance of stabilized approach criteria and wind shear recognition during final approach.

6.4 Manufacturer and Supplier Documentation
Boeing’s flight crew operations manual (FCOM) provided guidance for crosswind landings, emphasizing the use of a wing-low technique and maintaining directional control through rudder and aileron inputs. The manual specified that touchdown should occur on the upwind main gear first, followed by a controlled lowering of the nose gear. Spirit AeroSystems provided structural analysis data confirming that the forward fuselage and door plug assembly were designed to withstand loads exceeding the maximum design landing weight. The aircraft’s maintenance program, as approved by the FAA, included periodic inspections of the nose landing gear shock strut and trunnion fittings. All documentation was reviewed and found to be consistent with regulatory requirements and manufacturer specifications. The operator’s technical library contained the latest revisions of the aircraft maintenance manual (AMM), fault isolation manual (FIM), and illustrated parts catalog (IPC), all of which were accessible to maintenance personnel at the time of the accident.

1. INTRODUCTION
This report documents the factual findings of the specialist examination conducted by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Structures Group, with technical support from the Materials Laboratory and Flight Data Recorder (FDR) Group, regarding the nose landing gear (NLG) collapse of a Boeing 737-800, registration N737XX, following a hard landing on August 15, 2021. The scope of the examination encompassed the physical inspection, dimensional measurement, non-destructive inspection (NDI), metallurgical evaluation, and flight data parameter analysis of the NLG assembly, associated airframe attachment points, and recorded operational telemetry. The primary laboratory examination was conducted between September 12 and October 4, 2021, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., with supplemental field documentation collected at the accident site on August 16, 2021. Items examined included the NLG strut assembly (Boeing P/N 65-43210-123, S/N 88421), torque link assembly (P/N 65-43215-45, S/N 77103), drag brace (P/N 65-43220-89, S/N 99214), forward and aft trunnion fittings, and the associated FDR and Quick Access Recorder (QAR) data modules. All examinations were performed in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols, Boeing Service Bulletins, and applicable ASTM/AMS material testing standards.

2. BACKGROUND
The Boeing 737-800 is a twin-engine, narrow-body transport category aircraft certified under 14 CFR Part 25, Amendment 25-108. The NLG system is designed to absorb landing impact energy through an oleo-pneumatic shock strut, maintain directional control during ground operations, and retract into the forward fuselage bay. The primary load-bearing components are manufactured from 7075-T7351 aluminum alloy forgings and 4340 steel alloy forgings, heat-treated to a minimum tensile strength of 180 ksi per AMS 2759/1 and Boeing BAC5000 specifications. The design certification basis requires the NLG to withstand a limit vertical sink rate of 10 ft/sec (3.05 m/s) at maximum design landing weight (146,300 lbs) without permanent deformation, and an ultimate load factor of 1.5 times the limit load. The system incorporates a dual-chamber shock absorber with nitrogen precharge pressure of 1,850 ± 50 PSI at 70°F, and hydraulic fluid (MIL-PRF-5606) for damping.

Maintenance records indicate the subject aircraft accumulated 42,118 flight hours and 28,945 flight cycles at the time of the accident. The most recent heavy maintenance visit, including a 6-year/12,000-cycle landing gear overhaul, was completed on March 14, 2020, by Island Express Helicopters, operating under FAA Part 145 Repair Station Certificate No. IEH-4421. The overhaul included strut disassembly, seal replacement, NDI of all primary structural members, and reassembly per Boeing Maintenance Planning Document (MPD) 737-800, Task 32-11-00-000-801. All maintenance actions were documented in accordance with 14 CFR 121.344, which mandates approved inspection programs and maintenance record retention for air carrier operations. Notably, the maintenance logbook contained a cross-referenced work order (WO-8842) that erroneously cited CFM International LEAP-1B engine installation procedures during a routine engine mount inspection; however, the aircraft was equipped with CFM56-7B26 engines (S/N 784421/784422), and the LEAP-1B reference was determined to be an administrative documentation error with no structural or operational impact on the NLG system.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS
The NLG assembly was recovered from the accident site and transported to the NTSB laboratory in a stabilized configuration. Initial visual inspection revealed catastrophic failure of the forward trunnion fitting (P/N 65-43225-11, S/N 88102) and complete separation of the drag brace from the lower shock strut cylinder. The strut cylinder exhibited severe axial compression, with a measured collapsed length of 14.2 inches, compared to the nominal extended length of 38.5 inches. The torque link assembly remained intact but showed plastic deformation at the upper and lower bearing interfaces, with measured angular deflection of 18.5° from the neutral axis.

Dimensional measurements were performed using calibrated coordinate measuring machine (CMM) equipment (Zeiss CONTURA G2, ±0.0002 in accuracy). The forward trunnion lug exhibited a through-thickness fracture originating at the inner radius of the forward bolt hole (Ø1.125 in). Fracture surface analysis revealed a classic fatigue initiation site measuring approximately 0.15 in², characterized by concentric beach marks and progressive crack growth. The final fracture zone, occupying approximately 65% of the cross-sectional area, displayed ductile dimple rupture morphology consistent with rapid overload. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) at 500x magnification confirmed intergranular cracking in the fatigue region, with secondary cracking along grain boundaries.

Metallurgical analysis was conducted per ASTM E3 and AMS 2680. A representative cross-section of the trunnion fitting was extracted and prepared for optical microscopy. The microstructure exhibited a fully recrystallized grain structure typical of 7075-T7351 aluminum alloy, with an average grain size of 45 μm. Hardness testing (Rockwell B scale) yielded an average value of 88.5 HRB, consistent with the T7351 temper specification (85–92 HRB). Chemical composition analysis via optical emission spectroscopy (OES) confirmed compliance with AMS 4045, with measured values of Zn: 5.82%, Mg: 2.41%, Cu: 1.58%, and Cr: 0.21%. No evidence of corrosion, hydrogen embrittlement, or manufacturing defects was identified.

Non-destructive inspection of the remaining NLG components was performed using eddy current (per Boeing BAC5650) and ultrasonic testing (per ASTM E114). The aft trunnion fitting, shock strut cylinder, and piston rod exhibited no detectable discontinuities. The drag brace clevis pin (P/N 65-43230-05) showed minor galling on the bearing surface, with a maximum material loss of 0.003 in, well within the allowable wear limit of 0.010 in per Boeing Structural Repair Manual (SRM) 32-11-00.

Photographic documentation (NTSB Photo Log Nos. 2021-08-15-001 through 2021-08-15-047) captures the fracture morphology, dimensional measurements, and component orientations. All measurements were verified by dual independent technicians and recorded in the NTSB Engineering Data Management System (EDMS).

4. DATA ANALYSIS
Flight data was extracted from the aircraft’s solid-state FDR (Honeywell SSFDR, P/N 060-0800-00, S/N 992144) and QAR (Teledyne QAR, P/N 822-1234-00, S/N 771022) using NTSB-approved data recovery protocols. The FDR recorded 88 parameters at a sampling rate of 1 Hz, with critical landing parameters captured at 4 Hz during the final approach phase. Data synchronization was achieved using time-correlated GPS position, radio altitude, and engine N1 parameters.

The final approach phase commenced at 1,500 ft MSL, with the aircraft established on a 3.0° glidepath. At 500 ft AGL, the recorded indicated airspeed was 142 KIAS, with a calculated crosswind component of 28 knots from 270° magnetic. Wind shear alerts were not triggered, but rapid fluctuations in vertical speed (±450 fpm) were recorded between 300 ft and 100 ft AGL, indicative of turbulent boundary layer conditions. At 50 ft AGL, the aircraft pitch attitude was 2.1° nose-up, with a vertical descent rate of 820 fpm (13.7 ft/sec). The NLG strut pressure transducer recorded a pre-impact nitrogen pressure of 1,842 PSI, within the specified tolerance.

At touchdown (T+0.00 sec), the main landing gear (MLG) contacted the runway first, followed by NLG contact at T+0.82 sec. The FDR recorded a peak vertical acceleration (Gz) of +2.84g at T+0.91 sec, exceeding the design limit load of 2.5g for the NLG system. The sink rate at NLG contact was calculated at 11.2 ft/sec, surpassing the 10 ft/sec certification limit. The crosswind component at touchdown was 31 knots, with a gust factor of 1.4, resulting in a lateral load vector of approximately 0.35g. The NLG strut compression rate exceeded 18 ft/sec, causing rapid fluid bypass through the metering pin and resulting in a loss of damping efficiency.

The QAR data corroborated the FDR parameters, with additional high-resolution pitch and roll attitude data. At T+0.75 sec, the aircraft experienced a 4.2° nose-down pitch excursion, followed by a rapid rebound to +1.8° at T+1.10 sec. The NLG forward trunnion load cell (simulated via strain gauge telemetry) indicated a peak compressive load of 142,500 lbs, approximately 1.68 times the limit load. The drag brace separation event was inferred from a sudden drop in NLG strut pressure (from 1,842 PSI to 410 PSI) and a corresponding spike in lateral acceleration (+0.62g) at T+1.05 sec.

Comparison with normal operational parameters (Boeing 737-800 Flight Crew Operations Manual, Section 5.10) indicates that the recorded sink rate, vertical acceleration, and crosswind component exceeded recommended landing limits. The aircraft’s autothrottle system remained engaged until T+0.30 sec, with thrust levers at idle. No system warnings or fault codes were recorded for the NLG or flight control systems prior to touchdown.

5. SUMMARY
The specialist examination of the Boeing 737-800 nose landing gear assembly and associated flight data yielded the following factual findings:
- The forward trunnion fitting (P/N 65-43225-11, S/N 88102) failed due to fatigue crack initiation at the inner radius of the forward bolt hole, followed by rapid ductile overload fracture.
- Metallurgical analysis confirmed the trunnion material met AMS 4045 specifications for 7075-T7351 aluminum alloy, with no evidence of corrosion, manufacturing defects, or improper heat treatment.
- The NLG shock strut collapsed to 14.2 inches, with the drag brace separating from the lower cylinder at approximately T+1.05 sec post-touchdown.
- Flight data recorded a peak vertical acceleration of +2.84g, a sink rate of 11.2 ft/sec at NLG contact, and a crosswind component of 31 knots with a 1.4 gust factor.
- The recorded loads exceeded the NLG design limit load of 2.5g and the 10 ft/sec sink rate certification basis.
- Maintenance records indicate the NLG was overhauled in March 2020 by Island Express Helicopters in compliance with 14 CFR 121.344, with all NDI and dimensional inspections documented as within limits.
- Administrative documentation referenced LEAP-1B engine procedures in a non-applicable maintenance log entry; this discrepancy did not affect NLG structural integrity or operational performance.
- No pre-existing structural anomalies, material degradation, or system malfunctions were identified in the NLG assembly prior to the hard landing event.
All findings are strictly factual and derived from physical examination, laboratory testing, and recorded flight data. No determination of probable cause is made in this report.

INTERVIEW OF CAPTAIN MARCUS THORNE, PILOT IN COMMAND
Date: August 17, 2023
Time: 14:30 Local
Location: NTSB Regional Field Office, Interview Room B
Interviewer: Senior Investigator Elena Rostova, NTSB Office of Aviation Safety

Q: Captain Thorne, thank you for making yourself available. I’m going to read you the standard NTSB advisory. You are not under oath, but your statement will become part of the official accident record. You may decline to answer any question, and you may stop the interview at any time. Do you understand?
A: Yes, ma’am. I understand completely. I want to be as clear as I can.

Q: Good. Let’s begin with your role on the flight. You were the pilot in command?
A: That’s correct. I was the captain, flying the left seat. First Officer was David Chen. We’d been flying together for about three months. Good rhythm. He’s sharp, knows the aircraft inside and out.

Q: Walk me through the pre-flight and initial approach. What were you seeing in terms of weather and aircraft status?
A: Okay. So, we pushed back around 14:15, I think. Maybe 14:20. We got the ATIS at the gate, and it was… it was already showing a pretty active wind. Northwest at twenty-two, gusting thirty-five. Crosswind component was right around twenty-eight knots. The 737-800’s demonstrated limit is thirty-three, so we were within limits, but it was definitely on the high side. We ran the performance numbers, checked the landing distance. Everything was green. I told David, “We’ll take it, but if it gets unstable below five hundred, we’re going around.” He nodded, said he’d call it if he saw anything.

Q: What did you observe as you descended through the final approach?
A: The wind was… it was really choppy. You could feel it in the yoke. Constant little kicks, you know? The autopilot was tracking okay until about a thousand feet, then I disconnected and took over manually. I prefer to hand-fly in those conditions anyway. Gives you better tactile feedback. We were on a stabilized approach, flaps thirty, speed around one-thirty-five. But then, at about four hundred feet, we hit a shear. A real nasty one. The airspeed just… dropped. Then surged. I added power, corrected the drift. The nose was yawing left, then right. I was fighting it with rudder and aileron. It was like the airplane was trying to dance.

Q: Describe the touchdown.
A: Yeah. So, we were maybe fifty feet, then thirty. I was trying to keep the wings level, but the gusts were just… relentless. I called “ten feet,” David called “retard,” I pulled the thrust levers back. We touched down… hard. I mean, really hard. It wasn’t a smooth flare. The main gear hit first, but then the nose came down like a hammer. There was this… this massive *crunch*. Not a thud. A crunch. Like metal folding. The whole airframe shuddered. I felt it through the seat, through my boots. Then the nose just… dropped. The yoke went forward, alarms started screaming. “PULL UP,” “TERRAIN,” all of it. I immediately cut the engines, hit the fuel cutoffs, and yelled “Evacuate! Evacuate! Evacuate!”

Q: What happened immediately after?
A: David was already on the comms, calling Mayday, but I was focused on the evacuation checklist. We had to get everyone out. The cabin crew… they were fantastic. I heard the slides deploy. That *whoosh* sound, you know? Like a giant air mattress inflating. I looked out the left window, saw the nose gear was completely gone. Just… collapsed inward. The nose was resting on the runway. There was a smell, too. Hydraulic fluid, maybe some burning rubber. Not smoke, not yet, but that sharp, acrid smell.

Q: How long did the evacuation take?
A: From the time I called it to the last passenger off? Maybe… I don’t know, four or five minutes. We had a full load, about a hundred and sixty souls. The flight attendants did their jobs. They were shouting, pointing, keeping people moving. No panic, really. People were scared, but they listened. We met at the rally point, did a headcount. Everyone was accounted for. Not a single serious injury. Just bumps, bruises, a couple of sprained ankles.

Q: Let’s talk about the aircraft’s maintenance history. Were there any recent inspections or modifications you were aware of?
A: Yeah, actually. We’d just come out of a heavy check. The maintenance logs showed a recent inspection on the forward fuselage section. I think it was… Spirit AeroSystems had done some work on the forward pressure bulkhead and the door plug area. Wait, no, not a door plug. I’m mixing it up. It was an emergency exit plug, or maybe a maintenance access panel. The paperwork referenced a service bulletin from Spirit AeroSystems. I remember seeing it in the tech log. They’d replaced some fasteners, checked the alignment. Everything was signed off.

Q: You mentioned a door plug. Can you clarify?
A: Right, sorry. I was thinking of the MAX fleet training we did last quarter. They were talking about the DOOR PLUG installations on the 737 MAX 9s, how to inspect the retention bolts. It’s just… it’s fresh in my head. But for this bird, it was a standard 737-800. No door plug. Just the regular overwing exits and the main doors. I think I just conflated the two in my head. Happens when you’re stressed.

Q: Understood. What about the engines? Any anomalies noted before or after the landing?
A: The engines were fine. We’re flying CFM56-7Bs on this model, but we’d just had a fleet-wide briefing on the new LEAP-1B powerplants for the MAX line. The training module covered crosswind landing techniques, engine-out procedures, and how the newer engines handle asymmetric thrust. I was thinking about that during the approach, actually. Wondering if the LEAP-1B’s faster spool-up would’ve helped in that shear. But that’s just… hindsight. The CFMs performed exactly as they should. No surges, no stalls. Just… we came down too fast, too hard.

Q: Let’s discuss the evacuation procedures. Were there any regulatory considerations you were following?
A: Absolutely. We’re trained to 14 CFR 121.344. That’s the emergency equipment requirement. We checked the slides, the life vests, the megaphones, the flashlights. All accounted for during the pre-flight. When the nose gear collapsed, the forward door was jammed, so we used the overwing exits and the aft doors. The regulation says you have to be able to evacuate within ninety seconds. We were well under that. Maybe sixty, sixty-five. The crew knew their stations. I didn’t have to tell them twice.

Q: How did you feel during the approach and landing?
A: Honestly? Tense. You know, you train for this stuff in the sim. You run the crosswind scenarios, the wind shear escapes, the hard landings. But when it’s real… it’s different. The wind was just… it was like the airplane was fighting you. I was sweating, my hands were tight on the yoke. I kept thinking, “Just keep it straight, don’t let it drift.” When the nose came down, I felt this… this jolt. Like a car hitting a curb at forty. Then the alarms, the smell, the realization that we were down. But the training kicked in. You don’t freeze. You run the checklist. You get people out.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add?
A: Just… I want to make sure the crew gets credit. David, the first officer, he was on the ball. The flight attendants, they were heroes. And maintenance, whoever signed off on that Spirit AeroSystems work, they did their job. The aircraft was airworthy. This was… this was weather. Pure and simple. A gusty crosswind, a microburst maybe, and a hard landing. We got lucky. Nobody got hurt. That’s what matters.

Q: Thank you, Captain. We’ll follow up if we need clarification.
A: Of course. I’ll be here.

FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION
OFFICE OF AVIATION SAFETY

TRANSPORT AIRPLANE DIRECTORATE

NTSB Safety Recommendation A-22-047 Response

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This correspondence constitutes the Federal Aviation Administration’s formal response to National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Safety Recommendation A-22-047, issued following the investigation of the August 15, 2021, runway excursion and structural failure event involving a Boeing 737-800, registration N738IE, operated by Island Express Air Services, Inc. (hereinafter "Island Express"). The subject matter addresses regulatory compliance with 14 CFR Part 121 operational mandates, structural integrity requirements under 14 CFR 25.571, and the continued airworthiness oversight of type certificate (TC) holders and tier-one suppliers. The referenced incident involved a hard landing during a gusty crosswind approach that resulted in the collapse of the nose landing gear, substantial airframe damage, and a successful emergency evacuation of all occupants. This document further addresses the integration of recent design modifications, including the mid-exit door plug configuration and propulsion system interfaces, within the broader 737 family certification framework.

2. BACKGROUND
The FAA exercises continuous regulatory oversight of air carrier operations and aircraft design under the authority of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations. The occurrence on August 15, 2021, was precipitated by meteorological conditions that exceeded the demonstrated crosswind limitations published in the approved Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM). The resulting vertical and lateral impact loads surpassed the design limit load factors for the nose landing gear assembly, initiating a progressive structural failure. Under 14 CFR 121.344, air carriers are mandated to establish and maintain a continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) that ensures all aircraft are serviced, inspected, and repaired in strict accordance with approved manufacturer data and applicable regulatory directives.

Historically, the FAA has addressed fatigue-related structural vulnerabilities in the 737 Next Generation series through targeted rulemaking. Airworthiness Directive 2012-09-04 was promulgated to mandate repetitive inspections and eventual structural reinforcement of primary fuselage elements susceptible to multi-site fatigue cracking. While the directive successfully mitigated legacy airframe degradation, subsequent operational data and type design evolutions have necessitated a comprehensive review of damage tolerance methodologies. Section 25.571 of Title 14 establishes the foundational requirements for fatigue evaluation and damage tolerance of transport category airplanes, requiring that all structural components demonstrate an adequate safety margin against catastrophic failure under repeated load cycles.

Concurrently, the FAA’s Aircraft Certification Service (AIR) has been evaluating manufacturing and certification processes for derivative airframe configurations. This includes the structural integration of the mid-cabin exit door plug, which introduces localized stress concentrations requiring enhanced load path analysis. Although the CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engine is not installed on the 737-800 variant, the regulatory framework governing engine-to-airframe vibration harmonics, thrust load distribution, and adjacent structural reinforcement remains directly applicable to the overarching 737 type certificate. The FAA has coordinated with Spirit AeroSystems, Inc. (Spirit) to ensure that all forward fuselage assemblies, including door plug interfaces and nose gear bay reinforcements, comply with the damage tolerance criteria mandated by § 25.571.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A thorough examination of the operator’s maintenance logs, flight data recorder (FDR) telemetry, and structural inspection records confirms that Island Express maintained baseline compliance with the minimum equipment list (MMEL) and CAMP requirements at the time of the occurrence. However, the investigation identified systemic deficiencies in the operator’s crosswind landing training curriculum and wind shear recovery protocols, which fall under the operational control and pilot qualification standards of Part 121. The assigned Principal Operations Inspector (POI) and Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) have documented these findings in the FAA’s surveillance database and initiated a targeted oversight review.

From an airworthiness standpoint, the nose landing gear collapse was attributed to dynamic load exceedance rather than a latent manufacturing defect or undetected fatigue crack. Nevertheless, the FAA’s fleet-wide analysis has identified regulatory gaps concerning the harmonization of fatigue evaluation requirements for modified fuselage sections. Specifically, the integration of the mid-exit door plug on certain 737 variants necessitates updated damage tolerance analysis to account for altered stress distribution under asymmetric loading conditions. While AD 2012-09-04 addressed historical fatigue concerns, the current regulatory framework requires supplemental compliance verification for newer structural modifications.

The FAA has also audited the quality assurance and production control protocols of Spirit AeroSystems, Inc. regarding the fabrication of forward fuselage assemblies. Audit findings indicate that Spirit’s non-conformance reporting system satisfies the baseline requirements of 14 CFR § 21.137; however, the FAA recommends enhanced traceability documentation for structural fasteners, load-bearing brackets, and door plug retention mechanisms. Furthermore, the certification basis for the LEAP-1B engine installation has been reviewed to ensure that engine-induced vibration spectra and thrust load harmonics do not adversely affect adjacent structural components, including the nose gear bay and forward pressure bulkhead.

Regulatory oversight actions have included the issuance of a Letter of Investigation (LOI) to the operator, a mandatory safety bulletin for all Part 121 certificate holders regarding crosswind approach limitations, and a fleet-wide review of nose landing gear inspection intervals. The FAA’s continued airworthiness assessment confirms that the existing regulatory architecture, when rigorously enforced, provides adequate safety margins. However, the incident underscores the necessity for proactive regulatory updates to address evolving operational environments and type design modifications.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
In direct response to the investigative findings and in alignment with NTSB Safety Recommendation A-22-047, the FAA hereby mandates the following corrective actions and compliance timelines:

a. **Operator Compliance (Island Express Air Services, Inc.):** Island Express shall revise its FAA-approved training program to incorporate advanced crosswind and wind shear recovery modules, in strict accordance with 14 CFR § 121.401 and § 121.409. The revised curriculum must be submitted to the assigned POI for approval no later than 90 days from the date of this correspondence. The operator shall additionally implement mandatory line-oriented flight training (LOFT) scenarios focusing on gusty crosswind approaches and stabilized approach criteria.

b. **Airworthiness Directive Implementation:** The FAA will issue a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) to amend the compliance requirements of Airworthiness Directive 2012-09-04, extending inspection intervals for forward fuselage stringers and reinforcing the damage tolerance evaluation criteria for the mid-exit door plug assembly. The proposed rule will be published in the Federal Register within 120 days, with a public comment period of 60 days. Final rulemaking is anticipated within 180 days.

c. **Manufacturer Quality Assurance Enhancements:** Spirit AeroSystems, Inc. shall implement enhanced non-destructive testing (NDT) protocols for all forward fuselage assemblies destined for 737 Next Generation and derivative variants. The manufacturer must submit a revised quality control manual to the FAA’s Manufacturing Inspection District Office (MIDO) within 150 days, demonstrating full compliance with 14 CFR § 21.137 and § 21.143.

d. **Fleet-Wide Structural Review:** The FAA’s Transport Airplane Directorate will conduct a comprehensive review of nose landing gear load path analysis and fatigue evaluation data for all 737-800 aircraft operating under 14 CFR Part 121. This review will incorporate updated gust load modeling and crosswind operational data. A final engineering report will be issued within 240 days, with any necessary service bulletins or supplemental type certificates (STCs) to be promulgated accordingly.

e. **Follow-Up Inspection and Oversight Schedule:** The FAA will conduct a targeted surveillance audit of Island Express within 180 days to verify compliance with the revised training program and maintenance procedures. Concurrently, the FAA will perform a manufacturing audit of Spirit AeroSystems, Inc. to validate the implementation of enhanced NDT protocols. All findings will be documented in the FAA’s Safety Management System (SMS) database and reported to the NTSB as part of the ongoing safety recommendation tracking process.

The FAA remains committed to the highest standards of aviation safety and will continue to collaborate with the NTSB, industry stakeholders, and international regulatory authorities to ensure the continued airworthiness of the global fleet. All compliance documentation shall be submitted to the Aircraft Certification Service, Docket Management Facility, under Docket No. FAA-2021-0892.

HEADLINE: Boeing 737 Nose Gear Collapses in Gusty Crosswind Landing; All 162 Aboard Evacuate Safely

BYLINE: Marcus Vance, National Aviation Correspondent
DATELINE: SEATTLE — 

A Boeing 737-800 carrying 156 passengers and six crew members suffered a hard landing that collapsed its nose landing gear during a turbulent crosswind approach at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on August 15, 2021. Despite substantial damage to the aircraft’s forward fuselage, emergency responders successfully evacuated everyone on board within minutes, with only minor injuries reported.

The incident unfolded as Flight 442 battled sudden wind shear and crosswinds exceeding 35 knots on final approach. The aircraft’s nose gear buckled upon touchdown, causing the forward section to scrape the runway and come to a halt. Airport operations were temporarily suspended, and emergency response teams deployed fire suppression foam as a precaution. All passengers and crew exited via emergency slides, with paramedics treating three individuals for minor sprains and smoke inhalation. No life-threatening injuries were reported.

Federal investigators and aviation regulators have launched a comprehensive review of the event. "The preliminary data indicates a combination of environmental factors and landing dynamics contributed to the gear collapse," said NTSB investigator-in-charge David Chen. "Our priority is securing the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder to reconstruct the final moments of the approach and determine whether operational limits were exceeded."

The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it is monitoring the probe. "The FAA is reviewing the operator’s compliance with all safety protocols and will take appropriate action based on the investigation’s findings," an FAA regional director stated in a written release.

Marcus Thorne, spokesperson for the operating carrier, expressed relief and gratitude. "We are profoundly thankful that every passenger and crew member walked away from this event," Thorne said. "Our emergency response teams executed their training flawlessly, and we are providing full support to those affected, including counseling and travel accommodations."

The flight was operated by Pacific Coast Airways, a regional carrier under the corporate umbrella of Island Express Helicopters, which expanded into fixed-wing commercial operations in 2018. The aircraft was en route from Portland, Oregon, to Seattle on a routine scheduled service. The carrier operates under Part 121 of the Federal Aviation Regulations, the strict set of rules governing scheduled commercial air carriers that mandate rigorous pilot training, maintenance schedules, and operational safety standards. While the 737-800 relies on older CFM56 turbofan engines, the airline has been gradually integrating newer aircraft equipped with the more fuel-efficient LEAP engine into its fleet as part of a broader modernization initiative.

Aviation safety experts note that crosswind landings require precise control inputs and strict adherence to manufacturer limits. "When wind gusts shift rapidly, pilots must constantly adjust the aircraft’s alignment to prevent side-loading on the landing gear," said Dr. Aris Thorne, a former commercial pilot and aviation safety consultant at the University of Washington. "If the touchdown is too firm or the aircraft isn't perfectly aligned with the runway centerline, the structural stress can exceed design tolerances."

Investigators will examine whether the landing gear assembly met the fatigue and damage tolerance standards outlined in 14 CFR 25.571, a federal regulation that requires aircraft structures to withstand repeated stress cycles without catastrophic failure. The First Officer, who was monitoring the approach and managing throttle inputs, immediately initiated a go-around procedure, but the aircraft had already committed to the runway. "The crew recognized the deteriorating conditions and attempted to abort the landing, but momentum and altitude constraints made it impossible to safely climb away," Chen noted during a preliminary press briefing.

For passengers aboard the flight, the moments following touchdown were marked by confusion and fear, quickly replaced by relief. "We hit the runway hard, and the whole plane shuddered like it was breaking apart," said passenger Clara Mendez, 42, who was traveling with her two children. "The lights flickered, and then we heard the captain tell us to brace. But the flight attendants were incredibly calm. They guided us to the exits, and we were on the tarmac within minutes. I’m just grateful we’re all here."

The Boeing 737-800 has a long operational history and remains one of the most widely flown commercial aircraft in the world. While nose gear collapses are rare, they have occurred in previous incidents involving heavy crosswinds, pilot technique deviations, or maintenance oversights. The National Transportation Safety Board has documented fewer than two dozen similar events involving 737 variants over the past two decades, with the vast majority resulting in safe evacuations and no fatalities. The aircraft’s forward fuselage section, manufactured by Spirit Aerosystems, sustained visible abrasions and minor structural deformation but remained intact, a factor investigators credit for the rapid and orderly evacuation.

Maintenance crews have already begun inspecting the aircraft’s hydraulic and landing gear systems, including the MED Plug—a specialized maintenance access component used to monitor fluid pressure and detect micro-fractures in the gear retraction mechanism. Early visual inspections revealed no signs of pre-existing corrosion or metal fatigue, though laboratory analysis of recovered components will take several weeks.

The NTSB investigation remains active. Investigators are currently downloading telemetry data, interviewing flight and cabin crew, and reviewing air traffic control recordings. A preliminary report is expected within 30 days, with a final determination likely taking 12 to 18 months. In the interim, the operating carrier has temporarily suspended flights to the affected route pending a fleet-wide inspection of landing gear assemblies and a review of crosswind training protocols.

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Aircraft Manufacturer’s Structural Engineering and Landing Gear Systems Division, acting as a designated party to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigation. Our role is to provide a comprehensive technical evaluation of the nose landing gear (NLG) collapse that occurred during the August 15, 2021, hard landing event involving a Boeing 737-800. The scope of this document encompasses structural load path analysis, certification compliance verification, operational data interpretation, and an assessment of environmental and human factors that contributed to the sequence of events. 

The manufacturer’s position is grounded in engineering data, flight data recorder (FDR) and quick access recorder (QAR) telemetry, maintenance documentation, and established certification frameworks. This submission addresses the structural response of the NLG assembly under exceedance conditions, evaluates the aircraft’s compliance with applicable airworthiness standards, and clarifies the relevance of ancillary components and regulatory references that have been raised during preliminary investigative discussions. Specifically, we address the role of Spirit AeroSystems (SAS) in fuselage section manufacturing, clarify the inapplicability of the LEAP-1B engine and mid-exit door plug configurations to this airframe, and contextualize the investigation within the requirements of 14 CFR 25.571 and 14 CFR part 121. References to unrelated operators, including Island Express Helicopters (IEH), are addressed solely to delineate the fixed-wing transport category scope of this inquiry. Our objective is to provide the Board with a technically rigorous, evidence-based foundation for determining probable cause and formulating actionable safety recommendations.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On August 15, 2021, at approximately 14:32 local time, the subject Boeing 737-800 (registration withheld per docket protocol) executed an approach to Runway 27L under deteriorating meteorological conditions. Surface winds were reported at 22 knots from 290 degrees, with gusts to 35 knots and a crosswind component of approximately 28 knots. The flight crew elected to continue the approach following a stabilized approach briefing. At touchdown, the aircraft experienced a high vertical descent rate, resulting in a hard landing that exceeded the design load limits of the nose landing gear. The NLG collapsed aft and downward, causing substantial damage to the forward fuselage, avionics bay, and lower lobe structure. All 162 passengers and 6 crew members evacuated via the main cabin doors without serious injury.

Docket materials, including NTSB Exhibit 12A (FDR/QAR Data Package), Exhibit 14C (Maintenance and Inspection Records), and Exhibit 18B (Meteorological and ATC Transcripts), confirm the following sequence: the aircraft crossed the threshold at 142 knots indicated airspeed, approximately 8 knots above the target Vref. The flare was initiated late, and the main landing gear (MLG) contacted the runway at a vertical acceleration of 2.1g. Within 0.8 seconds, the NLG contacted the surface at a calculated sink rate of approximately 1,150 feet per minute, significantly exceeding the 600 fpm design limit for the NLG oleo strut. The forward drag brace buckled, the torque link assembly separated, and the strut cylinder bottomed out, resulting in structural collapse.

The airframe’s forward fuselage sections were manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems (SAS) under established production agreements. Post-incident non-destructive inspection (NDI) of the SAS-supplied panels, longerons, and bulkhead interfaces revealed no evidence of pre-existing fatigue cracking, corrosion, or manufacturing anomalies. The aircraft is equipped with CFM International CFM56-7B turbofan engines; the LEAP-1B powerplant is not installed on this variant and is exclusive to the 737 MAX family. Similarly, the 737-800 configuration does not incorporate a mid-exit door plug (Type III emergency exit configuration), which is a structural feature specific to the 737 MAX 9. Regulatory compliance for this aircraft is governed by 14 CFR 25.571 (Damage-Tolerance and Fatigue Evaluation of Structure) and operational oversight falls under 14 CFR part 121. The operator’s training, dispatch, and maintenance programs were audited and found to be in compliance with Part 121 requirements. References to Island Express Helicopters (IEH) or rotary-wing operations are outside the scope of this fixed-wing transport category investigation and do not intersect with the technical or operational parameters of this event.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The collapse of the nose landing gear must be evaluated through the lens of structural design limits, dynamic load response, and operational envelope exceedance. The 737-800 NLG is engineered to absorb vertical and drag loads within certified parameters, utilizing a dual-chamber oleo-pneumatic strut, a forward drag brace, and a torque link assembly that maintains wheel alignment and steering geometry. Certification testing, conducted in accordance with §25.571, establishes ultimate load factors at 1.5 times limit load, with fatigue life validated through full-scale static testing and crack propagation modeling.

FDR and QAR telemetry (Docket Exhibit 12A) indicate that the NLG experienced a vertical impact velocity of approximately 19.2 feet per second, translating to a dynamic load factor of 2.8g at the strut attachment points. This exceeds the limit load condition by approximately 40 percent and approaches ultimate load thresholds. Finite element analysis (FEA) of the post-impact damage pattern confirms that the forward drag brace experienced compressive buckling at the lower clevis pin interface, initiating a progressive failure sequence. The torque link assembly subsequently sheared due to uncontrolled lateral displacement, and the strut cylinder bottomed out, transferring residual energy into the forward fuselage structure.

Wind tunnel and flight simulation data corroborate that the reported crosswind and gust conditions created a complex aerodynamic environment. The aircraft encountered a 12-knot wind shear layer at 200 feet AGL, which disrupted the glide path and required rapid control inputs. The QAR data shows a 4-degree nose-up pitch attitude at touchdown, followed by a rapid pitch-down moment as the MLG absorbed the initial impact. The delayed NLG contact, combined with the high sink rate, prevented the oleo strut from fully extending and absorbing energy through its designed stroke. This is a known aerodynamic and kinematic phenomenon in high-crosswind, gusty conditions, where ground effect, wind gradient, and pilot control timing interact nonlinearly.

From a certification standpoint, the airframe fully complies with 14 CFR 25.571 damage-tolerance requirements. The fatigue evaluation program, which includes scheduled inspections of the NLG trunnion, drag brace, and forward bulkhead, was current. Maintenance records (Exhibit 14C) show no deferred defects, no repeat write-ups related to the NLG, and all recent heavy checks were completed within regulatory intervals. The structural response observed is consistent with an operational exceedance rather than a latent manufacturing or maintenance deficiency.

It is necessary to address several configuration and regulatory clarifications that have emerged during preliminary hearings. The LEAP-1B engine, while a highly efficient next-generation powerplant, is not installed on the 737-800 and therefore played no role in thrust management, engine-out performance, or weight distribution during this event. The mid-exit door plug, a structural modification introduced on the 737 MAX 9 to accommodate variable cabin configurations, is absent from this airframe; the 737-800 utilizes standard Type III emergency exits with certified load paths that were unaffected by the NLG collapse. Spirit AeroSystems (SAS) fuselage sections underwent standard production acceptance testing and post-incident NDI confirmed structural continuity. Regulatory oversight under 14 CFR part 121 was appropriately applied by the operator, and the flight crew’s decision to continue the approach, while ultimately resulting in an exceedance, was made within the bounds of company standard operating procedures (SOPs) and FAA-approved crosswind limitations.

Comparative industry data from similar hard landing events indicates that NLG collapses in the 737-800 fleet are rare and almost exclusively associated with sink rate exceedances above 900 fpm, often compounded by crosswind drift correction errors or delayed thrust reduction. The manufacturer’s fleet monitoring program has identified that real-time sink rate awareness and gust response training are critical mitigations. The aircraft’s design margins, as validated under §25.571, are robust, but they are not intended to accommodate repeated or extreme operational exceedances. The structural failure observed is a direct consequence of kinetic energy transfer exceeding the NLG’s certified absorption capacity.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the engineering data, flight telemetry, maintenance documentation, and certification analysis, the manufacturer concludes that the primary contributing factor to the nose landing gear collapse was an operational exceedance of the aircraft’s design envelope. The combination of a high vertical descent rate (~1,150 fpm), delayed flare initiation, and gusty crosswind conditions resulted in dynamic loads that surpassed the NLG’s limit load capacity. The structural failure sequence—drag brace buckling, torque link separation, and strut bottoming—is consistent with certified load path behavior under extreme impact conditions.

Secondary contributing factors include environmental complexity (low-level wind shear and rapid gust variation) and the inherent challenges of manual crosswind landing techniques under high workload. The aircraft’s systems, including the flight control computers, autothrottle, and wind shear detection, functioned within design parameters. The operator’s compliance with 14 CFR part 121 training and maintenance requirements was verified, and no systemic deficiencies were identified.

It is critical to clarify that the LEAP-1B powerplant, the mid-exit door plug configuration, and Spirit AeroSystems (SAS) manufacturing processes were not involved in this event. The 737-800 airframe is structurally distinct from the 737 MAX family, and the failure mode observed is unrelated to those configurations. Similarly, references to Island Express Helicopters (IEH) or rotary-wing operational paradigms are outside the technical and regulatory scope of this investigation. The event is firmly situated within fixed-wing transport category operations, governed by 14 CFR 25.571 structural certification standards and Part 121 operational oversight.

The manufacturer recommends targeted safety improvements focused on operational awareness, training refinement, and enhanced monitoring. These include the integration of predictive sink rate alerting, revised crosswind and gust response training modules, and expanded QAR threshold monitoring for hard landing precursors. Structural design margins remain validated, but operational risk can be further mitigated through procedural and technological enhancements.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

The manufacturer has already implemented several corrective and preventive measures in response to this event and related fleet data. A Service Bulletin (SB 737-32-XXXX) was issued within 30 days of the incident, mandating enhanced post-hard-landing inspections of the NLG drag brace, torque link, and forward trunnion fittings. The bulletin includes updated torque specifications, NDI protocols, and replacement criteria for components exhibiting plastic deformation. Additionally, the Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM) was revised to emphasize early flare initiation, crosswind drift correction timing, and thrust reduction sequencing in gusty conditions. The manufacturer’s Fleet Health Monitoring (FHM) program has been updated to flag QAR parameters indicative of high sink rate approaches, enabling proactive operator intervention.

Looking forward, the manufacturer proposes the following safety improvements:
1. Integration of a Real-Time Sink Rate Advisory System: A software enhancement to the flight deck display that provides visual and aural alerts when vertical descent rates exceed 800 fpm below 500 feet AGL, allowing crews to execute a timely go-around.
2. Enhanced Crosswind and Gust Training Modules: Development of a Level D full-flight simulator scenario package focusing on wind shear recovery, late flare mitigation, and manual landing techniques under rapidly changing wind conditions. This package will be made available to all Part 121 operators at no additional licensing cost.
3. NLG Load Telemetry Expansion: Implementation of strain gauge instrumentation on the NLG drag brace and oleo strut for select fleet aircraft, enabling continuous load monitoring and predictive maintenance scheduling. Data will be shared with operators and the FAA to refine fatigue tracking under §25.571.
4. Regulatory Collaboration: Engagement with the FAA to review and update 14 CFR part 121 training requirements for crosswind and gusty approach operations, ensuring alignment with current meteorological forecasting capabilities and aircraft performance data.
5. Industry Safety Forum Participation: Active contribution to the Commercial Aviation Safety Team (CAST) working group on hard landing prevention, sharing anonymized QAR data and engineering insights to develop standardized mitigation strategies across the transport category fleet.

The manufacturer remains committed to aviation safety, continuous engineering improvement, and transparent collaboration with the NTSB, regulatory authorities, and operator partners. The structural integrity of the 737-800 has been validated through decades of service, rigorous certification testing, and ongoing fleet monitoring. By addressing operational exceedance risks through enhanced training, real-time alerting, and data-driven maintenance, the industry can further reduce the likelihood of similar events while preserving the proven safety record of the aircraft family.

TO: Fleet Maintenance Engineering, Line Maintenance Supervisors, Quality Assurance Division, Flight Operations Training, Airworthiness Compliance Office
FROM: Director of Maintenance Quality & Airworthiness, Pacific Regional Operations
DATE: 22 August 2021
SUBJECT: Quality Alert – Post-Hard Landing Inspection Protocols & Forward Fuselage/NLG Load Assessment
REF: QA-2021-089, WO-77432-NLG, AMM Rev. 44, SB-737-32-1145

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert establishes immediate inspection, reporting, and maintenance actions following the 15 August 2021 hard landing event. It supersedes previous guidance in QA-2021-072 and mandates updated structural assessment criteria for all 737-800 and 737 MAX aircraft in our fleet. The objective is to ensure continued airworthiness, standardize post-event teardown procedures, and align our maintenance program with current regulatory expectations.

BACKGROUND:
On 15 August 2021, a Boeing 737-800 (Reg. N737XX) experienced a hard landing during a gusty crosswind approach at 14:32 local time. The aircraft sustained a vertical acceleration event exceeding 2.8G, resulting in collapse of the nose landing gear (NLG) and substantial damage to the forward fuselage, NLG bay, and adjacent avionics racks. All passengers and crew evacuated safely via forward and overwing exits. Preliminary QAR data indicates the First Officer was pilot flying and executed a stabilized approach until encountering a 28-knot crosswind with gusts to 35 knots. Initial teardown under WO-77432-NLG revealed trunnion fitting deformation, forward bulkhead web cracking, and drag brace attachment point yielding.

While this event involves a CFM56-7B powered airframe, the forward load path assessment methodology applies across our narrowbody fleet, including LEAP-1B equipped MAX variants. Structural interfaces supplied by Spirit AeroSystems (Spirit) require enhanced non-destructive inspection (NDI) thresholds. Additionally, our contracted NDT provider, Island Express Helicopters (IEH), has been mobilized to support phased-array ultrasonic scanning of primary longerons. This alert ensures compliance with Section 25.783 of the certification basis, which governs structural integrity under abnormal and emergency loading conditions, and aligns with 14 CFR 121.344 continuous airworthiness maintenance program obligations. All findings must be evaluated against established damage tolerance requirements to prevent undetected crack propagation.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, implement the following procedures for any aircraft reporting a hard landing, bounce, or crosswind excursion exceeding manufacturer thresholds:

1. Immediate Grounding & Initial Assessment
   • Any aircraft with QAR-recorded vertical acceleration ≥ 2.0G or reported NLG impact must be removed from service until completion of the Level 3 Structural Inspection.
   • Line Maintenance shall initiate WO-77432-NLG (or equivalent fleet-specific work order) and secure the aircraft with NLG safety pins and forward fuselage shoring per AMM 32-11-00.
   • The First Officer and Captain must submit a mandatory ASRS-style internal report within 4 hours of block-in, including wind data, approach configuration, and touchdown parameters.

2. Structural & NLG Teardown Requirements
   • Remove NLG shock strut, drag brace, and trunnion assembly. Inspect all attachment lugs for elongation, fretting, or micro-cracking.
   • Perform eddy current and fluorescent penetrant inspection on forward pressure bulkhead (Station 240–280) and Spirit-supplied fuselage skin panels. Reference AMM 53-10-00 for access and removal.
   • Cross-check pylon and forward engine mount interfaces. While the LEAP-1B powerplant utilizes a different pylon architecture than the -800, the forward load transfer path through the keel beam and bulkhead remains structurally analogous. Apply identical NDI thresholds to both variants.
   • All NDI beyond standard line capabilities shall be routed to the IEH specialized inspection team. Coordinate scheduling through Maintenance Control (Ext. 4410).

3. Regulatory & Airworthiness Compliance
   • Section 25.783 mandates that primary structure maintain load-carrying capability under emergency conditions. Any deformation exceeding 0.050" permanent set requires engineering disposition before return to service.
   • Per 14 CFR 121.344, our maintenance program must incorporate updated inspection intervals following fleet-wide structural events. The Airworthiness Compliance Office will issue a temporary MPD revision within 10 days.
   • All repair schemes must satisfy current damage tolerance requirements. Crack arrest features, fastener hole cold expansion, and doubler installations require dual-signature approval from Structures Engineering and QA.

4. Documentation & Traceability
   • All inspection results, NDI reports, and engineering dispositions must be logged in the electronic maintenance tracking system under Event Code HL-2021-08.
   • Retain all removed components, including fractured pins and deformed brackets, in the QA evidence locker for 90 days. Do not scrap or return to vendor without written authorization.

ACTION REQUIRED:
• Line Maintenance Supervisors: Complete initial Level 3 inspections on all aircraft with QAR flags ≥ 1.8G within 48 hours of this bulletin. Submit compliance checklist to QA by 24 August 2021.
• Structures Engineering: Issue revised repair disposition matrix and update AMM cross-references by 30 August 2021. Validate all Spirit AeroSystems panel repair limits against updated fatigue data.
• Training & Standards: Distribute updated crosswind landing and hard landing reporting procedures to all flight crews by 25 August 2021. Schedule mandatory simulator debrief modules for the First Officer and Captain training tracks.
• Quality Assurance Division: Conduct random audits of 15% of completed WO-77432-NLG work packages by 10 September 2021. Verify NDI traceability, engineering sign-offs, and regulatory alignment.
• Maintenance Control: Coordinate with Island Express Helicopters (IEH) to prioritize ultrasonic phased-array scans for aircraft with forward bulkhead access limitations. Provide daily status updates to the Director of Maintenance.

Failure to comply with these directives will result in immediate grounding of the affected aircraft and escalation to the VP of Maintenance. All personnel are reminded that airworthiness decisions must prioritize structural integrity over schedule pressure. Direct technical questions to the Structures Engineering Help Desk (Ext. 5520) or QA Compliance (Ext. 4405).

1. SYNOPSIS
On August 15, 2021, at approximately 1432 local time, a Boeing 737-800 operated by Island Express Helicopters (IEH) experienced a hard landing during a gusty crosswind approach at the destination airport. The impact resulted in the collapse of the nose landing gear and substantial damage to the forward fuselage and lower wing structure. All occupants successfully evacuated via emergency slides, and no serious injuries were reported.
