This preliminary document outlines the initial factual data, establishes the investigative framework, and documents early procedural determinations pending the completion of the full inquiry.

2. INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary information indicates that the flight was operating under instrument flight rules when it encountered rapidly changing wind conditions during the final approach phase. Initial witness accounts from ground personnel and air traffic control staff suggest the aircraft exhibited a pronounced lateral drift and a higher-than-normal descent rate prior to touchdown. Meteorological data retrieved from the airport’s automated weather observing system indicates sustained winds of approximately 18 knots, with gusts reported up to 28 knots, and a crosswind component that approached the operational limits documented in the aircraft flight manual.

Preliminary examination of the accident site revealed that the nose landing gear assembly separated from the forward fuselage attachment points upon initial ground contact. The main landing gear remained extended and appeared to have sustained localized structural deformation, though initial assessments suggest they remained largely intact. The forward fuselage skin, lower lobe structure, and adjacent avionics bays sustained substantial damage consistent with a high-energy vertical and longitudinal impact. Initial review of maintenance and configuration records indicates the aircraft was equipped with CFM International LEAP-1B engines, though this designation is currently under verification against the airframe serial number and type certificate data sheet to resolve preliminary discrepancies in the equipment manifest.

Regulatory compliance considerations have been preliminarily noted for the structural evaluation. The investigation team will reference 14 CFR 25.571 (Title 14 CFR § 25.571) regarding damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation of metallic structures to assess whether pre-existing conditions or operational stress cycles contributed to the observed failure modes. Additionally, Section 25.783 (FAR 25.783), pertaining to fuselage doors and emergency exits, will be examined to verify the integrity and operational status of the evacuation pathways during the post-impact sequence. Initial interviews with the flight crew indicate that standard crosswind landing techniques were initiated, though precise control inputs and system responses remain under review. All preliminary observations are subject to revision as additional data is recovered and analyzed.

3. INVESTIGATION STATUS
The National Transportation Safety Board has activated the following investigative groups to address the scope of this event: Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Flight Data Recorder/Cockpit Voice Recorder, Human Performance, and Weather. Each group has been assigned a designated lead investigator and is operating under established NTSB protocols for preliminary data collection, preservation, and chain-of-custody documentation.

Parties to the investigation have been formally notified and include representatives from the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, the operator (Island Express Helicopters), the Federal Aviation Administration, and the relevant pilot and flight attendant labor organizations. All parties have been briefed on their roles, responsibilities, and the requirement to maintain strict confidentiality regarding preliminary findings. The party system will be utilized to facilitate technical expertise sharing while ensuring the independence of the investigative process.

Evidence secured to date includes the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, which have been transported to the NTSB laboratory for readout and preliminary analysis. The wreckage has been secured at the accident site under continuous surveillance, and a detailed photographic and three-dimensional mapping survey has been completed. Critical components, including the collapsed nose gear strut, torque links, and forward fuselage attachment fittings, have been tagged, documented, and prepared for transport to a secure examination facility. Maintenance logs, dispatch records, and crew training files have been obtained and are undergoing initial review. Planned examinations include metallurgical analysis of the failed gear components, non-destructive testing of the forward fuselage structure, and a comprehensive review of the aircraft’s weight and balance calculations for the accident flight.

4. NEXT STEPS
The immediate priority for the investigative teams is the completion of the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder readouts, which are anticipated to yield critical parameters regarding airspeed, vertical acceleration, control surface positions, and crew communications during the final approach and landing sequence. Concurrently, the Structures and Systems groups will conduct detailed teardown and dimensional inspections of the nose landing gear assembly to identify primary failure initiation points and assess the sequence of structural collapse.

Weather analysis will continue with a focus on microscale wind shear phenomena, boundary layer turbulence, and the accuracy of terminal area forecasting models. The Human Performance group will conduct structured interviews with the flight crew, cabin crew, and air traffic controllers to reconstruct the operational timeline and evaluate decision-making processes under the reported environmental conditions. All data collection efforts will be cross-referenced against applicable airworthiness directives, service bulletins, and manufacturer operational guidance.

A preliminary factual report is expected to be released within 30 days, pending the completion of initial data downloads and component examinations. Subsequent updates will be issued as the investigation progresses, with a formal public hearing and final report timeline to be established once the scope of the inquiry is fully defined. All findings documented herein remain preliminary and are subject to change as additional evidence is evaluated, tested, and validated. The investigation will proceed in accordance with established NTSB procedures, with an emphasis on factual accuracy, methodical analysis, and the preservation of all relevant data.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 On August 15, 2021, at 1432 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), a Boeing 737-800, registration N842IE, experienced a hard landing that resulted in the collapse of the nose landing gear (NLG) assembly during a visual approach to runway 27L at Coastal Regional Airport (CRA), Charleston, South Carolina. The aircraft touched down at 1431:45 EDT, followed by immediate structural failure of the forward landing gear. The aircraft slid approximately 1,850 feet along the runway pavement before coming to rest at coordinates 32.8912° N, 80.0401° W.

1.2 The flight was conducted under the provisions of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121 as a scheduled passenger service, designated as flight IE 4412. The aircraft departed Orlando International Airport (MCO), Florida, at 1245 EDT, with a scheduled arrival time of 1430 EDT. The flight was operated by Island Express Air, Inc., a certificated air carrier holding operating certificate number IEX-8842.

1.3 The aircraft sustained substantial damage to the forward fuselage, NLG, lower wing-to-fuselage fairings, and both engine nacelles. All 162 passengers and 6 flight crewmembers evacuated the aircraft via the forward left, forward right, and overwing emergency exits. Emergency medical services and airport rescue and firefighting (ARFF) units arrived on scene within 2 minutes and 45 seconds of the aircraft coming to rest. No serious injuries were reported.

1.4 The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) was notified at 1455 EDT. An investigator-in-charge and a multidisciplinary investigative team were dispatched to the accident site. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the operator’s safety management system (SMS) personnel were notified concurrently. The accident site was secured, and evidence preservation protocols were initiated in accordance with NTSB investigative procedures.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 The captain, age 48, held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate, certificate number 2845192, with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The captain possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on May 12, 2021, with no limitations or waivers. Total flight time was recorded at 14,250 hours, with 6,800 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The captain was designated as the pilot flying (PF) for the accident flight.

2.2 The first officer, age 34, held a commercial pilot certificate, certificate number 3198445, with multi-engine land and instrument ratings, and a Boeing 737 type rating. The first officer possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on June 3, 2021. Total flight time was 4,120 hours, with 1,850 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The first officer was designated as the pilot monitoring (PM) for the accident flight.

2.3 Both pilots completed recurrent training and proficiency checks in accordance with the operator’s FAA-approved training program. The captain’s most recent line check was completed on June 18, 2021, with satisfactory results in all evaluated maneuvers. The first officer’s most recent simulator evaluation was completed on July 2, 2021, which included crosswind landing scenarios, wind shear recovery, and rejected landing procedures. Both pilots completed the operator’s annual line-oriented flight training (LOFT) module on August 1, 2021.

2.4 Duty time records indicate the flight crew reported for duty at 0930 EDT on the day of the accident. The scheduled block time for the flight was 2 hours and 15 minutes. The crew had 11 hours and 15 minutes of rest prior to the duty period, in compliance with 14 CFR § 117.25. Crew scheduling logs, fatigue risk management system (FRMS) reports, and post-accident interviews revealed no evidence of fatigue, illness, or medication use that would have impaired performance.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 The accident aircraft was a Boeing 737-800, manufacturer serial number 38452, line number 4122. It was manufactured in 2014 and delivered to the operator in March 2015. At the time of the accident, the airframe had accumulated 42,180 total flight hours and 28,940 total flight cycles. The aircraft was registered to Island Express Air, Inc., and operated under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program.

3.2 Maintenance records were reviewed and found to be current. The most recent heavy maintenance check (C-check) was completed on April 10, 2021, at 41,850 flight hours. All deferred maintenance items (MEL/CDL) were within allowable limits. The aircraft’s maintenance tracking system indicated compliance with all manufacturer service bulletins and FAA directives. The operator’s reliability program reported no recurring discrepancies for the landing gear or flight control systems in the 90 days preceding the accident.

3.3 The aircraft was equipped with two CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, serial numbers 88421 (left) and 88423 (right). The LEAP-1B engine model was installed as part of a performance enhancement retrofit program completed in 2019. Engine maintenance logs indicated compliance with all applicable time-limited components and on-condition maintenance intervals. The left engine had accumulated 18,450 hours since new, and the right engine had accumulated 17,920 hours since new. Both engines were operating within manufacturer-specified parameters at the time of the accident, with no fault codes recorded in the engine indication and crew alerting system (EICAS).

3.4 The forward fuselage section, including the nose landing gear bay, forward pressure bulkhead, and lower skin panels, was manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems, Inc. (Spirit). The operator’s maintenance tracking system indicated that all structural inspections mandated by Airworthiness Directive 2012-09-04 had been completed. The directive required repetitive eddy current and ultrasonic inspections of the forward fuselage lap joints, stringer terminations, and frame-to-skin attachments. The most recent inspection was performed on March 22, 2021, at 41,650 flight hours, with no discrepancies noted.

3.5 The aircraft’s weight and balance calculations indicated a takeoff weight of 158,400 pounds, with a center of gravity at 24.8% mean aerodynamic chord (MAC). The landing weight was calculated at 142,100 pounds, within the maximum certified landing weight of 146,300 pounds. The aircraft was configured for landing with flaps set to 30 degrees, slats extended, and speed brakes armed. The landing gear was extended and indicated down and locked at 1,500 feet above ground level (AGL).

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 At the time of the accident, the airport was experiencing gusty crosswind conditions associated with a passing cold front. The Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) recorded a wind direction of 240 degrees at 18 knots, gusting to 28 knots, with a crosswind component of approximately 16 knots relative to runway 27L. The wind direction remained steady between 235 and 245 degrees for the 30 minutes preceding the accident.

4.2 The 1430 EDT METAR for CRA read: KCRA 151430Z 24018G28KT 10SM FEW035 SCT050 BKN120 28/18 A2992 RMK AO2 PK WND 25032/1415 SLP128 T02830183. The 1400 EDT TAF forecasted winds of 23015G25KT, with a temporary condition of 24020G30KT valid through 1600 EDT. Barometric pressure was recorded at 29.92 inches of mercury, with a temperature of 28°C and a dew point of 18°C, yielding a relative humidity of 54%.

4.3 The Automatic Terminal Information Service (ATIS) broadcast at 1425 EDT reported wind 240 at 17 gusting 26, visibility 10 statute miles, ceiling broken at 5,000 feet, temperature 28°C, dew point 18°C, altimeter 29.92 inches of mercury. The ATIS also included a NOTAM regarding wind shear advisories for the final approach corridor. The flight crew acknowledged the ATIS and wind shear advisory during the approach briefing at 1418 EDT.

4.4 Pilot reports (PIREPs) from preceding aircraft indicated moderate turbulence on final approach and a 15-knot crosswind component. The aircraft’s flight data recorder (FDR) indicated a peak vertical acceleration of 2.8g at touchdown, with a lateral load factor of 0.4g during the initial ground roll. The aircraft’s weather radar system recorded no precipitation or convective activity within 20 nautical miles of the airport.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 The wreckage was distributed along a linear path aligned with runway 27L. Initial touchdown marks were observed 1,200 feet from the runway threshold, followed by a secondary impact scar 1,240 feet from the threshold, consistent with NLG collapse. The aircraft slid 1,850 feet before coming to rest 3,050 feet from the threshold, 15 feet left of the centerline. The runway surface exhibited parallel gouge marks extending 1,850 feet, with an average depth of 0.25 inches.

5.2 Examination of the runway surface revealed no evidence of tire blowouts, brake system failures, or anti-skid system malfunctions prior to the NLG collapse. The main landing gear (MLG) tires exhibited asymmetric wear patterns consistent with differential braking during the slide. The MLG struts remained intact, with no evidence of structural compromise.

5.3 The nose landing gear assembly was separated from the forward fuselage and located 45 feet aft of the final resting position. The NLG strut exhibited compressive buckling at the upper cylinder, with fracture surfaces consistent with overload failure. The drag brace and side brace linkages showed plastic deformation. The NLG retraction actuator was found in the extended position, with hydraulic fluid leakage noted at the piston seal. The NLG steering actuator and torque tube assembly were intact, with no evidence of pre-impact failure.

5.4 The forward fuselage structure, manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems, sustained substantial damage to the lower skin panels, frame 12, and the forward pressure bulkhead. The damage pattern was consistent with a high-rate vertical impact followed by forward sliding. The skin panels exhibited buckling and tearing along the longitudinal stringers. The forward pressure bulkhead showed localized deformation at the lower quadrant, with no evidence of fatigue cracking or corrosion.

5.5 Post-accident examination of the flight control systems revealed no pre-impact anomalies. The elevator, aileron, and rudder control cables were intact, with proper tension and routing. The LEAP-1B engines were secured, with fan blades exhibiting minor leading-edge nicks consistent with foreign object debris (FOD) ingestion during the slide. Both engines were removed for teardown inspection. The hydraulic, pneumatic, and electrical systems were isolated and found to be within operational limits prior to impact.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 The operator, Island Express Air, Inc., maintained a crosswind landing policy in accordance with the Boeing 737 Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM). The policy specified a maximum demonstrated crosswind component of 33 knots for dry runways and 25 knots for wet runways. The operator’s standard operating procedures (SOPs) required a stabilized approach by 1,000 feet above ground level (AGL), with a go-around mandated if airspeed, descent rate, or lateral deviation exceeded established tolerances. The operator’s training department conducted quarterly crosswind landing proficiency evaluations for all line pilots.

6.2 A review of the operator’s safety reporting system identified three previous hard landing events involving Boeing 737-800 aircraft within the preceding 24 months. All three events occurred during gusty crosswind conditions, with vertical accelerations ranging from 2.1g to 2.6g. In each case, the aircraft remained within structural limits, and no landing gear failures were reported. Corrective actions included enhanced simulator training for crosswind landings, revised approach stabilization criteria, and mandatory post-flight maintenance inspections following vertical accelerations exceeding 2.0g.

6.3 The aircraft was certified under 14 CFR Part 121. Section 25.571 of the Code of Federal Regulations establishes the fatigue and damage tolerance requirements for transport category airplanes. The operator’s maintenance program incorporated the supplemental structural inspection program (SSIP) as required by the regulation. The most recent structural integrity assessment was completed in accordance with the manufacturer’s service bulletin, with no findings of widespread fatigue damage. The operator’s engineering department conducted a post-accident review of the forward fuselage inspection intervals, confirming compliance with all regulatory mandates.

6.4 Section 25.783 of the regulations addresses fuselage door and emergency exit requirements. The accident aircraft was equipped with four Type I emergency exits and two overwing exits. Post-accident inspection confirmed that all exit doors operated normally during the evacuation. The evacuation slide deployment times were recorded at 6.2 seconds for the forward left door and 7.1 seconds for the forward right door, within manufacturer specifications. The cabin crew reported no obstructions or malfunctions during the evacuation sequence.

6.5 The operator’s maintenance program was approved under Section 121.344, which requires a continuous airworthiness maintenance program for scheduled air carriers. The program included mandatory inspections, component life limits, and reliability monitoring. The aircraft’s maintenance records were audited and found to be in compliance with all applicable FAA directives and manufacturer service letters. The operator’s quality assurance department conducted a post-accident audit of the NLG maintenance logs, confirming that all required inspections, lubrication, and component replacements were performed within specified intervals.

6.6 The flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) were recovered and transported to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for readout. Preliminary data indicated that the aircraft was on a 3.0-degree glide path at 140 knots indicated airspeed (KIAS) at 500 feet AGL. At 100 feet AGL, the descent rate increased to 1,200 feet per minute (fpm), and the airspeed decreased to 132 KIAS. The pilot flying applied aft control column input at 50 feet AGL, followed by a flare maneuver that resulted in a touchdown vertical velocity of approximately 1,150 fpm. The FDR recorded a peak vertical acceleration of 2.8g at 1431:45 EDT, followed by a rapid decrease in pitch attitude and forward fuselage contact with the runway surface.

6.7 The National Transportation Safety Board investigator-in-charge coordinated with the FAA, the operator, and the aircraft manufacturer to secure the accident site and preserve evidence. All personnel were interviewed, and maintenance logs, training records, and weather data were collected. The factual information contained in this report is based on the preliminary examination of the wreckage, review of operational records, and analysis of flight recorder data. No conclusions or probable cause determinations are presented herein.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination and analysis conducted by the Structures/Materials Group, in coordination with the Flight Data Recorder (FDR) Group, regarding the nose landing gear (NLG) collapse of a Boeing 737-800, registration N737AE, following a hard landing on August 15, 2021. The scope of this examination encompasses the physical and metallurgical evaluation of the NLG assembly, forward fuselage attachment structure, and associated flight data parameters. The investigation was initiated under NTSB docket number DCA21MA089.

Items examined include the NLG shock strut assembly (Boeing P/N 65-43210-123, S/N 88421), torque link assembly (P/N 65-43211-045, S/N 77201), drag brace (P/N 65-43212-011, S/N 66109), forward fuselage bulkhead 240, and the Honeywell Solid State Flight Data Recorder (SSFDR, P/N 060-0800-00, S/N 9921A). The physical examination was conducted from September 12 through September 24, 2021, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory, Washington, D.C., with supplemental structural measurements performed at Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Everett, Washington. All procedures were executed in accordance with NTSB Group Chairman's Manual, Chapter 4, and applicable ASTM/AMS testing standards.

2. BACKGROUND

The Boeing 737-800 NLG is a dual-wheel, oleo-pneumatic shock strut system designed to absorb vertical landing energy and provide ground steering capability. The system is certified under 14 CFR Part 25, specifically §§ 25.473, 25.723, and 25.729, with a design limit sink rate of 10 ft/sec (600 ft/min) at maximum design landing weight (MDLW) of 146,300 lbs. The outer cylinder is manufactured from 300M vacuum-melted steel per AMS 6414, while the inner piston utilizes 4340 steel per AMS 6415. Torque links are fabricated from 7075-T6 aluminum alloy (AMS 4045), and the drag brace employs 15-5PH stainless steel (AMS 5659). The forward fuselage wheel well structure, including bulkhead 240 and the NLG attachment lugs, was manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems (SAS) under Boeing drawing 65-43000-100. SAS provided material certifications and dimensional inspection reports confirming compliance with Boeing D6-17487 structural requirements.

The accident aircraft accumulated 42,118 flight hours and 28,942 flight cycles at the time of the event. The NLG assembly underwent its last scheduled overhaul at 25,000 cycles in accordance with the Boeing Maintenance Planning Document (MPD) 737-800, Task 32-11-00-001. Routine servicing included nitrogen charging to 1,850 PSI ± 50 PSI and hydraulic fluid replenishment per MIL-PRF-5606G specifications. Maintenance records indicate that a phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) inspection of the drag brace and torque link lugs was outsourced to Island Express Helicopters (IEH) on May 14, 2021. IEH utilized rotorcraft-grade inspection protocols adapted for fixed-wing landing gear components, reporting no detectable discontinuities or crack propagation at that time.

Engine performance data for the incident flight was cross-referenced with the operator's fleet-wide aerodynamic modeling database, which utilizes LEAP-1B turbofan performance curves as a baseline for comparative crosswind and gust load factor calculations across mixed-fleet operations. Although the accident aircraft is equipped with CFM56-7B26 engines, the LEAP-1B dataset was referenced to validate aerodynamic damping coefficients under high-crosswind touchdown conditions. The aircraft's operational history shows no prior NLG structural repairs, with all recorded maintenance actions falling within manufacturer-specified intervals.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

The NLG assembly was received in a collapsed configuration, with the strut displaced approximately 142 mm aft of its fully extended position. Visual inspection revealed catastrophic failure of the outer cylinder at the lower bearing housing interface. The fracture surface was sectioned and prepared for metallurgical analysis per ASTM E340. Macroscopic examination identified a primary fatigue crack originating at the 3 o'clock position, 12.4 mm below the lower dynamic seal groove. The crack propagated circumferentially through approximately 65% of the cross-sectional area before transitioning to a final ductile overload fracture. Beach marks were clearly visible under low-magnification stereomicroscopy, indicating progressive cyclic loading.

Hardness testing was performed on the outer cylinder using a Rockwell C scale indenter per ASTM E18. Ten measurements yielded an average of 48.5 HRC (range: 47.8–49.1 HRC), which falls within the AMS 6414 specification of 46–50 HRC. Tensile testing of extracted coupon samples (ASTM E8) demonstrated a yield strength of 1,480 MPa and an ultimate tensile strength of 1,620 MPa, consistent with heat-treated 300M steel. Fracture toughness testing per ASTM E399 yielded a K_IC value of 78 MPa√m, confirming adequate resistance to crack propagation under static loading conditions.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the fatigue initiation site revealed no evidence of corrosion, pitting, or manufacturing defects. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) per ASTM E1508 confirmed elemental composition within AMS 6414 limits (C: 0.42%, Si: 0.25%, Mn: 0.78%, Cr: 0.82%, Mo: 0.38%, Ni: 1.85%, V: 0.10%). Fretting wear was observed at the lower bearing interface, with oxide debris accumulation indicating micro-movement under high cyclic loads. The torque link upper lugs exhibited plastic deformation measuring 3.2 mm at the pin bore, with secondary cracking detected via fluorescent penetrant inspection (AMS 2644, Type I, Method A). The drag brace remained intact, with no evidence of buckling or fastener failure.

Dimensional inspection of the forward fuselage attachment structure revealed 0.8 mm of plastic deformation at bulkhead 240 lug interfaces, with all 12 attachment bolts (NAS1306-12) remaining torqued within specification (185–205 ft-lbs). No fastener shear or thread stripping was observed. The Spirit AeroSystems (SAS) forward fuselage section maintained structural continuity, with no evidence of skin buckling or frame distortion beyond the immediate NLG bay.

Photographic documentation (Figs. 1–15) captures fracture morphology, strut compression measurements, torque link deformation, and bulkhead attachment integrity. All measurements were recorded using calibrated digital calipers (±0.01 mm) and laser profilometry. The examination confirmed that the NLG failure was initiated by fatigue crack propagation, accelerated by impact loads exceeding design limits.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

Flight data was extracted from the Honeywell SSFDR using the NTSB-approved readout system (v4.2.1) and decoded per ARINC 717 standards. The QAR (Quick Access Recorder) provided supplementary high-frequency parameters at 256 Hz sampling rate. Key parameters analyzed included vertical acceleration (Gz), pitch attitude, radio altitude, NLG strut pressure, wheel speed, and crosswind component.

Timeline reconstruction indicates the following sequence:
- 14:32:18.4 UTC: 500 ft AGL, 145 KIAS, crosswind 22 kts from 270°, crab angle 8°.
- 14:32:24.1 UTC: 100 ft AGL, sink rate 850 ft/min, Gz 1.1, pitch attitude -0.8°.
- 14:32:26.3 UTC: 50 ft AGL, sink rate 1,250 ft/min, Gz 2.4, pitch attitude -1.2°, crosswind gusting to 35 kts.
- 14:32:27.0 UTC: Main gear touchdown, NLG strut pressure 2,850 PSI (normal range: 1,800–2,100 PSI), wheel speed 0 kts.
- 14:32:27.4 UTC: NLG impact, Gz spike to 4.8, strut pressure 4,100 PSI, strut compression 142 mm.
- 14:32:28.1 UTC: NLG collapse, forward fuselage pitch-down moment 1.8°, thrust reverser deployment inhibited by NLG weight-on-wheels signal loss.

The recorded sink rate of 1,250 ft/min at touchdown exceeds the FAR 25.473 design limit of 600 ft/min by approximately 108%. Energy absorption calculations indicate the oleo-pneumatic system was subjected to 2.1 times its rated capacity, resulting in complete strut bottoming-out. The crosswind component of 35 kts, combined with a 12° crab angle at touchdown, induced asymmetric loading on the NLG, as evidenced by the 3 o'clock fatigue crack initiation site.

Engine parameters (CFM56-7B26) show N1 at 42% and N2 at 68% at touchdown, with thrust lever position at idle. The operator's fleet performance database, which incorporates LEAP-1B aerodynamic damping models for crosswind validation, confirmed that the recorded wind shear profile exceeded the aircraft's certified crosswind landing envelope. The NLG steering bypass valve activation was recorded 0.4 seconds prior to touchdown, consistent with standard crosswind landing procedures.

FDR data also indicates that the NLG strut pressure transducer (P/N 65-43215-002) registered a rapid pressure spike from 1,850 PSI to 4,100 PSI within 0.3 seconds, confirming hydraulic fluid compression and nitrogen gas over-pressurization. The QAR wheel speed channels remained at 0 kts throughout the touchdown sequence, indicating no tire spin-up prior to structural failure. All data parameters were cross-verified against Boeing 737-800 Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM) normal operating limits and structural design envelopes.

5. SUMMARY

The physical and metallurgical examination of the nose landing gear assembly revealed a fatigue crack originating at the lower bearing housing of the outer cylinder, propagating through 65% of the cross-section before final ductile overload. Material testing confirmed that the 300M steel outer cylinder met all AMS 6414 specifications, with hardness, tensile strength, and fracture toughness values within certified limits. No manufacturing defects, corrosion, or pre-existing structural anomalies were identified.

Dimensional measurements indicated strut compression of 142 mm, exceeding the design maximum of 115 mm by 23.5%. The forward fuselage bulkhead 240 attachment structure sustained 0.8 mm of plastic deformation but maintained structural integrity, with all fasteners remaining within torque specifications. Non-destructive inspection records from Island Express Helicopters (IEH) confirmed the drag brace and torque link assemblies were free of detectable cracks at the time of the last scheduled inspection.

Flight data analysis established a touchdown sink rate of 1,250 ft/min and a crosswind component of 35 kts, resulting in vertical impact energy exceeding the NLG design limit by approximately 108%. The recorded strut pressure spike to 4,100 PSI and absence of wheel spin-up confirm immediate structural overload upon ground contact. Comparative aerodynamic modeling utilizing LEAP-1B performance baselines validated the operator's crosswind load factor calculations. Spirit AeroSystems (SAS) forward fuselage attachment points exhibited no fastener failure or bulkhead separation.

All findings are documented in accordance with NTSB investigative procedures and are presented as factual observations. No determination of probable cause is included in this report.

INTERVIEW OF MARCUS THORNE, GROUND OPERATIONS SUPERVISOR
Date: August 17, 2021
Time: 14:30 Eastern Daylight Time
Location: Airport Operations Conference Room B, Terminal 3
Interviewer: Investigator Sarah Chen, NTSB Office of Aviation Safety
Witness: Marcus Thorne, Ground Operations Supervisor, Island Express

Q: Mr. Thorne, thank you for making yourself available. For the official record, please state your full name, your current title, and your employer.

A: Yeah, absolutely. Marcus Thorne. I’m the Ground Operations Supervisor for Island Express. We’re the contracted ground handling provider for Spirit Airlines at this station. I’ve been in this role for about four years now, and I’ve been on the ramp for twelve total.

Q: And on August 15, 2021, what was your specific duty assignment and physical location when the incident occurred?

A: I was working the afternoon shift. It was… let me check my notes… I was actually out on the south apron, near the taxiway intersection for Runway 27L. I’d walked out there to verify a delayed baggage transfer, so I was roughly two hundred yards from the threshold. I had a direct, unobstructed view of the final approach path.

Q: Can you walk me through what you observed from the moment you first noticed the aircraft on approach?

A: Sure. It was… I’d say around 16:42, maybe 16:43 local time. The weather had been deteriorating all afternoon. We were getting constant wind advisories, gusts shifting from the northwest. I looked up because I heard the engines spooling down, and I saw the 737 coming in. It was a Spirit flight, obviously, but we just track it by the tail number in our system. The approach looked… unstable, honestly. It was crabbing pretty aggressively. You could see the wings dipping, then the pilot correcting, then dipping again. The crosswind was just brutal. I’ve seen a lot of rough landings, but this one… it just didn’t look right. The nose was pitched up, but the descent rate seemed high. Too high. I remember thinking, “They’re going to have to go around.” But they didn’t.

Q: What happened when the aircraft made contact with the runway?

A: It hit… hard. I mean, really hard. There was this deep, metallic *thud*. Not like a normal touchdown. It sounded like a heavy vehicle hitting a concrete barrier, but… heavier, if that makes sense. Then immediately after, there was a screech, like metal grinding on asphalt, and a puff of dark smoke from the nose area. I saw the nose gear just… fold. It didn’t bounce. It just collapsed forward. The aircraft nosed down, scraped the forward fuselage, and slid maybe… I don’t know, a hundred, hundred-fifty feet before it stopped. The engines were still running for a few seconds, then they spooled down. I could smell jet fuel and… burnt rubber, definitely. And this acrid, hot metal smell. It was pretty intense.

Q: What was your immediate response once you realized what had happened?

A: I keyed my radio right away. Called out “hard landing, nose gear collapse, Runway 27L, south apron.” Dispatch confirmed. I started moving toward the aircraft, but I kept my distance because of the fuel leak risk and the potential for fire. I could see the evacuation slides deploying on the left side. The overwing exits opened too. Passengers were coming out, some were sliding down, others were just… jumping. It was chaotic but… controlled, I guess. The crew was doing their job. I saw the lead flight attendant at the L1 door, waving people away from the wing and toward the triage zone. I grabbed the nearest emergency response kit from the service vehicle and headed over to assist.

Q: Did you interact with any specific equipment or personnel during the evacuation and initial response?

A: Yeah. Once the aircraft was stationary and the engines were shut down, I coordinated with the ARFF trucks. They were on scene in under two minutes. I helped direct the triage area. We pulled out the MED Plug from the ground response cart—uh, the medical emergency plug, it’s part of our standard ground medical kit, connects to the portable oxygen and suction units. We used it to stabilize a passenger who’d twisted an ankle and was having trouble breathing. Just a precaution, really. Also, I had to verify that the ground power unit wasn’t connected, obviously, and that the area was clear of FOD. I made sure the ramp crew stayed behind the safety line until ARFF gave the all-clear.

Q: Were you aware of any regulatory or procedural requirements that came into play during or after the event?

A: Oh, absolutely. I mean, we’re trained on 14 CFR part 121 for all our ground handling procedures. Specifically, when it comes to emergency evacuations and post-incident reporting, we follow the guidelines under 14 CFR 121.344. That’s the one about emergency equipment and evacuation duties, right? I had to make sure our ground crew didn’t interfere with the evacuation, that we maintained the safety perimeter, and that we documented everything for the FAA and the airline’s safety office. Island Express has a strict protocol for this, but it’s all built around those regs. I remember thinking, “Okay, don’t touch the aircraft, don’t cross the yellow line, just secure the area and log the times.” We also had to ensure the MED Plug and all other emergency gear were accounted for and logged per the manual.

Q: Can you give me a rough timeline of the events from touchdown to full evacuation?

A: Let’s see… Touchdown was around 16:43. The slides deployed within… maybe ten, fifteen seconds. The first passengers were on the ground by 16:44. ARFF arrived at 16:45. I’d say the last passenger was clear by 16:52, maybe 16:53. The crew came out last, around 16:54. So, roughly ten to eleven minutes total. It felt longer, obviously, when you’re out there, but the clock says about that. I’ve got the exact times logged in my shift report if you need them. I can pull that up.

Q: Did you notice anything unusual about the aircraft’s systems or the ground conditions that might have contributed?

A: The wind was the main thing. We had gusts up to twenty-five, thirty knots, shifting direction. The runway was dry, but the crosswind component was definitely pushing the limits. I didn’t see any hydraulic fluid spraying before touchdown, just the smoke after. And the nose gear… it just didn’t absorb the impact. I’m not a mechanic, but I’ve seen gear failures before. This looked like a structural overload. The forward fuselage was scraped, paint stripped, but no fire. Thank God. I also noticed the windsock was practically horizontal. It was just… nasty out there.

Q: Were you involved in any post-incident briefings or documentation?

A: Yeah. I filed the initial ground incident report with Island Express and copied Spirit’s station manager. We had a debrief the next morning. I had to reference the 14 CFR part 121 requirements again for the official statement. Also, we checked all our ground equipment, made sure the MED Plug and the rest of the emergency medical gear were accounted for and functional. Everything was logged. I also spoke with the NTSB field investigator who came out on the 16th. Gave him my radio recordings and the timeline. I think I covered everything, but if you need me to clarify the exact sequence of the slide deployment or the triage setup, I can walk through it again.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Thorne. We’ll take a copy of that report. Do you have any questions for us?

A: No, I think that’s it. Just… let me know if you need me to clarify anything. I’ll be around the station for the rest of the week.

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
Docket No. FAA-2021-0892; NTSB Safety Recommendation A-22-014
NTSB Accident Number: DCA21MA087
Date of Occurrence: August 15, 2021
Regulatory References: 14 CFR Part 121, Subpart L; 14 CFR 25.783; Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2012-09-04
Subject: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Regulatory Oversight Report and Safety Recommendation Response Regarding Hard Landing and Nose Landing Gear Structural Failure Involving Island Express Air, Inc.

2. BACKGROUND
On August 15, 2021, a Boeing 737-800, registered to and operated by Island Express (hereinafter referred to as “the Operator” or “IEA”), sustained substantial damage following a high-energy hard landing event during a gusty crosswind approach. The incident resulted in the catastrophic collapse of the forward landing gear assembly, triggering an emergency evacuation. All passengers and crew evacuated safely without serious injury. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) initiated a major accident investigation under 49 U.S.C. § 1131, assigning docket number DCA21MA087.

The regulatory framework governing this occurrence is established under Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR), specifically Part 121, which prescribes operating requirements for domestic, flag, and supplemental operations. The Operator’s approved maintenance program, as mandated by 14 CFR 121.344, requires continuous airworthiness monitoring, adherence to manufacturer service bulletins, and strict compliance with applicable Airworthiness Directives. Historically, the Federal Aviation Administration has issued AD 2012-09-04 to address fatigue cracking and structural degradation in main and nose landing gear trunnion assemblies for Boeing 737 Next Generation series aircraft. Compliance with this directive is mandatory for continued airworthiness under 14 CFR 39.13.

Furthermore, the structural design certification of the airframe is governed by 14 CFR 25.783, which establishes load factor and structural integrity requirements for fuselage doors and adjacent pressure bulkhead interfaces. While 14 CFR 25.783 primarily addresses door retention and emergency egress pathways, the structural load paths evaluated under this section are intrinsically linked to the forward fuselage and nose gear attachment points during high-impact vertical and lateral loading events. The investigation also examined the Operator’s fleet modernization initiatives, including the integration of CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines on select airframes under a supplemental type certificate (STC) program. The LEAP-1B powerplant installation necessitates revised weight and balance calculations, which directly influence landing gear stress tolerances during abnormal approach profiles.

Prior to this occurrence, the NTSB issued Safety Recommendation A-19-042, urging enhanced crosswind training and real-time meteorological data integration for Part 121 operators. The FAA’s response, documented in Docket No. FAA-2019-0551, acknowledged the recommendation and initiated rulemaking under 14 CFR 121.400 to standardize adverse weather dispatch protocols. The current incident necessitates a reevaluation of those protocols, particularly concerning Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) dispatch authorizations and operational control procedures under 14 CFR 121.373.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive review of Island Express Air, Inc.’s operational and maintenance records indicates partial compliance with established regulatory mandates. The Operator’s maintenance tracking system confirms that AD 2012-09-04 was executed within the prescribed compliance window, and all required non-destructive testing (NDT) inspections of the nose landing gear trunnion and drag brace assemblies were documented in accordance with the approved maintenance program. However, the investigation revealed that the Operator’s dispatch release procedures under 14 CFR 121.373 failed to adequately account for rapidly deteriorating crosswind components exceeding the aircraft’s demonstrated crosswind limitations. The flight crew’s decision to continue the approach, despite wind shear advisories and gust factors exceeding 25 knots, contravened the Operator’s own Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and the manufacturer’s Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM).

From a structural engineering perspective, the collapse of the nose landing gear was determined to be a consequence of dynamic vertical and lateral load factors that exceeded the design ultimate load limits established under the type certificate data sheet (TCDS). While 14 CFR 25.783 does not explicitly govern landing gear structural certification, the forward fuselage load path analysis demonstrated that the impact forces propagated through the door sill and adjacent longeron structures, exacerbating the NLG failure mode. The investigation further identified that the Operator’s fleet-wide integration of the LEAP-1B engine variant introduced incremental forward center-of-gravity (CG) shifts, which altered the static and dynamic load distribution on the nose gear during touchdown. Although the supplemental type certificate (STC) for the LEAP-1B installation was approved under 14 CFR 21.113, the Operator’s weight and balance control program did not adequately update the landing gear stress tolerance matrices to reflect the modified CG envelope.

Regulatory oversight actions initiated by the FAA’s Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) included an immediate ramp inspection, a Principal Operations Inspector (POI) review of dispatch records, and a Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) audit of the Operator’s continuing analysis and surveillance system (CASS). These actions confirmed that while the Operator maintained baseline compliance with 14 CFR Part 121, Subpart L, significant deficiencies existed in the integration of real-time meteorological data into the operational control framework. Furthermore, the Operator’s MMEL dispatch authorizations permitted the deferral of certain weather radar and wind shear detection systems, which, when combined with the gusty crosswind environment, degraded situational awareness and compromised approach stability.

A critical gap in the current regulatory framework pertains to the lack of mandatory, real-time crosswind component monitoring and automated dispatch inhibition protocols for Part 121 operators. Existing guidance under Advisory Circular (AC) 120-71A provides recommended practices but does not establish enforceable standards for wind shear and gust factor integration into the flight release process. Additionally, the current MMEL framework under 14 CFR 121.628 does not sufficiently restrict dispatch when multiple weather-related systems are deferred in high-risk meteorological environments.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
In response to the findings detailed herein, the Federal Aviation Administration mandates the following corrective actions and compliance timelines for Island Express Air, Inc. and all similarly certificated Part 121 operators:

1. Revised Dispatch and Operational Control Procedures: The Operator shall amend its General Operations Manual (GOM) and dispatch protocols to incorporate mandatory crosswind component verification and automated wind shear inhibition thresholds. Compliance with 14 CFR 121.373 shall be demonstrated through a revised operational control checklist that requires dual verification of gust factors and demonstrated crosswind limits prior to final approach clearance. This action shall be completed within 90 days of this directive’s issuance.

2. Enhanced Training and Proficiency Requirements: Pursuant to 14 CFR 121.400, the Operator shall implement a mandatory recurrent training module focused on high-energy hard landings, crosswind recovery techniques, and go-around decision-making in gusty conditions. Training shall include full-flight simulator (FFS) scenarios replicating the dynamic load profiles observed in DCA21MA087. Initial compliance shall be achieved within 120 days, with full fleet proficiency verification completed within 180 days.

3. Structural and Maintenance Program Updates: The Operator shall conduct a fleet-wide review of nose landing gear stress tolerance matrices, specifically accounting for forward CG shifts associated with the LEAP-1B engine installation. All affected aircraft shall undergo enhanced NDT inspections of the NLG trunnion, drag brace, and forward fuselage attachment points in accordance with the revised compliance schedule for AD 2012-09-04. The Operator shall submit a revised Continuing Airworthiness Maintenance Program (CAMP) to the PMI for approval within 60 days.

4. MMEL and System Deferral Restrictions: The Operator shall revise its Minimum Equipment List (MEL) to prohibit the simultaneous deferral of weather radar, predictive wind shear systems, and crosswind landing guidance systems when operating in terminal areas with forecasted gust factors exceeding 20 knots. This restriction shall be implemented within 45 days and shall be subject to quarterly FAA compliance audits.

5. Regulatory Oversight and Follow-Up Schedule: The FAA’s FSDO shall conduct a comprehensive surveillance audit of the Operator’s operational control and maintenance programs at 90-day, 180-day, and 365-day intervals. The Principal Operations Inspector (POI) and Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) shall submit consolidated compliance reports to the FAA’s Office of Aviation Safety (AVS) and the NTSB’s Office of Aviation Safety. Failure to meet the stipulated compliance milestones will result in enforcement action under 14 CFR 13.19, including potential suspension of the Operator’s Part 121 certificate.

This directive is issued under the authority of 49 U.S.C. § 44701 and 14 CFR Part 119. All correspondence, compliance documentation, and audit submissions shall be directed to the FAA Docket Management System under Docket No. FAA-2021-0892. The Federal Aviation Administration remains committed to ensuring the highest standards of airworthiness, operational safety, and regulatory compliance across the National Airspace System.

HEADLINE: All 162 Survive After Boeing 737 Nose Gear Collapses in Gusty Crosswind Landing

BYLINE: Elena Rostova, Global Aviation News
DATELINE: CHICAGO, Ill. —

A Boeing 737-800 carrying 156 passengers and six crew members suffered a hard landing and collapsed its nose landing gear on Sunday, Aug. 15, 2021, at O’Hare International Airport. Despite the violent touchdown and substantial airframe damage, emergency crews successfully evacuated everyone aboard without serious injury.

The incident occurred during a turbulent approach marked by sudden, gusty crosswinds that pushed the aircraft off its stabilized glide path. As the jet touched down, the forward landing gear buckled under the impact, sending the nose slamming onto the concrete runway. The aircraft skidded several hundred feet before coming to a halt, triggering an immediate emergency response. Fire crews and paramedics were on scene within minutes, deploying evacuation slides and assisting passengers to safety.

“We are relieved to report that all souls on board have been accounted for and are receiving medical evaluation,” said NTSB Investigator-in-Charge David Chen during a Monday press briefing. “The National Transportation Safety Board has dispatched a go-team to Chicago to begin a comprehensive examination of the wreckage, flight data recorders, and cockpit voice recordings.” Federal Aviation Administration officials confirmed the runway was closed for nearly 12 hours for debris removal and forensic documentation. “The crew followed established emergency protocols, and the evacuation was executed efficiently,” FAA regional director Maria Gonzalez stated. “We are working closely with the NTSB to determine the exact sequence of events.” Airline spokesperson Thomas Vance added, “Our priority remains the well-being of our passengers and crew. We are providing full support, including accommodations and counseling, as we cooperate with investigators.”

The aircraft, operated by a major U.S. carrier under 14 CFR Part 121 regulations—which govern commercial airline operations, crew training, and maintenance standards—was completing a routine domestic flight from Denver to Chicago. The Boeing 737-800, a workhorse of modern commercial aviation, is powered by CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, known for their fuel efficiency and reliability. The airframe’s forward fuselage section, including critical structural components, was manufactured by Spirit Aerosystems, a leading aerospace supplier based in Kansas. While the airline has not yet released maintenance logs, the aircraft was reportedly up to date on all scheduled inspections prior to departure.

Aviation safety analysts suggest the combination of severe weather and landing dynamics likely played a central role. “A hard landing in a crosswind can place extreme stress on the nose gear, especially if the aircraft touches down with excessive vertical speed or if the pilot struggles to maintain directional control,” said Dr. Alan Mercer, a former commercial pilot and aviation safety professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. “The nose gear is designed to absorb significant force, but there are limits. If the aircraft bounced or landed nose-heavy, the structural load could exceed design parameters.” Mercer cautioned that investigators will need to review telemetry data to determine whether wind shear, pilot technique, or a mechanical anomaly contributed to the collapse. He also noted that modern aircraft are equipped with a MED Plug—a specialized cabin safety device designed to isolate smoke or hazardous fumes from the passenger compartment—though it was not activated during this incident.

For those on board, the final moments of the flight were terrifying. “We hit the runway like a truck,” said passenger Marcus Lin, 34, who was traveling for a family wedding. “The plane shuddered violently, the nose dropped, and sparks flew past the windows. But the flight attendants were incredible. They kept us calm, opened the doors, and got everyone out in under two minutes.” Lin’s wife, Sarah, who was waiting at the gate, described the agonizing wait. “When the emergency sirens started, my heart stopped. I just kept praying. Seeing him walk out with a blanket and a paramedic was the best moment of my life.” Several passengers reported minor bruises and sprains from the evacuation slides, but no life-threatening injuries were reported.

Nose gear collapses, while dramatic, are relatively rare in commercial aviation. The Boeing 737-800 has an extensive safety record, with millions of flights logged worldwide since its introduction in the late 1990s. However, similar incidents have occurred under adverse weather conditions. In 2018, a 737-800 operated by a European carrier experienced a nose gear failure during a storm in Istanbul, resulting in minor injuries and a lengthy runway closure. The NTSB and FAA have historically emphasized that modern training programs rigorously prepare pilots for crosswind landings and hard touchdown scenarios. Airlines operating under Part 121 must adhere to strict maintenance schedules, and any structural anomaly triggers immediate grounding until cleared by regulators.

The investigation remains in its early stages. NTSB technicians are currently downloading data from the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, which will be analyzed at the agency’s laboratory in Washington, D.C. Weather data from the airport’s automated surface observing system will be cross-referenced with the aircraft’s approach profile. The airline has voluntarily grounded the specific aircraft for a thorough structural inspection, while the broader fleet continues normal operations pending regulatory review. “We expect preliminary findings within 30 days, but a final report could take up to a year,” Chen said. “Our focus is on understanding exactly what happened so we can prevent it from happening again.”

1. INTRODUCTION

On behalf of the Operator’s Engineering and Maintenance Division, I submit this technical analysis as a formal party submission to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigative hearing regarding the August 15, 2021, hard landing and subsequent nose landing gear (NLG) collapse involving a Boeing 737-800. As Chief Structural and Systems Engineer for the carrier, my role in this investigation encompasses the review of maintenance records, structural integrity assessments, regulatory compliance documentation, and operational data correlation. This submission is intended to provide a comprehensive, evidence-based evaluation of the aircraft’s airworthiness status, maintenance history, and structural response to the landing event.

The scope of this document is strictly limited to the technical and engineering factors within the Operator’s purview. It addresses the condition of the aircraft prior to the incident, the structural and mechanical response during the landing sequence, and the alignment of our maintenance and operational programs with applicable Federal Aviation Regulations (FARs) and industry standards. While the investigation will undoubtedly examine meteorological conditions, flight crew decision-making, and aircraft design parameters, this submission focuses on demonstrating that the aircraft was maintained in full compliance with its approved maintenance program, that no latent structural or mechanical deficiencies contributed to the NLG collapse, and that the failure mode is consistent with a single-event overload exceeding certified design limits. The analysis draws upon flight data recorder (FDR) parameters, post-accident metallurgical examinations, maintenance tracking logs, and regulatory compliance documentation, all of which have been entered into the public docket.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On August 15, 2021, at approximately 14:32 local time, the subject Boeing 737-800 (Registration N-XXXX) was conducting a scheduled passenger flight under instrument meteorological conditions. The aircraft was on final approach to Runway 27L when it encountered rapidly shifting wind conditions, including a sustained crosswind component of 28 knots with gusts reported up to 38 knots. The aircraft touched down with a recorded vertical sink rate of approximately 1,150 feet per minute, followed by a peak vertical acceleration of 3.8 G. The nose landing gear collapsed aft and slightly leftward, resulting in substantial damage to the forward fuselage, nose gear well, and lower avionics bay. All 162 passengers and 6 crew members evacuated safely via the forward and overwing exits.

Key docket materials relevant to this submission include:
- Docket Exhibit 12-A: FDR and CVR parameter logs, including vertical acceleration, pitch attitude, lateral drift, and control surface deflections.
- Docket Exhibit 15-C: Post-accident structural inspection and metallurgical analysis report.
- Docket Exhibit 18-B: Complete maintenance history and deferred defect log for the preceding 12 months.
- Docket Exhibit 21-D: Meteorological data, including terminal aerodrome forecasts (TAFs), automated weather observing system (AWOS) recordings, and pilot reports (PIREPs).

The aircraft’s maintenance program is fully approved under 14 CFR § 121.344, which mandates a continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) tailored to the operator’s fleet and operational environment. All scheduled inspections, component overhauls, and service bulletin implementations were current at the time of the incident. The forward fuselage and nose section, originally manufactured by Spirit Aerosystems (SA), were inspected per the OEM’s structural repair manual (SRM) and showed no evidence of manufacturing anomalies, corrosion, or fatigue cracking. The nose gear trunnion, drag brace, and steering actuator were all within service life limits and had been inspected during the most recent C-check.

While this specific airframe is equipped with CFM56-7B turbofans, the Operator’s engineering division maintains a cross-platform structural health monitoring program that incorporates vibration and load-tracking methodologies originally developed for CFM LEAP-1B equipped aircraft. This comparative data framework has been instrumental in validating our predictive maintenance algorithms and ensuring consistent load-path monitoring across the fleet. Furthermore, the aircraft’s fuel system wiring, bonding, and tank venting configurations were verified compliant with Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88 (SFAR 88), which governs fuel tank system fault tolerance and ignition source prevention. Post-impact inspection confirmed that fuel system integrity was maintained, with only minor seepage from a fractured vent line, and no ignition sources were present during or after the evacuation.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

The technical evaluation of this event requires a multidisciplinary synthesis of aerodynamic loading, structural mechanics, maintenance compliance, and operational data. The primary objective is to determine whether the NLG collapse resulted from a progressive structural deficiency, maintenance oversight, or a single-event overload condition.

3.1 Landing Dynamics and Load Path Analysis
FDR data (Docket Exhibit 12-A) indicates that the aircraft crossed the threshold at 142 knots indicated airspeed, with a lateral drift angle of approximately 6 degrees. The flight crew initiated a crab-to-sideslip transition during the flare, but rapid wind shear and directional gusts disrupted the alignment sequence. At touchdown, the main landing gear contacted the runway first, followed by a delayed nose gear contact 1.4 seconds later. The vertical acceleration trace shows a sharp spike to 3.8 G, significantly exceeding the 2.5 G static certification limit for the NLG assembly. Concurrently, lateral load sensors recorded a 1.9 G side-load component due to the asymmetric touchdown and continued crosswind drift.

The combined vertical and lateral loading created a resultant bending moment at the NLG trunnion and drag brace attachment points that exceeded the yield strength of the 300M steel components. Metallurgical analysis (Docket Exhibit 15-C) confirms that the fracture surfaces exhibit classic ductile overload characteristics, including microvoid coalescence and shear lip formation. There is no evidence of fatigue striations, stress corrosion cracking, or improper heat treatment. The failure initiated at the lower drag brace clevis pin, propagated through the trunnion housing, and resulted in aft collapse of the gear assembly. This failure mode is entirely consistent with a single-event exceedance of the certified design envelope, not a progressive degradation.

3.2 Maintenance and Airworthiness Compliance
The Operator’s maintenance program, approved under Section 121.344, follows a reliability-centered maintenance (RCM) framework aligned with MSG-3 principles. All scheduled inspections, including the 600-flight-hour NLG lubrication and torque verification, were completed within the required intervals. Docket Exhibit 18-B confirms zero open deferred items related to the landing gear, steering system, or forward fuselage structure. Non-destructive testing (NDT) records from the most recent heavy maintenance visit show no anomalies in the nose gear well, bulkhead attachments, or Spirit Aerosystems-manufactured forward fuselage panels.

The Operator’s engineering division has implemented a fleet-wide structural health monitoring (SHM) program that tracks load cycles, vibration spectra, and component wear rates. This program, which incorporates data analytics originally validated on LEAP engine-equipped airframes, has demonstrated high predictive accuracy for identifying early-stage fatigue and wear. In the 12 months preceding the incident, the subject aircraft’s NLG load cycle count was 14,200, well below the 25,000-cycle overhaul threshold. No maintenance actions or service bulletins were pending that would have altered the structural integrity of the nose gear assembly.

3.3 Regulatory and Industry Standard Alignment
The aircraft’s maintenance and operational procedures are fully compliant with FAA Advisory Circular 120-71A, which outlines standard operating procedures for crosswind and gusty wind landings. The Boeing 737-800 Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM) specifies a maximum demonstrated crosswind component of 33 knots, with gusts not to exceed 10 knots above the steady-state value. The reported conditions on August 15, 2021, approached and intermittently exceeded these limits. While the aircraft is certified to withstand higher loads during emergency or abnormal conditions, the FCOM explicitly recommends a go-around if crosswind components exceed 30 knots with gusts above 35 knots, or if sink rate exceeds 800 fpm during the flare.

The Operator’s compliance with SFAR 88 requirements further demonstrates a robust approach to post-impact safety. The regulation mandates rigorous evaluation of fuel tank wiring, bonding, and venting to prevent ignition sources. Post-accident inspection confirmed that all SFAR 88-mandated modifications were installed, and the fuel system’s fault-tolerant design prevented catastrophic fuel release or fire, directly contributing to the successful evacuation.

3.4 Comparative Engineering Assessment
Industry data from similar hard landing events involving narrow-body aircraft indicates that NLG collapse typically occurs when vertical acceleration exceeds 3.2 G in combination with lateral drift angles greater than 5 degrees. The subject event’s 3.8 G vertical load and 6-degree drift angle place it in the upper percentile of documented exceedances. Structural finite element analysis (FEA) conducted by the Operator’s engineering team, using OEM-provided load path models, confirms that the nose gear assembly would have remained intact under normal operational parameters. The collapse is attributable to the simultaneous application of extreme vertical and lateral forces, which created a moment arm that exceeded the drag brace’s ultimate load capacity.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on a comprehensive review of flight data, structural analysis, maintenance records, and regulatory compliance documentation, the Operator’s Engineering and Maintenance Division concludes the following:

1. The nose landing gear collapse was the direct result of a single-event structural overload caused by combined vertical and lateral landing forces that exceeded the certified design limits of the NLG assembly.
2. There is no evidence of manufacturing defects, maintenance deficiencies, or progressive structural degradation that contributed to the failure. The aircraft was maintained in full compliance with its FAA-approved maintenance program under 14 CFR § 121.344, and all inspections, service bulletins, and airworthiness directives were current.
3. The forward fuselage structure, manufactured by Spirit Aerosystems, performed as designed. No anomalies were identified in the nose gear well, bulkhead attachments, or surrounding airframe structure.
4. The aircraft’s fuel system, maintained in accordance with SFAR 88 requirements, maintained post-impact integrity, preventing ignition and facilitating a safe evacuation.
5. The primary contributing factors to the event were meteorological conditions (rapidly shifting crosswinds and gusts exceeding 35 knots) and operational parameters (high sink rate, delayed flare, and asymmetric touchdown) that collectively exceeded the aircraft’s certified landing envelope.

The Operator acknowledges the complexity of crosswind landing operations and the inherent challenges of real-time wind shear assessment. However, the technical evidence clearly demonstrates that the aircraft’s structural and maintenance systems functioned within their designed parameters until the moment of exceedance. The failure mode is consistent with a rare, high-energy landing event rather than a systemic or maintenance-related deficiency.

To enhance safety and mitigate the risk of similar events, the Operator recommends the following industry-wide improvements:
- Implementation of real-time, predictive crosswind and wind shear alerting systems integrated with electronic flight bags (EFBs) and flight management computers (FMCs).
- Standardization of mandatory go-around criteria across operators, with explicit thresholds for sink rate, lateral drift, and gust intensity during the flare phase.
- Enhanced flight data monitoring (FDM) parameters to track crosswind landing performance and provide targeted training feedback.
- Collaboration with OEMs and regulatory bodies to develop next-generation landing gear load monitoring systems capable of providing real-time structural health feedback during high-energy landings.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In response to the August 15, 2021, incident, the Operator has implemented immediate and long-term corrective actions to reinforce operational safety, enhance training protocols, and improve predictive maintenance capabilities.

5.1 Actions Already Taken
- Fleet-Wide Safety Bulletin: Issued within 72 hours of the incident, emphasizing strict adherence to crosswind landing limits, mandatory go-around criteria, and proper crab-to-sideslip transition techniques.
- Updated Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs): Revised the B737-800 crosswind landing checklist to include explicit sink rate and lateral drift thresholds. Pilots are now required to initiate a go-around if vertical speed exceeds 800 fpm at 50 feet AGL or if crosswind gusts exceed 35 knots.
- Enhanced Flight Data Monitoring (FDM): Deployed new FDM algorithms to track crosswind landing parameters, including touchdown sink rate, lateral drift angle, and control surface deflection. Data is reviewed weekly by the Flight Operations Quality Assurance (FOQA) team.
- Simulator Training Integration: All B737-800 captains and first officers have completed mandatory simulator sessions focusing on high-crosswind approaches, wind shear recovery, and go-around decision-making under degraded weather conditions.
- Maintenance Program Audit: Conducted a comprehensive audit of all landing gear maintenance records, torque verification logs, and NDT reports across the fleet. No discrepancies were identified, and all records were verified against Section 121.344 compliance requirements.

5.2 Proposed Future Improvements
- Predictive Load Monitoring System: The Operator is collaborating with OEMs and avionics suppliers to develop a real-time landing gear load monitoring system. This system will utilize strain gauge telemetry and machine learning algorithms to predict structural stress accumulation and provide maintenance alerts before component limits are approached.
- Enhanced Weather Data Integration: Working with meteorological service providers to integrate high-resolution, runway-specific wind shear and crosswind data into the EFB. This will provide flight crews with real-time, predictive wind trend analysis during final approach.
- Regulatory Advocacy: The Operator will submit a formal recommendation to the FAA and IATA to update crosswind landing guidance, including standardized go-around thresholds and enhanced training requirements for gusty wind operations.
- Cross-Platform Engineering Synergy: The Operator will expand its structural health monitoring program to include data sharing across CFM56-7B and LEAP-1B equipped aircraft. This will improve predictive maintenance accuracy and enable earlier detection of load-path anomalies across the fleet.
- Human Factors and Decision Support: Implementation of a cockpit decision-support tool that provides real-time feedback on approach stability, sink rate, and crosswind components. The system will issue aural and visual alerts if parameters approach go-around thresholds, reducing reliance on subjective pilot assessment during high-workload phases.

The Operator remains fully committed to aviation safety, regulatory compliance, and continuous improvement. The technical evidence presented in this submission demonstrates that the aircraft was airworthy, properly maintained, and operated within established parameters until the moment of exceedance. By implementing the corrective actions outlined above, the Operator aims to enhance pilot decision-making, improve predictive maintenance capabilities, and contribute to industry-wide safety advancements. We stand ready to provide additional technical data, maintenance records, or expert testimony as required by the NTSB investigative process.

TO: All Maintenance Control, Line Maintenance, Base Maintenance, Quality Assurance, and Flight Operations Liaison Personnel
FROM: Director of Maintenance & Engineering / Quality Assurance Division
DATE: 22 August 2021
SUBJECT: QUALITY ALERT QA-2021-084: Post-Hard Landing Nose Landing Gear Inspection & Crosswind Approach Protocol Updates
REF: WO-21-8842, SB-737-32-1145, Internal Memo ENG-2021-07, NTSB Docket Entry DCA21MA089

PURPOSE:
This Quality Alert mandates immediate inspection protocols for the nose landing gear (NLG) assembly following the 15 August 2021 hard landing event. It establishes revised work instructions, clarifies component handling procedures, and reinforces compliance with 14 CFR part 121 operational and maintenance standards. All affected personnel must implement these directives by the close of business 25 August 2021.

BACKGROUND:
On 15 August 2021, a Boeing 737-800 (Registration N737XX) experienced a hard landing during a gusty crosswind approach at [Redacted] International Airport. The aircraft sustained substantial damage, including a complete collapse of the nose landing gear. All passengers and crew evacuated safely without injury. Preliminary data from the Quick Access Recorder (QAR) and initial teardown inspections indicate vertical and lateral load factors exceeded design limits during touchdown, compounded by asymmetric weight distribution and delayed thrust reverser deployment.

While the primary failure mode is attributed to operational exceedance, our internal review identified secondary concerns regarding maintenance documentation, component traceability, and inspection rigor for forward fuselage and NLG interface structures. Spirit AeroSystems (SAS) manufactured the forward fuselage section and NLG door assemblies for this airframe. Historical service bulletins and our internal reliability tracking show that repeated high-load events can induce micro-fractures in the NLG trunnion mount and adjacent fuselage frames. Additionally, recent audits revealed inconsistencies in the installation and torque verification of the Main Engine Deck (MED) Plug during post-flight inspections, which can obscure access to critical forward bulkhead fasteners.

DETAILS:
Effective immediately, the following directives apply to all 737 Classic/NG and MAX fleet aircraft under our maintenance control:

1. Post-Hard Landing NLG Inspection Protocol (Ref: WI-MNT-737-044 Rev. C)
   - Any landing exceeding 2.0G vertical acceleration or 1.5G lateral acceleration, as recorded by the Flight Data Recorder (FDR) or QAR, triggers a mandatory Level 3 NLG inspection.
   - Inspectors must perform eddy current testing on the NLG trunnion lugs, drag brace fittings, and forward fuselage frame 40-42 interface.
   - All findings must be documented in the Aircraft Maintenance Log (AML) and cross-referenced with Work Order WO-21-8842.
   - If crack propagation is suspected, the aircraft must be grounded until a non-destructive testing (NDT) Level III technician completes a phased array ultrasonic inspection.

2. Spirit AeroSystems Component Traceability & Handling
   - All SAS-supplied forward fuselage panels and NLG door assemblies must be verified against the latest revision of the Component Maintenance Manual (CMM 32-11-00).
   - Any replacement part must carry a valid FAA Form 8130-3 or EASA Form 1. Parts lacking proper certification tags will be quarantined per QA-PROC-09.
   - SAS has issued a service advisory (SAS-ADV-2021-07) regarding fastener torque values on the NLG door hinge brackets. Maintenance crews must apply the updated torque specification of 185 ± 5 in-lbs using calibrated torque wrenches (Cal Due: within 30 days).

3. MED Plug Installation & Access Verification
   - The Maintenance Equipment Deck (MED) Plug (P/N 737-ENG-PLUG-04) must be removed prior to any forward bulkhead or NLG interface inspection.
   - Reinstallation requires a dual-verification sign-off by a certified airframe mechanic and a quality inspector.
   - Torque sequence must follow the star-pattern method outlined in AMM 71-00-00. Failure to properly seat the MED Plug can compromise aerodynamic sealing and restrict access to critical structural inspection points.

4. Regulatory & Operational Compliance
   - All maintenance actions must comply with 14 CFR part 121, specifically §121.363 (Maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations) and §121.373 (Continuing analysis and surveillance).
   - Flight Operations has been directed to reinforce crosswind landing technique training and go-around decision criteria. Maintenance Control will coordinate with Dispatch to ensure QAR data is downloaded and analyzed within 24 hours of any reported hard landing.

ACTION REQUIRED:
- Line Maintenance Supervisors: Distribute this alert to all shift personnel. Verify completion of mandatory read-and-sign acknowledgment via the LMS portal by 25 August 2021.
- Quality Assurance Inspectors: Audit 100% of open NLG-related work orders. Flag any non-compliant torque records or missing MED Plug verification tags. Submit audit findings to QA-Reports@company.com by 27 August 2021.
- Engineering & Reliability Team: Update the fleet reliability tracking database to include the new G-load thresholds. Cross-reference LEAP-1B and CFM56-7B engine mount stress data to determine if shared inspection intervals require adjustment. While the subject aircraft is NG-series, the forward fuselage architecture and inspection jigs are standardized across our entire 737 fleet, including LEAP-1B powered variants.
- Training Department: Develop a 2-hour recurrent module on post-hard landing structural assessment and crosswind approach limitations. Roll out to all A&P technicians and IA inspectors by 15 September 2021.
- All Personnel: Do not release any aircraft to service until the revised inspection checklist (Form QA-CHK-737-NLG-02) is completed and countersigned. Any deviation requires written approval from the Director of Maintenance.

This alert will remain active until superseded by a formal Service Bulletin or FAA Airworthiness Directive. All documentation generated under this directive will be retained per our records retention policy and may be subject to regulatory review.

Questions regarding technical implementation should be directed to the Engineering Support Desk (Ext. 4402) or the Quality Assurance Hotline (Ext. 4410).
