SYNOPSIS
On August 15, 2021, at approximately 1432 local time, a Boeing 737-800, registered NXXXXX, operated under 14 CFR Part 121, experienced a hard landing at a regional commercial airport resulting in the collapse of the nose landing gear. Initial information indicates the aircraft was conducting a scheduled passenger flight during a period of gusty crosswind conditions. All occupants evacuated without serious injury, and the aircraft sustained substantial damage to the forward fuselage and nose gear assembly.

INITIAL FINDINGS
Preliminary factual information has been compiled from flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) downloads, air traffic control communications, and initial maintenance log reviews. Early data suggests the aircraft approached the runway with a lateral wind component that may have approached or exceeded the operator’s published crosswind limitations, though exact values remain under verification. Initial witness accounts from ground personnel and passengers describe a firm touchdown followed by a pronounced forward pitch and a distinct metallic impact sound. Weather observations recorded at the time of the event indicate surface winds of 22 knots gusting to 34 knots, with a crosswind component of approximately 18 knots, alongside scattered precipitation and reduced visibility.

Preliminary examination of the airframe revealed substantial deformation to the nose landing gear strut, forward pressure bulkhead, and lower forward fuselage skin. The main landing gear remained extended and structurally intact. Initial maintenance record reviews indicate compliance with applicable airworthiness directives, including Airworthiness Directive 2012-09-04, which pertains to specific structural inspection intervals for the forward fuselage section. The aircraft’s powerplant configuration has been verified as CFM56-7B series; documentation confirms that LEAP-1B engines are not installed on this airframe variant, though engine maintenance logs and fleet-wide parts tracking protocols are being reviewed for any anomalous thrust or autothrottle behavior during the final approach phase. Fuel system integrity was assessed in accordance with Special Federal Aviation Regulation No. 88 guidelines, and no evidence of fuel leakage or ignition source was identified during the initial site survey. Structural damage assessment is being conducted with reference to 14 CFR 25.571 damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation requirements to determine the extent of primary and secondary structural compromise.

INVESTIGATION STATUS
The National Transportation Safety Board has activated the following investigative groups: Operations, Structures, Systems, Flight Recorders, Weather, and Human Performance. The investigation is being conducted in accordance with established NTSB protocols, with participation from designated parties including the Federal Aviation Administration, the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, the operator, and Spirit AeroSystems, Inc., which is providing technical support regarding forward fuselage and nose gear attachment structures.

All critical evidence has been secured at the accident site. The FDR and CVR have been transported to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for readout and analysis. The collapsed nose landing gear assembly, associated hydraulic lines, and forward fuselage components have been documented, tagged, and preserved for metallurgical and mechanical examination. Maintenance records, crew training files, and dispatch documentation have been collected and are undergoing preliminary review. The operator’s standard operating procedures for crosswind landings and go-around criteria are being evaluated against Part 121 operational requirements.

Initial examinations are focused on determining the sequence of events leading to the hard landing and subsequent gear collapse. The Structures Group is conducting a detailed survey of the nose gear trunnion, drag brace, and forward bulkhead attachment points. The Systems Group is analyzing hydraulic pressure data, brake application records, and nose wheel steering inputs. The Operations Group is reviewing crew communications, approach briefings, and decision-making processes during the final approach segment. All findings at this stage remain preliminary and are subject to revision as additional data is processed and analyzed.

NEXT STEPS
Planned investigative activities include the completion of FDR and CVR data transcription, detailed metallurgical analysis of the failed nose gear components, and computational modeling of the landing impact loads. The Weather Group will finalize a microscale meteorological analysis to characterize wind shear and gust profiles along the final approach path. The Human Performance Group will conduct confidential interviews with the flight crew, cabin crew, and air traffic control personnel to establish operational context and workload factors.

A preliminary factual report is anticipated within 30 days, pending laboratory results and party submissions. The investigation will continue to evaluate maintenance compliance, structural integrity, and operational decision-making in accordance with established regulatory frameworks. All conclusions regarding the sequence of events, contributing factors, and probable cause will be deferred until the completion of comprehensive testing, data correlation, and public hearing proceedings. This document serves as an initial procedural record and does not constitute a final determination. Further updates will be issued as the investigation progresses and additional evidence is evaluated.

GROUP CHAIRMAN’S FACTUAL REPORT
OPERATIONAL FACTORS, AIRCRAFT SYSTEMS, AND WRECKAGE EXAMINATION
NTSB ACCIDENT NUMBER: DCA21MA087
DATE OF REPORT: October 12, 2021

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On August 15, 2021, at 14:32:15 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT), a Boeing 737-800, registration N737IE, experienced a hard landing resulting in the collapse of the nose landing gear during the landing roll. The accident occurred on Runway 27L at Coastal Regional International Airport (KCRI), located at latitude 33°56′45″N, longitude 118°24′12″W. The runway elevation is 125 feet mean sea level (MSL). The accident site was situated approximately 1,850 feet beyond the runway threshold, within the designated touchdown zone.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator
The aircraft was a Boeing 737-800, serial number 34567, manufactured in 2008. The aircraft was registered to a commercial leasing entity and operated under a wet lease agreement by Island Express. The operator maintained an FAA-approved Operations Specification (OpSpec) authorizing scheduled passenger transport services. The aircraft was configured for 162 passenger seats, with a standard two-class cabin layout.

1.3 Flight Operations and Regulatory Framework
The flight was conducted as Island Express Flight 442, a scheduled domestic passenger service from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (KATL) to Coastal Regional International Airport (KCRI). The flight operated under the provisions of 14 CFR Part 121, specifically as a scheduled air carrier operation. The flight plan was filed under Instrument Flight Rules (IFR), with an estimated en route time of 2 hours and 14 minutes. The flight departed KATL at 11:48:30 EDT and arrived at KCRI at 14:32:15 EDT. The flight was conducted in accordance with the operator’s General Operations Manual (GOM) and the Boeing 737-800 Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM).

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Experience
The Captain, age 48, held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The Captain possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on March 12, 2021, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 14,820 hours, with 6,450 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The Captain’s most recent line check was completed on May 18, 2021, with satisfactory performance noted in all evaluated maneuvers. The Captain’s proficiency check was current and valid through November 2021.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Experience
The First Officer, age 34, held an ATP certificate with multi-engine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The First Officer possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on June 5, 2021, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 4,120 hours, with 1,890 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The First Officer’s most recent line check was completed on July 22, 2021, with satisfactory performance documented. The First Officer’s proficiency check was current and valid through January 2022.

2.3 Duty/Rest and Training Records
Both flight crewmembers were within the duty and rest limitations prescribed by 14 CFR Part 121, Subpart Q. The Captain reported 10 hours and 15 minutes of rest prior to reporting for duty. The First Officer reported 11 hours and 40 minutes of rest. Both crewmembers completed recurrent training at an FAA-approved training center on April 10, 2021. Training records indicate completion of simulator sessions covering adverse weather operations, crosswind landing techniques, wind shear recovery, and rejected landing procedures. The training syllabus included 4.0 hours of simulator time dedicated to gusty crosswind approaches and landings, with performance metrics meeting operator standards.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Specifications and History
The accident aircraft was a Boeing 737-800 equipped with CFM56-7B26 engines. The airframe accumulated 42,115 total flight hours and 28,940 total flight cycles at the time of the accident. The aircraft was maintained under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) approved by the FAA. The last heavy maintenance check (C-check) was completed on February 14, 2021, at 41,890 flight hours. The aircraft was released to service with no outstanding deferred maintenance items.

3.2 Maintenance and Airworthiness Directives
Maintenance records indicate compliance with all applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) and Service Bulletins (SBs) as of the date of the accident. Specifically, the aircraft was in compliance with Airworthiness Directive 2012-09-04, which mandated repetitive inspections of forward fuselage structural fasteners and door plug attachment points. The most recent inspection per AD 2012-09-04 was performed on June 30, 2021, at 41,980 flight hours, with no discrepancies noted. All inspection results were documented in the operator’s maintenance tracking system and signed off by an FAA-certified Airframe and Powerplant (A&P) mechanic with Inspection Authorization (IA).

3.3 Systems and Component Configuration
The aircraft was equipped with a standard dual-channel autopilot, dual flight management computers, and a digital flight data acquisition unit. The landing gear system consisted of a retractable tricycle configuration with dual-wheel main landing gear (MLG) and a dual-wheel nose landing gear (NLG). The NLG was equipped with a shimmy damper, steering actuator, and downlock mechanism. The aircraft was fitted with a DOOR PLUG assembly (part number 65-43210-1) installed on the forward left fuselage, designated as a structural access panel replacement for a former emergency exit. The DOOR PLUG was secured with 24 high-shear titanium fasteners and inspected per manufacturer structural repair manual (SRM) guidelines. All primary flight control surfaces, hydraulic systems (A and B), and electrical buses were operational at the time of departure.

3.4 Weight, Balance, and Performance Data
The aircraft’s takeoff weight was 148,200 pounds, with a calculated center of gravity (CG) at 24.8% MAC. The landing weight was calculated at 136,450 pounds, with a CG at 25.1% MAC. The calculated Vref speed for the landing configuration was 138 knots. The approach speed (Vapp) was set at 148 knots, incorporating a 10-knot additive for gusty wind conditions per Boeing FCOM procedures. The aircraft’s performance calculations indicated a required landing distance of 5,850 feet on a dry runway, well within the available 10,500 feet of Runway 27L.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Synoptic Conditions and Surface Observations
A surface high-pressure system was centered over the central United States, with a cold front advancing from the northwest. The frontal passage resulted in rapidly shifting wind directions and increased gust factors across the terminal area. Surface observations indicated a crosswind component from the west-northwest, with sustained winds and significant gusts reported throughout the approach phase.

4.2 METAR/TAF and Automated Weather Data
The Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR) for KCRI at 14:25 EDT, seven minutes prior to the accident, was recorded as: KCRI 151425Z 27022G35KT 10SM SCT035 BKN050 24/12 A2998 RMK AO2 PK WND 28038/1418 SLP148 T02440122. The Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) issued at 11:00 EDT forecasted winds from 260° at 18 knots, gusting to 30 knots, with temporary conditions of 270° at 25 knots, gusting to 38 knots, valid through 18:00 EDT. The Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) recorded a peak wind gust of 38 knots at 14:18 EDT, with a sustained wind direction of 270° and a crosswind component of approximately 24 knots relative to Runway 27L.

4.3 Pilot Reports and Wind Shear Indicators
Multiple pilot reports (PIREPs) were filed between 13:45 and 14:20 EDT indicating moderate turbulence and occasional wind shear on final approach to Runway 27L. One report from a preceding aircraft noted a 15-knot airspeed fluctuation at 500 feet above ground level (AGL). The Low-Level Wind Shear Alert System (LLWAS) at KCRI recorded a 12-knot wind shear alert at 14:28 EDT, with a differential between the runway centerline and threshold sensors. The flight crew acknowledged the LLWAS alert and wind shear advisory during the approach briefing.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Impact Site and Debris Distribution
The initial touchdown point was located 1,250 feet beyond the runway threshold, marked by a 4-foot-long rubber deposit on the runway surface. The aircraft contacted the runway with a vertical acceleration of 2.8 G, as recorded by the flight data recorder. Following initial touchdown, the aircraft bounced approximately 12 feet before a second, more forceful impact occurred 320 feet further down the runway. The second impact resulted in the collapse of the nose landing gear. The aircraft subsequently slid forward for 1,100 feet, leaving a continuous gouge mark in the runway surface measuring 18 inches in width and 0.5 inches in depth. Debris was confined to a linear distribution along the runway centerline, with no off-runway scatter.

5.2 Landing Gear and Structural Examination
Examination of the nose landing gear revealed a complete aft collapse of the strut assembly. The NLG downlock mechanism was found in the unlocked position, with the shear pin fractured at the primary load-bearing interface. The steering actuator cylinder exhibited plastic deformation consistent with a high-energy vertical impact. The main landing gear remained fully extended and locked, with no evidence of structural failure or tire deflation. The MLG shock struts showed compression marks within normal operational limits. The NLG wheel well structure sustained localized buckling of the forward bulkhead and adjacent longeron sections.

5.3 DOOR PLUG and Fuselage Assessment
The DOOR PLUG assembly on the forward left fuselage was examined post-accident. The plug remained securely attached to the airframe, with all 24 fasteners intact and showing no signs of fatigue cracking or shear failure. The surrounding skin exhibited minor cosmetic abrasion from runway debris, but no structural compromise was identified. The plug’s internal pressure relief valve and sealing gasket were inspected and found to be within manufacturer specifications. The forward fuselage skin sustained a 14-inch longitudinal tear adjacent to the NLG wheel well, consistent with the upward displacement of the collapsed strut.

5.4 Flight Data and Cockpit Voice Recorder Review
The flight data recorder (FDR) captured 256 parameters at a sampling rate of 1 Hz. Data indicated that the aircraft crossed the runway threshold at 152 feet AGL, with an indicated airspeed of 151 knots and a descent rate of 850 feet per minute. At touchdown, the pitch attitude was 2.1 degrees nose-up, and the vertical acceleration peaked at 2.8 G. The autothrottle system was in the IDLE mode, and the thrust levers were positioned at 15 degrees aft of idle. The cockpit voice recorder (CVR) captured standard approach callouts, including “minimums,” “runway in sight,” and “wind shear alert.” No abnormal system warnings or crew distress calls were recorded prior to touchdown.

5.5 Evacuation and Emergency Response
Following the cessation of forward motion, the flight crew initiated an emergency evacuation. All eight passenger slides deployed successfully. The evacuation was completed in 78 seconds, with 142 passengers and 6 crewmembers exiting the aircraft. Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting (ARFF) units arrived on scene within 45 seconds of the initial alert. No post-impact fire occurred, and all occupants were accounted for without serious injury. The evacuation complied with the operator’s emergency procedures and met the 90-second regulatory benchmark.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Standard Operating Procedures
Island Express maintained a comprehensive Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) manual for adverse weather operations. The SOP specified a maximum demonstrated crosswind component of 33 knots for dry runway conditions, with a recommended go-around threshold of 25 knots for sustained crosswinds exceeding 20 knots with gust factors greater than 10 knots. The operator’s GOM required flight crews to execute a stabilized approach by 1,000 feet AGL, with specific parameters for airspeed, descent rate, and configuration. The flight crew’s approach briefing documented the crosswind conditions, and the crew elected to continue the approach in accordance with company policy.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents and Safety Data
A review of the NTSB aviation accident database and FAA Service Difficulty Reports (SDRs) identified 14 similar hard landing events involving Boeing 737-800 aircraft in gusty crosswind conditions between 2015 and 2020. Of these, 6 resulted in nose landing gear collapse, and 3 resulted in substantial fuselage damage. Common contributing factors documented in these reports included high descent rates at touchdown, delayed thrust reduction, and wind shear encounters below 500 feet AGL. The operator’s internal safety management system (SMS) had previously issued a safety bulletin in 2019 emphasizing crosswind landing techniques and go-around decision-making, which was incorporated into recurrent training curricula.

6.3 Regulatory Compliance and Advisory Guidance
The aircraft and operator were in compliance with 14 CFR Part 121 requirements for airworthiness, crew qualifications, and operational procedures. Specifically, the aircraft’s emergency equipment configuration met the requirements of 14 CFR 121.344, which mandates the stowage, accessibility, and inspection of emergency equipment for passenger evacuation. All life vests, oxygen masks, and evacuation slides were inspected within the required intervals and were fully functional during the accident evacuation. The operator’s maintenance program adhered to FAA Advisory Circular 120-16E, which provides guidance on continuous airworthiness maintenance programs. Additionally, the operator’s flight operations manual incorporated guidance from FAA Advisory Circular 120-71A, which addresses standard operating procedures for flight deck crewmembers, including crosswind approach and landing techniques.

6.4 Fuel System and SFAR 88 Compliance
The aircraft’s fuel system was inspected in accordance with Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 (SFAR 88), which mandates fuel tank ignition prevention measures for transport category aircraft. Compliance with SFAR 88 was verified through the operator’s maintenance records, which documented the installation of fuel quantity indicating system (FQIS) wiring modifications, fuel tank vent line inspections, and lightning protection enhancements. Post-accident examination of the fuel tanks revealed no evidence of fuel leakage, vapor ignition, or structural compromise. The fuel system remained intact, and all fuel lines, pumps, and valves were secured within their designated mounting brackets. The aircraft’s fuel quantity at the time of the accident was recorded at 18,400 pounds, with a balanced distribution between the left and right main tanks.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination, testing, and data analysis conducted by the NTSB Structures and Materials Group in support of the investigation into the August 15, 2021, hard landing event involving a Boeing 737-800, registration N737XX. The scope of this examination encompasses the forward fuselage lower lobe structure, nose landing gear (NLG) assembly, associated attachment fittings, and the correlation of physical damage with recorded flight data parameters. The examination was conducted between August 20 and August 28, 2021, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., and at the operator's primary maintenance facility in Seattle, Washington.

The investigation team reviewed maintenance records, engineering drawings, and operational logs provided by Island Express Helicopters (IEH), the certificate holder operating the aircraft under a 14 CFR Part 121 air carrier certificate. The examination focused on determining the structural response of the NLG assembly to the recorded impact loads, evaluating material properties against original equipment manufacturer (OEM) specifications, and documenting fracture morphology, crack propagation characteristics, and fastener hole deformation. All testing and analysis were performed in accordance with NTSB investigative protocols, ASTM International standards, and Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) aerospace material specifications. Photographic documentation, dimensional measurements, and metallurgical cross-sections were cataloged under NTSB exhibit numbers 2021-08-15-STR-001 through 2021-08-15-STR-047.

2. BACKGROUND

The accident aircraft, a Boeing 737-800, was manufactured under Type Certificate A16WE and certified in accordance with 14 CFR 25.571, which establishes damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation requirements for transport category aircraft structures. The nose landing gear assembly, Boeing Part Number 65-43210-1, Serial Number 789012, was originally manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems (SAS) as a major structural subassembly and delivered to the final assembly line in 2008. The NLG strut, torque links, drag brace, and upper/lower trunnion fittings are fabricated from vacuum-arc remelted 300M steel, conforming to AMS 6415, with a specified minimum ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 260 ksi and a yield strength of 220 ksi. The assembly is heat-treated per AMS 2750E and shot-peened to induce compressive residual stresses in high-stress transition zones.

The aircraft accumulated 42,150 flight hours and 28,400 flight cycles at the time of the event. The operator's maintenance program, approved under 14 CFR Part 121, mandated supplemental structural inspection program (SSIP) compliance, including eddy current and ultrasonic inspections of the NLG trunnion lugs at 15,000-cycle intervals. The most recent heavy maintenance visit, completed 1,240 flight hours prior to the accident, included a full NLG overhaul, bearing replacement, and non-destructive testing (NDT) of all primary load paths. Maintenance logs confirm compliance with Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2012-09-04, which required repetitive inspections of the rudder power control unit and associated control linkages; this directive was completed 142 flight hours prior to the event and documented in the aircraft's continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP).

The operator's engineering department had previously evaluated a fleet modernization initiative involving LEAP-1B powerplant integration for improved fuel efficiency and emissions compliance. However, the accident aircraft retained its original CFM56-7B26 engine configuration, and no structural modifications to the NLG or forward fuselage were implemented as part of the powerplant evaluation. Fuel system safety compliance, including wiring harness routing and vent line isolation within the NLG wheel well, was maintained in accordance with Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 (SFAR 88) requirements, with the most recent fuel tank system review completed 890 flight hours prior to the event.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

Physical examination of the recovered NLG assembly revealed catastrophic failure of the lower trunnion fitting, with complete separation of the forward lug from the main strut body. The fracture surface exhibited distinct regions of fatigue crack propagation and final ductile overload. Macroscopic examination identified a primary fatigue crack originating at the 3 o'clock position of the forward lug bore, measuring 1.24 inches in length along the circumferential axis. Secondary cracking was observed at the 9 o'clock position, measuring 0.68 inches. The fracture surface was cleaned per ASTM E114 ultrasonic cleaning protocols and examined under stereomicroscopy at 10x to 50x magnification. Beach marks were clearly visible, indicating progressive crack growth over multiple loading cycles.

Dimensional measurements of the lug bore revealed localized plastic deformation, with an ovality of 0.018 inches exceeding the OEM tolerance of 0.005 inches. Fastener hole diameters measured 0.3125 inches nominal, with no evidence of fretting corrosion or bearing wear. The torque link assembly exhibited permanent set, with the upper link deflected 14.2° from its neutral position. Drag brace pivot pins showed scoring consistent with high-impact loading, but no fracture or material loss was observed.

Material analysis was conducted to verify compliance with AMS 6415 specifications. Specimens were extracted from the non-fractured regions of the lower trunnion and subjected to tensile testing per ASTM E8. Results indicated a yield strength of 224 ksi and an ultimate tensile strength of 268 ksi, within the specified range. Hardness testing per ASTM E18 yielded an average Rockwell C value of 52.4, consistent with the required 50-54 HRC range. Chemical analysis via optical emission spectroscopy (OES) confirmed composition within AMS 6415 limits: 0.42% C, 1.65% Si, 0.78% Mn, 0.82% Cr, 0.41% Mo, 1.58% Ni, and 0.008% P.

Fracture mechanics evaluation was performed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). The fatigue initiation site exhibited intergranular cracking with secondary oxide formation, indicating exposure to atmospheric moisture during service. The final fracture zone displayed dimpled rupture morphology, characteristic of ductile overload. No evidence of hydrogen embrittlement, stress corrosion cracking, or manufacturing defects was identified. Dye penetrant inspection per AMS 2644 Type II, Method C, revealed no additional surface-breaking cracks in the remaining NLG structure.

Photographic documentation (NTSB-2021-08-15-001 through 045) captures the fracture morphology, lug deformation, and surrounding structural damage. The forward fuselage lower lobe skin exhibited localized buckling and fastener hole elongation, with maximum deformation measuring 0.032 inches. The NLG bay door hinges were sheared, and the hydraulic retraction actuator cylinder was bent 18.5° from its longitudinal axis. All measurements were recorded using calibrated digital calipers (±0.001 in) and coordinate measuring machine (CMM) verification.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

Flight data recorder (FDR) parameters were extracted from the solid-state memory unit and decoded using NTSB-approved software. The FDR recorded 88 parameters at a sampling rate of 4 Hz for critical flight dynamics and 1 Hz for system status indicators. Data synchronization with the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) and quick access recorder (QAR) was verified using time-code alignment and radio altitude cross-referencing.

The approach phase was characterized by a stabilized descent until 500 feet above ground level (AGL), at which point the aircraft encountered a 28-knot crosswind gusting to 35 knots, with a 15° crosswind component relative to runway heading. The First Officer, serving as pilot flying, maintained a 145-knot indicated airspeed (KIAS) on final approach, consistent with the calculated Vref + 10 knots for the reported weight and configuration. At 200 feet AGL, the vertical speed increased to 850 feet per minute (fpm), and the pitch attitude decreased to -1.8°. Control column inputs recorded a 12° aft deflection at 50 feet AGL, followed by a rapid 8° forward input at touchdown.

Touchdown occurred at 14:23:17 local time, with a recorded sink rate of 1,250 fpm and a vertical acceleration (Gz) peak of +3.4g. The NLG squat switch transitioned from "air" to "ground" at 14:23:17.3, followed by a rapid Gz spike to +3.8g at 14:23:17.6. The pitch attitude at touchdown was -2.1°, and the aircraft yawed 4.2° to the right, consistent with the crosswind component. The main landing gear (MLG) touchdown preceded NLG contact by 0.4 seconds, with MLG Gz peaking at +2.1g.

Comparison with normal operational parameters indicates the sink rate exceeded the 600 fpm threshold that triggers a hard landing inspection per Boeing Service Bulletin 737-32-1245. The recorded Gz of +3.4g surpassed the 14 CFR 25.571 limit load factor of 2.5g for landing gear certification, approaching the ultimate load factor of 3.75g. The crosswind component of 28 knots remained within the 33-knot demonstrated crosswind limit for dry runway operations, but the gust profile and rapid sink rate created a combined loading condition that exceeded the design envelope for the NLG lower trunnion.

FDR data also recorded hydraulic system pressure fluctuations, with NLG retraction line pressure dropping from 3,000 PSI to 1,850 PSI within 0.2 seconds of touchdown, indicating structural failure of the hydraulic manifold or line rupture. The NLG steering angle remained at 0.0° throughout the event, and the anti-skid system did not activate prior to NLG collapse. The First Officer's control inputs, while within normal operational ranges for crosswind correction, did not mitigate the excessive vertical descent rate.

Data correlation with structural analysis confirms that the fatigue crack in the lower trunnion reduced the residual load-carrying capacity of the fitting. Finite element modeling (FEM) of the lug geometry, using the measured crack length of 1.24 inches, indicates a stress intensity factor (K) of 42 ksi√in, approaching the fracture toughness (KIC) of 300M steel at 55 ksi√in. The impact load of +3.4g, combined with the crosswind-induced bending moment, exceeded the remaining structural margin, resulting in catastrophic failure.

5. SUMMARY

The examination of the nose landing gear assembly and associated forward fuselage structure revealed a fatigue crack originating at the forward lug bore of the lower trunnion fitting, measuring 1.24 inches in length. Material testing confirmed compliance with AMS 6415 specifications, with yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, hardness, and chemical composition within OEM tolerances. Fracture surface analysis indicated progressive fatigue crack propagation followed by ductile overload failure.

Flight data recorder parameters recorded a touchdown sink rate of 1,250 fpm and a peak vertical acceleration of +3.4g, exceeding the 600 fpm hard landing threshold and the 2.5g limit load factor specified in 14 CFR 25.571. The aircraft encountered a 28-knot crosswind gusting to 35 knots, with a 15° crosswind component, during the final approach phase. The First Officer's control inputs were consistent with standard crosswind correction techniques, but did not arrest the excessive vertical descent rate.

Maintenance records demonstrate compliance with 14 CFR Part 121 requirements, including completion of AD 2012-09-04 and adherence to the operator's supplemental structural inspection program. The aircraft's fuel system safety configuration remained in compliance with SFAR 88, and no structural modifications related to the LEAP-1B powerplant evaluation were implemented on this airframe. The NLG assembly, manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems, exhibited no manufacturing defects or material anomalies outside of the documented fatigue crack.

The structural failure of the nose landing gear lower trunnion resulted from the combined effects of pre-existing fatigue crack propagation and impact loads exceeding the residual strength of the fitting. All measurements, test results, and data correlations are documented in the referenced exhibits and laboratory reports.

INTERVIEW OF DAVID CHEN, SENIOR MAINTENANCE CONTROLLER
Date: August 16, 2021
Time: 09:30 Local
Location: Airport Operations Building, Conference Room B
Interviewer: NTSB Investigator J. Vance
Witness: David Chen, Senior Maintenance Controller, Ramp & Line Maintenance

Q: Please state your full name and current position for the record.
A: David Chen. I’m the Senior Maintenance Controller for line operations here at the hub. Basically, I oversee the ramp technicians, coordinate with dispatch and flight ops, and handle any unscheduled maintenance events that pop up during the day.

Q: Can you describe your location and what you were doing on August 15, 2021, around the time of the incident?
A: Yeah. I was in the maintenance control office, which is on the second floor overlooking the south ramp. It was... let me think... around 14:45, maybe 14:50 local time. We had a pretty active afternoon. The weather was deteriorating, wind picking up out of the west. I remember looking out the window because the windsock was practically horizontal. We were tracking a Boeing 737-800 inbound from the coast. Flight 442, I believe. Or maybe 447. Doesn’t really matter, it was the one that came in hard.

Q: Walk me through what you observed as the aircraft approached and landed.
A: Okay. So, I’m watching the final approach. The tower had already switched to the crosswind runway, 27L. You could see the crab angle, the nose was pointed into the wind, but the wings were level. Standard technique. Then, maybe... I’d say about two hundred feet out, there was a sudden gust. The aircraft just... dropped. Not a lot, but enough. The main gear touched down first, which is normal, but it was heavy. Really heavy. I heard it through the glass, honestly. A deep, metallic thud that you feel in your chest. Then the nose came down. Too fast. Way too fast. It slammed. I saw the nose strut compress, then just... fold. Like a lawn chair giving out. The nose dropped onto the runway, sparks flew, and it started sliding.

Q: What happened immediately after touchdown?
A: The pilots got it stopped. I’d say within... maybe three, four hundred feet of the touchdown point. The engines spooled down, you could hear the reversers kick in, but then they cut them. Probably because of the nose gear collapse, didn’t want to ingest debris. Then the evacuation started. I saw the slides deploy on the left side. The right side... I think the forward door was jammed or something, but the aft doors opened. Passengers started coming out. It was chaotic but controlled. No fire, just a lot of smoke from the tires and maybe some hydraulic fluid burning off.

Q: Did you respond to the scene?
A: Yeah, I grabbed my radio and headed out with two line techs, Miller and Rodriguez. We met the ARFF trucks at the perimeter. By the time we got there, it was about 15:10. The aircraft was sitting on its nose, forward fuselage resting on the concrete. The nose gear was completely collapsed, strut bent back, wheel well door torn. We did a quick walk-around to check for fuel leaks, hot brakes, anything immediate. Everything seemed contained. The captain was already doing his headcount. All souls accounted for.

Q: You mentioned maintenance procedures. Were there any specific regulatory or maintenance considerations that came to mind during your initial assessment?
A: Oh, absolutely. First thing I’m thinking is, we’re operating under 14 CFR part 121, so the maintenance release and dispatch requirements are strict. But this was an unscheduled event, obviously. My immediate concern was securing the aircraft and starting the damage assessment. I pulled up the maintenance logs on my tablet. I was cross-referencing the last heavy check. We’d just come out of a C-check about six weeks prior. I remember looking at the forward fuselage section—Spirit Aerosystems builds those, right? Yeah, the 41 section. I was checking for any stress fractures or skin buckling around the nose gear well. The impact was severe, but the structure held. No catastrophic failure, just localized damage.

Q: Were there any specific airworthiness directives or service bulletins you considered relevant to the landing gear or fuselage?
A: Yeah, I was thinking about Airworthiness Directive 2012-09-04. That’s the one covering the nose gear downlock and actuator inspections. We’d complied with it during the last check, but after a hard landing like that, you always go back to the ADs. I made a note to pull the gear log and verify the downlock pin installation and the actuator torque values. Also, I was looking at the emergency exit operation. Section 25.783 covers the door mechanisms and evacuation requirements. The slides deployed fine, but the forward left door was sluggish. I suspect the impact distorted the door frame slightly, which is common in nose-gear collapses. We had to manually override it to get the last few passengers out.

Q: You mentioned checking logs. Were there any other aircraft or equipment you were managing that day that might be relevant?
A: Well, it was a busy day. We had a mixed fleet on the ramp. I was also tracking a couple of 737 MAXs that had just arrived. Those have the LEAP-1B engines, which are completely different from the CFM56s on the 800. I was actually reviewing a maintenance deferral on one of the MAXs earlier that morning, something about a MED plug on the engine cowl. Not related to this incident, but it’s just... it’s all running through your head when you’re managing the board. You’re juggling multiple aircraft, different systems, different compliance requirements.

Q: Did you interact with any other organizations or personnel on scene?
A: Yeah. ARFF was first, obviously. Then the airline’s safety team showed up. We also had Island Express Helicopters on standby for a potential medevac, but thankfully, nobody needed it. They were hovering near the perimeter for about ten minutes, then they stood down. I spoke with the lead paramedic, and he confirmed all passengers were ambulatory. Minor injuries, mostly bumps and bruises from the slide deployment. The captain was cooperative, gave us the quick debrief. He mentioned the crosswind was gusting to 35 knots, with a 15-knot cross component. He said he tried to de-crab, but the wind shear caught him on final.

Q: Can you describe the condition of the aircraft when you first got close enough to inspect it?
A: Sure. The nose was resting on the runway, forward fuselage skin was scraped, but no penetration. The nose gear strut was buckled, the torque link was sheared. The wheel well doors were hanging open, hydraulic lines were weeping, but the main reservoirs were intact. I remember the smell—burnt rubber, hot metal, and that sharp ozone smell from the electrical systems. The left main gear looked fine, right main was a little hot, but within limits. We chocked the mains, installed the tow bar, and started the jacking procedure. It took about two hours to get it stabilized and ready for tow to the hangar.

Q: Is there anything else you’d like to add about the sequence of events or your observations?
A: Just that... it was a textbook hard landing in bad weather, but the crew handled it well. The evacuation was fast. I’ve seen worse, but this one... the nose gear just gave out. I think the impact load exceeded the design limits, but the structure did its job. We followed all the protocols, documented everything, and handed it over to the heavy maintenance team. I’ll be pulling the QAR data later, but from a line maintenance perspective, we secured the scene, verified no immediate hazards, and started the damage assessment per the AMM. That’s about it.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Chen. We’ll follow up if we need clarification.
A: Yeah, no problem. I’ll be around.

TO: National Transportation Safety Board, Office of Aviation Safety
FROM: Federal Aviation Administration, Aircraft Certification Service, Transport Standards Branch
RE: Response to Safety Recommendation A-22-045; Compliance Review Docket No. FAA-2022-0845
REFERENCE: NTSB Accident Number DCA21MA187; Date of Occurrence: August 15, 2021

1. SUBJECT / REFERENCE
This correspondence constitutes the Federal Aviation Administration’s formal response to National Transportation Safety Board Safety Recommendation A-22-045, issued pursuant to the investigation of the August 15, 2021, hard landing event involving a Boeing 737-800, Type Certificate No. A16WE. The referenced incident occurred during a gusty crosswind approach, resulting in a high-energy touchdown, collapse of the nose landing gear (NLG), and substantial airframe damage. All occupants successfully evacuated via approved emergency egress routes. This document addresses regulatory compliance, airworthiness directives, and structural certification requirements as they pertain to 14 CFR 25.783, 14 CFR Part 121.344, and associated maintenance program oversight. Docket No. FAA-2022-0845 has been established to track all corrective actions, manufacturer data submissions, and operator compliance milestones.

2. BACKGROUND
The Boeing 737-800 is certified under 14 CFR Part 25, Airworthiness Standards: Transport Category Airplanes. The aircraft’s type design incorporates multiple fuselage access panels, including the Maintenance Equipment Door (MED) plug, which is manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems, Inc. (SAS) and installed during final assembly. Under the certification basis, the MED plug is evaluated in accordance with 14 CFR 25.783, which establishes structural, latching, and load-bearing requirements for fuselage doors and equivalent access closures. The regulation mandates that such components must withstand ultimate loads without failure, maintain positive latching under dynamic stress, and not impede emergency evacuation procedures.

Island Express Air, Inc. (hereinafter referred to as Island Express, IEA, or the Operator) operates the subject aircraft under 14 CFR Part 121, Air Carrier and Operator Certification. The Operator’s approved maintenance program, developed pursuant to 14 CFR Part 121.344, incorporates manufacturer service bulletins, Airworthiness Directives (ADs), and Master Minimum Equipment List (MMEL) provisions. Prior to the August 15, 2021, occurrence, AD 2019-14-08 required repetitive inspections of forward fuselage structural interfaces, including access panel fastener torque verification. No outstanding AD compliance deficiencies were recorded in IEA’s maintenance tracking system at the time of the event.

The NTSB’s preliminary findings indicated that during the asymmetric NLG collapse, the forward fuselage experienced localized load redistribution that exceeded the certified static margins for the MED plug latching assembly. The plug exhibited permanent deformation, raising questions regarding the applicability of 14 CFR 25.783(c) to non-primary access closures under combined vertical and lateral impact vectors. The FAA initiated a targeted regulatory review to evaluate whether the existing type design data, supplemental type certificate (STC) modifications, and operator maintenance protocols adequately address high-energy landing scenarios.

3. FINDINGS / ANALYSIS
A comprehensive review of maintenance records, forensic metallurgical analysis, and manufacturer engineering documentation has been completed. The analysis yields the following determinations:

a. Compliance Status of the Operator/Manufacturer: Island Express demonstrated substantial compliance with 14 CFR Part 121.344 maintenance scheduling and recordkeeping requirements. All mandated inspections were performed within prescribed intervals. However, post-accident teardown revealed that the MED plug latching mechanism, as supplied by Spirit AeroSystems, Inc., did not retain positive engagement when subjected to the dynamic load spectrum generated during the NLG collapse sequence. The plug’s retention hardware exhibited shear deformation consistent with loads exceeding the ultimate design limits specified in § 25.783. Spirit AeroSystems’ production quality assurance records confirm that the component met static certification criteria at the time of manufacture, but the type design data package lacks explicit dynamic load correlation for asymmetric gear failure modes.

b. Regulatory Oversight Actions Taken: The FAA conducted an unannounced surveillance audit of IEA’s maintenance control center and line maintenance facilities. The audit verified adherence to approved procedures, MMEL dispatch limitations, and AD compliance tracking. Concurrently, the Aircraft Certification Service initiated a design review under 14 CFR 21.21 to evaluate whether the existing type certificate adequately addresses structural load path redistribution during high-impact landings. The review identified a regulatory gap: current certification standards do not explicitly require dynamic impact testing of secondary fuselage access panels under combined vertical and lateral loading conditions. While 14 CFR 25.783 establishes ultimate load requirements, the test methodology historically relies on static load application, which may not fully capture transient impact forces.

c. Gaps Identified in Regulatory Framework: The investigation highlights a deficiency in the integration of emergency evacuation integrity and structural load certification. The MMEL for the 737-800 permits dispatch with certain access panel discrepancies under specific conditions, but does not account for degraded structural margins during abnormal landing events. Furthermore, the absence of a mandatory dynamic load evaluation for the MED plug under § 25.783 creates an oversight vulnerability. The FAA acknowledges that the current regulatory framework requires enhancement to ensure that all fuselage closures, regardless of primary or secondary classification, maintain positive latching and structural continuity under high-energy impact scenarios.

4. ACTIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
To address the identified deficiencies and ensure continued airworthiness, the FAA has initiated the following corrective actions and compliance mandates:

a. Corrective Actions Required: The FAA will issue Emergency Airworthiness Directive (EAD) 2022-18-09, effective immediately upon publication in the Federal Register. The directive mandates a one-time detailed inspection of all MED plug latching assemblies on affected 737-800 series aircraft, followed by installation of a reinforced retention bracket and upgraded torque-verified fasteners. Operators must revise their maintenance programs in accordance with 14 CFR Part 121.344 to incorporate the new inspection criteria and torque verification procedures. Spirit AeroSystems, Inc. will submit revised engineering data to the Transport Standards Branch, including dynamic load test results and updated installation instructions, to support a supplemental type certificate (STC) or type design amendment.

b. Timeline for Compliance: Initial inspection and temporary reinforcement must be completed within 30 calendar days of EAD publication. Permanent modification and updated maintenance documentation must be implemented within 90 calendar days. Operators must submit compliance verification reports to the FAA Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) within 10 business days of completion. The FAA will track compliance through Docket No. FAA-2022-0845 and will issue enforcement actions for non-compliance pursuant to 14 CFR 39.13.

c. Follow-up Inspection or Review Schedule: The FAA will conduct biannual compliance audits of Island Express and other affected operators to verify adherence to the revised maintenance program and MMEL restrictions. A comprehensive regulatory review of 14 CFR 25.783 will be initiated within 180 days to evaluate the incorporation of dynamic load testing requirements for all fuselage access panels. The NTSB will receive quarterly progress reports detailing manufacturer data submissions, operator compliance rates, and any emergent safety trends. The FAA will coordinate with the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) and Transport Canada to harmonize certification standards and ensure global regulatory alignment.

This response satisfies the requirements of Safety Recommendation A-22-045 and establishes a structured compliance pathway to mitigate identified airworthiness risks. The FAA remains committed to maintaining the highest standards of aviation safety through rigorous regulatory oversight, continuous design evaluation, and proactive industry collaboration.

Island Express Jet Collapses Nose Gear in Gusty Crosswind Landing; All 142 Aboard Evacuate Safely

Elena Rostova, The National Chronicle
PORTLAND, Maine — An Island Express Boeing 737-800 suffered a hard landing that collapsed its nose landing gear on Sunday, August 15, 2021, after battling severe crosswinds on final approach. All 134 passengers and eight crew members escaped the damaged aircraft without serious injury, though the jet sustained substantial structural damage that will require extensive repairs.

The incident occurred at approximately 4:15 p.m. local time as Flight 882 touched down on Runway 11. Witnesses reported the aircraft bounced heavily before slamming onto the tarmac, causing the front landing gear to buckle and the nose to scrape the pavement. Emergency crews deployed within minutes, and passengers evacuated via inflatable slides as strong winds continued to buffet the airfield. The runway was immediately closed, diverting dozens of flights and prompting a temporary ground stop at the regional hub.

“We are relieved to confirm that every person on board walked away from this event,” said Marcus Thorne, chief operations officer for Island Express. “Our crew executed emergency procedures flawlessly, and we are deeply grateful to the first responders who secured the scene.” The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) dispatched a go-team to Portland to lead the investigation. “Preliminary data indicates a high-energy touchdown in challenging meteorological conditions,” said NTSB spokesperson Dr. Aris Chen. “We are examining flight data recorder information, maintenance logs, and pilot training records to determine the exact sequence of events.” The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) confirmed it is monitoring the probe and will review the airline’s compliance with federal operating standards.

The aircraft, a 12-year-old Boeing 737-800, was operating a scheduled domestic route from Chicago O’Hare to Portland. The narrow-body jet is equipped with CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines, a modern high-bypass propulsion system designed to improve fuel efficiency and reduce emissions. Island Express, a regional carrier that expanded rapidly over the past decade, operates under strict federal guidelines. The airline’s maintenance and flight operations are governed by 14 CFR Part 121, the FAA’s comprehensive regulatory framework for scheduled commercial air carriers, which mandates rigorous pilot training, aircraft inspections, and operational safety protocols.

Aviation safety analysts suggest the combination of a gusty crosswind and a firm touchdown likely exceeded the structural limits of the nose gear. “When an aircraft lands with a significant crosswind component, pilots must use a technique called a crab or sideslip to keep the plane aligned with the runway,” explained Dr. Sarah Lin, a former commercial pilot and aviation safety professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. “If the aircraft isn’t properly de-crabbed before touchdown, or if it hits the runway too hard, the vertical and lateral forces can overwhelm the landing gear. The nose strut is particularly vulnerable to these kinds of dynamic loads.” Lin cautioned that while pilot technique is often scrutinized, maintenance history and component fatigue also play critical roles.

For those on board, the moments after impact were chaotic but ultimately survivable. “We hit the ground like a dropped suitcase,” said passenger David Chen, 42, who was traveling with his family. “The nose dropped, there was a loud metallic crunch, and then the captain calmly told us to brace. The slides deployed, and we just ran. I’m just thankful my kids are safe.” Family members waiting at the terminal described a tense but orderly scene. “We heard the sirens and saw the emergency vehicles, but the airline staff kept us informed every step of the way,” said Maria Gonzalez, whose sister was on the flight. “It’s terrifying, but the crew’s training clearly made the difference.”

Hard landings resulting in gear collapse are rare but not unprecedented in commercial aviation. The Boeing 737 family has a long operational history, and manufacturers have issued numerous service bulletins and airworthiness directives to address landing gear stress. Notably, Airworthiness Directive AD 2012-09-04, issued by the FAA, previously mandated enhanced inspections of certain 737 landing gear components to detect early signs of fatigue cracking. While that directive primarily targeted older variants, it underscores the industry’s ongoing focus on structural integrity. Additionally, major airframe components for the 737 series, including fuselage sections and structural supports, have historically been manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems, a key aerospace supplier whose parts undergo rigorous quality control before integration. Despite the dramatic nature of Sunday’s incident, commercial aviation remains exceptionally safe, with fatal accidents occurring at a rate of less than one per several million flights globally.

The NTSB investigation remains active, with investigators currently downloading data from the cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder. Maintenance crews are working to safely tow the aircraft to a secure hangar for a detailed structural examination. The FAA has not issued any immediate operational restrictions for the 737-800 fleet, but regulators are reviewing Island Express’s recent training records and weather dispatch procedures. “We will follow the evidence wherever it leads,” Chen said. “Our priority is understanding what happened so we can prevent it from happening again.” The airline has arranged hotel accommodations and counseling services for affected passengers, while engineers assess the full extent of the damage to the airframe and landing gear assembly.

1. INTRODUCTION

This submission is presented by the Chief Engineer, Fleet Airworthiness and Safety Management Division, on behalf of the aircraft operator. As the designated technical representative for the operator in this NTSB investigative proceeding, our engineering and flight operations group has conducted a comprehensive review of the August 15, 2021, hard landing event involving a Boeing 737-800. Our mandate encompasses the continuous airworthiness of our fleet, the validation of maintenance programs, the optimization of operational procedures, and the integration of human factors engineering into our safety management system (SMS). The scope of this document is to present a technically grounded assessment of the factors contributing to the nose landing gear (NLG) collapse, evaluate the interplay between environmental conditions, aircraft systems, and crew performance, and articulate our position on the primary and secondary causal elements. We further outline corrective measures already implemented and propose forward-looking safety enhancements aligned with industry best practices.

We recognize the inherent complexity of this event. A hard landing in gusty crosswind conditions represents a convergence of aerodynamic, structural, and human performance variables. Our analysis does not seek to isolate a single failure mode but rather to evaluate the system-of-systems response under off-nominal conditions. By synthesizing flight data recorder (FDR) telemetry, cockpit voice recorder (CVR) transcripts, maintenance documentation, and comparative engineering data from our broader 737 family program, we aim to provide the Board with a clear, evidence-based technical position that supports both investigative clarity and proactive safety advancement.

2. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On August 15, 2021, at approximately 14:32 local time, the subject Boeing 737-800 (Registration N-XXXX, Serial Number 38XXX) was conducting a scheduled passenger flight to a coastal airport experiencing rapidly deteriorating meteorological conditions. The final approach was flown to Runway 27L with reported surface winds of 250° at 25 knots, gusting to 35 knots, yielding a calculated crosswind component of approximately 22 knots. The aircraft touched down with a vertical acceleration peak of 2.8G, resulting in the collapse of the NLG, substantial airframe damage, and a successful emergency evacuation with no serious injuries.

Key docket materials referenced in this analysis include:
- Docket Item 2021-08-15-042: FDR and QAR (Quick Access Recorder) data package, including 1-second and 4-second parameter sampling.
- Docket Item 2021-08-15-051: CVR transcript and audio spectral analysis.
- Docket Item 2021-08-15-067: Maintenance log excerpts, MSG-3 task compliance records, and structural inspection reports.
- Docket Item 2021-08-15-073: Meteorological data, ATC communications, and pilot post-flight statements.
- Docket Item 2021-08-15-089: OEM structural load analysis and landing gear certification test data.

The aircraft’s maintenance history, as documented in Docket Item 2021-08-15-067, reveals no deferred defects, no outstanding airworthiness directives, and full compliance with all scheduled heavy checks. The forward fuselage and landing gear attachment structures were originally manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems, whose design specifications and load-path documentation have been reviewed in conjunction with the operator’s structural integrity program. While the accident aircraft is a 737-800 variant, our engineering division manages a unified 737 family program that includes next-generation aircraft equipped with the CFM LEAP-1B engine and the Main Equipment Door (MED) plug. Cross-fleet data from these platforms has been incorporated into our comparative analysis to contextualize thrust response characteristics, structural load distribution, and standardized training protocols across our operational fleet.

The flight crew consisted of a Captain and a Second-in-Command (SIC). CVR data indicates standard approach briefings, configuration callouts, and stabilized approach criteria were initially met. However, telemetry reveals a rapid increase in sink rate during the flare phase, coinciding with a sudden crosswind gust and delayed thrust adjustment. The SIC’s monitoring role, as captured in the audio transcript, included standard altitude and airspeed callouts, but no explicit intervention or go-around recommendation was vocalized prior to touchdown.

3. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS

Our technical assessment is structured around three interdependent domains: aerodynamic and operational performance, structural and maintenance integrity, and human factors/crew resource management (CRM). Each domain is evaluated against certification standards, OEM service documentation, and industry safety benchmarks.

Aerodynamic and Operational Performance
FDR data (Docket Item 2021-08-15-042) indicates that at 50 feet radio altitude, the aircraft was within stabilized approach parameters: airspeed Vref+12, flaps 30, landing gear down, and vertical speed approximately 650 fpm. However, between 30 and 10 feet, a rapid crosswind shift and vertical gust component induced a momentary loss of lift and an increase in sink rate to 1,150 fpm. The pilot flying initiated a flare with aft yoke input, but the aircraft’s pitch attitude peaked at only 4.2 degrees, insufficient to arrest the descent rate. The resulting touchdown vertical acceleration of 2.8G exceeded the 2.0G design limit for the NLG, triggering structural overload.

The gust factor applied during the approach was calculated at 10 knots, consistent with operator SOPs and FAA Advisory Circular 120-71A. However, the actual wind shear profile, as reconstructed from terminal Doppler weather radar and FDR wind vector data, exhibited a transient 15-knot vertical component that exceeded the stabilized approach envelope. Industry best practices, including Boeing’s Flight Crew Training Manual (FCTM) and IATA’s Crosswind Landing Guidelines, emphasize that when sink rate exceeds 800 fpm below 50 feet in gusty conditions, a go-around is the preferred risk mitigation strategy. The decision to continue the approach, while within regulatory crosswind limits, introduced a high-probability exceedance scenario.

Structural and Maintenance Integrity
The NLG collapse was a direct consequence of vertical load exceedance, not a latent maintenance defect or material fatigue failure. The landing gear assembly, designed to withstand a 2.0G limit load with a 1.5x safety factor, experienced a peak load of approximately 3.1G equivalent during the impact sequence. Post-accident structural inspection (Docket Item 2021-08-15-089) confirmed that the failure initiated at the NLG trunnion attachment lugs, consistent with overload fracture mechanics rather than fatigue crack propagation.

The forward fuselage structure, originally engineered and manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems, maintains a continuous load path from the NLG through the keel beam and bulkhead stations. Our engineering review confirms that the structural design performed as certified; the failure mode was load-driven, not design-driven. For comparative context, our fleet-wide structural monitoring program includes data from 737 MAX variants featuring the MED plug configuration. The Main Equipment Door plug, while altering local fuselage skin continuity, does not affect the primary NLG load path. Finite element analysis (FEA) cross-referenced with Spirit’s original design documentation confirms that the 737-800’s forward fuselage architecture remains structurally isolated from the MED plug’s load distribution, reinforcing that the collapse was not attributable to airframe modification or manufacturing variance.

Maintenance records show full compliance with MSG-3 tasking, including NLG shock strut servicing, torque checks, and non-destructive testing (NDT) of attachment points. No deferred maintenance items or repeat write-ups were present. The operator’s reliability program, which tracks landing gear events across 1.2 million flight hours, shows a hard landing rate of 0.0004 per 1,000 departures, well below industry averages. This event represents a statistical outlier driven by operational conditions rather than systemic maintenance degradation.

Human Factors and Crew Resource Management
CVR analysis (Docket Item 2021-08-15-051) reveals that the SIC maintained standard monitoring duties, providing altitude, airspeed, and configuration callouts. However, during the critical 30-to-10-foot window, the SIC did not issue a “sink rate” or “go-around” callout, despite the FDR indicating a rapid descent rate increase. This aligns with documented CRM challenges in high-workload, gusty crosswind scenarios, where monitoring pilots may experience cognitive tunneling or defer to the pilot flying’s authority.

The operator’s training program emphasizes assertive monitoring and standardized intervention protocols. However, simulator data from our recent Line Operations Safety Audit (LOSA) indicates that only 68% of SICs consistently initiate go-around recommendations when sink rate exceeds 900 fpm below 50 feet. This gap suggests a need for reinforced behavioral training, particularly in dynamic wind conditions where automation dependency and manual flying skills intersect.

Additionally, while the 737-800 utilizes CFM56-7B engines, our cross-fleet engineering review includes thrust response modeling from the LEAP-1B powerplant. The FADEC logic and spool-up characteristics of the LEAP-1B engine demonstrate faster thrust response during wind shear recovery, which has informed our updated go-around decision matrices. Although not directly applicable to the accident aircraft, this comparative propulsion data underscores the importance of standardizing thrust management training across our mixed fleet to ensure consistent pilot response profiles during unstable approaches.

4. CONCLUSIONS

Based on the synthesis of flight data, maintenance records, structural analysis, and human factors evaluation, the operator’s technical position is as follows:

The primary contributing factor to the NLG collapse was an excessive sink rate during the flare phase, induced by a transient crosswind gust and compounded by delayed corrective pitch and thrust inputs. The aircraft’s vertical acceleration exceeded certified structural limits, resulting in an overload failure of the NLG trunnion attachment. This was not a maintenance deficiency, airworthiness defect, or design flaw. The forward fuselage and landing gear systems, including components originally produced by Spirit AeroSystems, performed within their certified parameters until the pilot-induced load exceedance occurred.

Secondary contributing factors include:
- Inadequate application of gust factor margins during the final approach phase, leading to continuation of an approach that transitioned from stabilized to unstable below 50 feet.
- CRM dynamics wherein the SIC, while performing standard monitoring duties, did not initiate a timely go-around recommendation despite observable sink rate degradation.
- Training gaps in high-gust crosswind landing techniques, particularly in manual flare execution and rapid thrust adjustment under wind shear conditions.

We acknowledge the complexity of real-world approach environments and the inherent challenges of manual flying in rapidly changing meteorological conditions. However, the data clearly indicates that adherence to stabilized approach criteria, timely go-around decision-making, and assertive CRM intervention would have prevented the structural exceedance. The aircraft’s design and maintenance posture were sound; the event was operationally driven.

Recommended safety improvements include:
- Mandatory go-around policy reinforcement when sink rate exceeds 800 fpm below 50 feet in gusty conditions.
- Enhanced simulator training focusing on manual flare techniques, crosswind gust response, and SIC intervention protocols.
- Integration of real-time wind shear and gust prediction algorithms into electronic flight bags (EFBs) to support approach stability monitoring.
- Cross-fleet standardization of thrust management and go-around decision matrices, leveraging data from both CFM56-7B and LEAP-1B equipped aircraft to optimize pilot response training.

5. CORRECTIVE ACTIONS

In response to this event, the operator has implemented the following immediate and near-term corrective actions:

1. Fleet Safety Bulletin 2021-09-01: Issued to all flight crews, emphasizing stabilized approach criteria, sink rate monitoring, and mandatory go-around execution when parameters degrade below 50 feet in gusty conditions.
2. Enhanced Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) Triggers: Updated QAR algorithms to flag vertical acceleration >2.0G, sink rate >800 fpm below 50 feet, and crosswind component >20 knots. All flagged events are now subject to mandatory safety review and instructor debrief.
3. CRM and SIC Intervention Training: Revised simulator curriculum to include assertive monitoring scenarios, standardized callout protocols, and role-specific decision-making exercises. Over 92% of active line pilots have completed the updated module as of Q4 2021.
4. Maintenance Program Review: Conducted a fleet-wide audit of NLG servicing intervals, shock strut pressure verification, and attachment lug NDT schedules. No systemic anomalies were identified; however, inspection frequency has been increased by 15% for aircraft operating in high-gust coastal environments.

Proposed future improvements include:
- Collaboration with OEM engineering and Spirit AeroSystems to develop a predictive NLG load monitoring system utilizing real-time FDR telemetry and machine learning algorithms to identify approach instability trends before touchdown.
- Standardization of crosswind landing techniques across the entire 737 family, incorporating thrust response data from the CFM LEAP-1B engine and structural load path analysis from MED plug-equipped variants to ensure consistent pilot training and operational procedures.
- Submission of a joint industry proposal to the FAA and IATA for revised guidance on gust factor application, emphasizing dynamic wind shear modeling over static surface wind reporting.
- Implementation of a mandatory “go-around authority” protocol, empowering the SIC to initiate a missed approach without requiring pilot flying concurrence when critical stability parameters are breached.

The operator remains fully committed to transparency, continuous safety improvement, and collaborative engagement with the NTSB, regulatory bodies, and industry partners. This event, while resulting in substantial airframe damage, provided critical data that has already strengthened our training, monitoring, and operational frameworks. We stand ready to provide additional technical documentation, engineering models, and maintenance records as requested by the Board, and we reaffirm our dedication to advancing aviation safety through evidence-based analysis and proactive risk mitigation.

PURPOSE:
This safety communication is issued to disseminate preliminary findings from the 15 August 2021 hard landing event, mandate immediate updates to nose landing gear (NLG) inspection protocols, and reinforce crosswind approach procedures across the 737-800 fleet. All maintenance, flight operations, and quality personnel must implement the directives outlined herein by the specified deadlines.

BACKGROUND:
On 15 August 2021, aircraft N737XX (Boeing 737-800) experienced a hard landing during a gusty crosswind approach at KSEA. The impact forces exceeded design limits, resulting in a complete collapse of the nose landing gear assembly. The aircraft sustained substantial structural damage to the forward fuselage and lower lobe. All passengers and crew evacuated safely without injury. Preliminary data from the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) indicate a combination of rapid wind shear, delayed flare initiation, and a vertical descent rate exceeding 1,200 fpm at touchdown.

While the primary investigation remains under the purview of the NTSB, our internal Quality Assurance team has completed an expedited review of maintenance records, pilot training logs, and recent airworthiness compliance audits. The review identified several procedural gaps that require immediate correction. Notably, the incident has prompted a broader cross-fleet safety assessment, including coordination with external partners such as Island Express Helicopters (IEH), who recently shared rotorcraft hard-landing mitigation data that proved applicable to fixed-wing gear load management. Additionally, while the affected airframe utilizes CFM56-7B powerplants, our engineering group is applying the same fatigue-tracking methodology currently deployed for the LEAP-1B engine program to standardize structural load monitoring across all platforms.

DETAILS:
The following findings and procedural updates are effective immediately:

1. Nose Landing Gear Inspection & Documentation
   - All 737-800 aircraft must undergo an expedited NLG structural inspection per Work Order WO-737-8892-REV3.
   - Inspectors must verify torque values on the NLG trunnion bolts (P/N 65-43210-12) and check for micro-fractures in the drag brace assembly.
   - Any aircraft with a recorded hard landing event (>1.5g vertical acceleration) in the past 180 days must be grounded until a Level 3 NDT inspection is completed and signed off by a Level III inspector.

   - Go-around decision authority is reinforced. If wind shear alerts activate or crosswind components exceed 25 knots with gusts >10 knots, a missed approach is mandatory.
   - Training records will be audited quarterly to ensure compliance with 14 CFR § 25.571 damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation requirements as they pertain to operational load limits.

   - All maintenance and flight operations personnel must verify that fuel tank system inspections align with Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 requirements.
