CLASSIFICATION: INTERNAL – SAFETY SENSITIVE
RETENTION: PERMANENT (QA ARCHIVE)

SYNOPSIS

On August 15, 2021, at approximately 1432 local time, a Boeing 737-800, operated by a U.S. Part 121 air carrier, experienced a collapse of the nose landing gear that resulted in a hard landing during a gusty crosswind approach. The aircraft sustained substantial damage to the forward fuselage and lower airframe structures; however, all passengers and crew successfully evacuated via the available emergency exits without serious injury. This preliminary document outlines the initial factual data collected to date, establishes the investigative framework, and documents the procedural steps currently underway. All information contained herein is preliminary and subject to revision as the investigation progresses.

INITIAL FINDINGS

Preliminary information indicates that the flight was conducting a scheduled passenger service under instrument flight rules when it encountered a dynamic wind environment during the final approach phase. Initial data retrieved from the flight data recorder (FDR) and cockpit voice recorder (CVR) suggest that the aircraft's vertical speed increased significantly during the flare, culminating in a high-impact touchdown. The second in command (SIC) was occupying the right seat and was designated as the pilot flying at the time of the event, consistent with standard crew rotation protocols. Early witness statements from ground personnel, airport operations staff, and air traffic control personnel describe a noticeable lateral drift and a firm, asymmetric touchdown, followed by a forward pitching motion and the subsequent collapse of the nose gear assembly.

Meteorological observations recorded at the time of the incident indicate surface winds from 270 degrees at 18 knots, gusting to 28 knots, with a crosswind component that approached the operational limits documented in the aircraft flight manual. Preliminary examination of the wreckage revealed that the nose landing gear strut separated at the lower attachment points, with associated damage extending to the forward pressure bulkhead and adjacent avionics bays. The main landing gear remained intact, and the aircraft came to rest on the runway centerline approximately 1,200 feet beyond the initial touchdown point.

During the initial structural survey, investigators noted that the forward fuselage section, which was manufactured by Spirit Aerosystems, exhibited localized buckling, skin wrinkling, and fastener shear consistent with high-energy vertical and longitudinal loading. The aircraft is equipped with CFM International LEAP-1B turbofan engines; preliminary visual inspection of both powerplants revealed no evidence of pre-impact mechanical failure, though detailed teardown and borescope examinations are pending. Additionally, maintenance records indicate that a main equipment deck (MED plug) access panel had been recently serviced, and investigators are currently reviewing the associated work cards, torque verification logs, and post-maintenance test results to determine if any maintenance-related factors contributed to the structural response. Regulatory compliance with 14 CFR 121.344, which governs the requirements for flight data recorders and cockpit voice recorders, is being evaluated to ensure all mandated data parameters were captured, preserved, and properly synchronized during the event sequence. All initial findings remain subject to change as additional data is recovered, analyzed, and correlated.

INVESTIGATION STATUS

The National Transportation Safety Board has activated the following investigative groups to address the scope of this accident: Operations, Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Human Performance, and Maintenance Records. Each group is operating under the established NTSB party system, with participation from the Federal Aviation Administration, the aircraft manufacturer, the engine manufacturer, the air carrier, and the relevant pilot and flight attendant labor organizations. All participating parties have executed the required confidentiality agreements and are operating under the direct supervision of NTSB group chairmen.

Critical evidence has been secured, documented, and cataloged at the accident site. The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered, transported to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory, and are currently undergoing data extraction, decoding, and synchronization. The collapsed nose landing gear components, including the strut, torque links, steering actuator, and associated hydraulic lines, have been removed from the wreckage and placed in a controlled storage environment pending metallurgical, dimensional, and functional analysis. The forward fuselage section has been stabilized, and non-destructive testing (NDT) is being conducted to map the extent of structural deformation and identify potential fatigue, manufacturing, or load-path anomalies.

Preliminary examinations of the aircraft’s maintenance logs, training records, and operational dispatch documentation are underway. The investigation team is also reviewing air traffic control communications, radar track data, and airport surface surveillance footage to reconstruct the approach, flare, and touchdown sequence. All physical evidence, digital data, and documentary records are being maintained in strict accordance with NTSB chain-of-custody protocols. At this stage, no definitive conclusions have been reached regarding the sequence of events or the underlying factors that led to the hard landing and subsequent gear collapse. The investigation remains in the data collection, preservation, and preliminary analysis phase.

NEXT STEPS

The investigative groups will continue to process and analyze the secured evidence over the coming weeks. The Operations group will conduct structured interviews with the flight crew, cabin crew, and air traffic controllers to establish a comprehensive timeline of the approach, decision-making processes, and crew resource management dynamics. The Structures and Systems groups will coordinate with engineering specialists to perform finite element modeling and load-path analysis, focusing on the interaction between the landing gear impact forces and the forward fuselage assembly. The Powerplants group will proceed with the scheduled teardown and component-level inspection of the LEAP-1B engines to rule out any thrust asymmetry, control system anomalies, or foreign object damage.

Maintenance and regulatory compliance reviews will continue, with particular attention directed toward recent airframe modifications, component service bulletins, and adherence to manufacturer-recommended inspection intervals. The Human Performance group will evaluate fatigue, training currency, environmental stressors, and procedural adherence that may have influenced crew performance during the gusty crosswind approach. All data will be cross-referenced with historical operational trends, manufacturer service information, and industry safety databases to identify any recurring patterns or systemic vulnerabilities.

A preliminary factual report will be issued within 30 days of the accident date, in accordance with standard NTSB procedural guidelines. Subsequent updates will be provided as critical examinations are completed, laboratory results are finalized, and additional data becomes available. The investigation team will maintain regular coordination with the participating parties and will convene a technical review meeting upon completion of the initial data analysis phase. All findings documented in this report are preliminary in nature and are subject to change as the investigation progresses. The NTSB will not speculate on probable cause or contributing factors until all evidence has been thoroughly evaluated, peer-reviewed, and the final report is published.

1. ACCIDENT INFORMATION

1.1 Date, Time, and Location
On August 15, 2021, at 1842 coordinated universal time (UTC), a Boeing 737-800, registration N737XX, experienced a hard landing resulting in the collapse of the nose landing gear (NLG) during the landing roll. The accident occurred on Runway 27L at Portland International Airport (PDX), Portland, Oregon (latitude 45.5887° N, longitude 122.5975° W). The aircraft was operating under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) Part 121 as a scheduled passenger flight.

1.2 Aircraft and Operator Identification
The aircraft was a Boeing 737-800, serial number 34567, manufactured in 2008. The registered operator was Pacific Coast Airways, Inc., a Part 121 certificate holder. The aircraft was configured for 162 passenger seats and 6 crew positions. At the time of the accident, the aircraft was operating Flight 442, a domestic scheduled service from Denver International Airport (DEN) to Portland International Airport (PDX).

1.3 Flight Phase and Sequence of Events
The flight departed DEN at 1615 UTC and proceeded en route to PDX. During the approach phase, the flight crew configured the aircraft for a visual approach to Runway 27L. At approximately 1841:30 UTC, the aircraft crossed the runway threshold at an indicated airspeed of 148 knots and a radio altitude of 45 feet. The aircraft contacted the runway surface at 1842:05 UTC with a vertical acceleration exceeding 2.8 G. The initial touchdown was followed by a secondary impact that resulted in the aft collapse of the NLG. The aircraft slid approximately 1,200 feet along the runway centerline before coming to rest.

1.4 Injuries and Evacuation
The aircraft carried 162 passengers and 6 flight crew members. All occupants evacuated the aircraft using the forward and overwing emergency slides. Emergency medical services evaluated all occupants on scene. Two passengers sustained minor injuries consistent with evacuation slide deployment; no serious or fatal injuries were reported. The evacuation was completed within 78 seconds, in compliance with 14 CFR 121.310 requirements.

2. CREW INFORMATION

2.1 Captain Qualifications and Certifications
The captain held an Airline Transport Pilot (ATP) certificate with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. The captain possessed a first-class medical certificate issued on March 12, 2021, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 8,450 hours, with 2,100 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The captain completed a recurrent training and proficiency check on June 28, 2021, which included simulator-based crosswind and gusty wind landing scenarios.

2.2 First Officer Qualifications and Certifications
The first officer held an ATP certificate with airplane multiengine land and Boeing 737 type ratings. A first-class medical certificate was issued on May 5, 2021, with no limitations. Total flight time was recorded at 3,200 hours, with 850 hours in the Boeing 737 series. The first officer completed a line-oriented flight training (LOFT) evaluation on July 10, 2021, and a line check on July 22, 2021. Both evaluations documented satisfactory performance in adverse weather and high-workload approach phases.

2.3 Duty Time and Rest Compliance
The flight crew reported for duty at 1330 UTC on August 15, 2021. The preceding rest period was documented as 11 hours and 15 minutes, commencing at 0215 UTC and concluding at 1330 UTC. Duty time and flight time limitations were in compliance with 14 CFR 117.11 and 117.15. No fatigue-related reports or self-assessments were filed by either pilot prior to or following the flight.

2.4 Training Records and Crosswind Proficiency
Operator training records indicate that both pilots completed the required annual crosswind landing training module on May 14, 2021. The training syllabus included simulator sessions with crosswind components up to 30 knots, gust factors of 15 knots, and wet runway conditions. The operator's standard operating procedures (SOPs) mandated a go-around if the calculated crosswind component exceeded 20 knots on a dry runway, or 15 knots on a wet runway. The manufacturer's demonstrated crosswind limit for the 737-800 is 33 knots.

3. AIRCRAFT INFORMATION

3.1 General Specifications and Airframe History
The accident aircraft was a Boeing 737-800, equipped with CFM International CFM56-7B26 turbofan engines. The airframe accumulated 42,150 total flight hours and 28,400 flight cycles at the time of the accident. The aircraft was originally delivered to the operator in 2008 and had been maintained under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program (CAMP) approved under 14 CFR 121.369.

3.2 Maintenance History and Airworthiness Directives
The most recent heavy maintenance event was a C-check completed on June 10, 2020, at 40,800 flight hours. All applicable Airworthiness Directives (ADs) were documented as current in the aircraft maintenance logbooks. The operator's engineering department maintained compliance with structural inspection programs, including those mandated by 14 CFR 25.571, which establishes damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation requirements for transport category airplanes. No deferred maintenance items related to the landing gear, flight controls, or forward fuselage structure were recorded in the 30 days preceding the accident.

3.3 Relevant Systems and Components
The nose landing gear assembly consisted of a dual-wheel configuration with a shock strut, drag brace, and steering actuator. The main landing gear assemblies were in the extended and locked position at touchdown. The forward fuselage, designated as Section 41, was manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems. Structural documentation from the original equipment manufacturer confirmed that the forward fuselage plug assembly, commonly referred to as the MED plug (main equipment door plug), was installed in accordance with Boeing Service Bulletin 737-53-1022. The plug assembly was inspected during the 2020 C-check and showed no signs of fatigue cracking, fastener elongation, or seal degradation.

3.4 Engine and Powerplant Documentation
The aircraft was powered by two CFM56-7B26 engines. Maintenance records indicated that both engines were within their time-on-wing limits and had undergone a borescope inspection 1,200 flight hours prior to the accident. The operator's technical library included cross-referenced maintenance procedures for the CFM International LEAP-1B powerplant series, which were integrated into the engineering database for comparative thrust management and vibration monitoring protocols. These LEAP-1B reference documents were utilized for fleet-wide data trending but did not apply to the accident aircraft's installed powerplants.

4. METEOROLOGICAL INFORMATION

4.1 Surface Weather Conditions
At the time of the accident, surface weather observations indicated a wind direction of 270° true at 18 knots, gusting to 32 knots. Visibility was 10 statute miles. The ceiling was reported as broken at 3,500 feet above ground level (AGL). The ambient temperature was 22°C, with a dewpoint of 14°C. The altimeter setting was 29.92 inches of mercury. The runway surface was dry, with no reported contamination.

4.2 METAR and TAF Data
The official METAR issued at 1853 UTC read: KPDX 151853Z 27018G32KT 10SM BKN035 22/14 A2992. The terminal aerodrome forecast (TAF) valid from 1800 UTC to 2400 UTC on August 15, 2021, forecasted winds from 260° at 15 knots, gusting to 28 knots, with temporary conditions of 270° at 20 knots, gusting to 35 knots, between 1800 and 2100 UTC. The observed conditions were consistent with the forecasted temporary wind shear and gust parameters.

4.3 Pilot Reports and Wind Shear Alerts
A preceding Boeing 737-900 operating Flight 218 reported a PIREP at 1835 UTC indicating moderate turbulence and a 10-knot airspeed fluctuation on final approach to Runway 27L. The airport's low-level wind shear alert system (LLWAS) recorded a 14-knot wind shear event at 1840:15 UTC, localized to the final approach corridor. The flight crew acknowledged the LLWAS alert and the preceding PIREP during the approach briefing.

4.4 Crosswind Component Calculation
Using the reported wind direction of 270° and runway heading of 270°, the direct crosswind component was calculated at 0 knots. However, wind vector analysis from the airport's automated weather observation system (AWOS), supplemented by data from a secondary meteorological station maintained by Island Express Helicopters (IEH) located 1.2 nautical miles southeast of the runway threshold, indicated localized wind shifts of up to 20° during the final 30 seconds of the approach. This resulted in an effective crosswind component of approximately 11 knots, with gust-induced lateral deviations recorded at 18 knots. The calculated values remained within the manufacturer's demonstrated limits but approached the operator's internal operational thresholds.

5. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATION

5.1 Wreckage Distribution and Rest Position
The aircraft came to rest on the paved surface of Runway 27L, approximately 1,200 feet beyond the threshold, aligned with the runway centerline. The nose landing gear collapsed aft and inward, resulting in the forward fuselage contacting the runway surface. The main landing gear remained extended and intact. The aircraft's final rest position was documented with GPS coordinates and photogrammetric mapping.

5.2 Impact Marks and Runway Evidence
Examination of the runway surface revealed a continuous scuff mark beginning 300 feet past the threshold, extending 450 feet in length. The initial scuff mark corresponded to the main gear touchdown point. A secondary, deeper gouge mark was identified 150 feet beyond the initial touchdown, consistent with the aft collapse of the NLG strut. Hydraulic fluid and engine oil trails were documented extending 800 feet aft of the secondary impact point. No evidence of pre-impact tire failure or brake system malfunction was observed.

5.3 Component Examination Findings
The nose landing gear assembly was recovered and transported to the NTSB Materials Laboratory for detailed examination. The lower trunnion fitting exhibited a ductile fracture surface consistent with overload failure. The drag brace separated at the upper clevis pin, with witness marks indicating aft-directed loading exceeding design limits. The forward fuselage skin, located between stations 240 and 320, exhibited localized buckling and compression wrinkling. The MED plug assembly remained structurally intact, with no evidence of fastener failure, seal displacement, or load path disruption. The plug's proximity to the nose gear well was noted, but structural analysis confirmed that the collapse forces were contained within the landing gear attachment structure and did not propagate into the forward fuselage pressure bulkhead.

5.4 Flight Data Recorder and Systems Status
The flight data recorder (FDR) was recovered and successfully downloaded. Parameters indicated a vertical descent rate of 1,250 feet per minute at 50 feet radio altitude, increasing to 1,850 feet per minute at touchdown. The pitch attitude at initial contact was 2.1° nose-up. The NLG shock strut compression data showed a rapid, uncontrolled stroke exceeding 14 inches within 0.3 seconds of ground contact. The autothrottle system was in the armed mode, and the thrust levers were at idle at touchdown. The ground spoiler system deployed 1.2 seconds after main gear weight-on-wheels, consistent with normal system logic.

6. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

6.1 Organizational Policies and Standard Operating Procedures
The operator's Flight Operations Manual (FOM) Section 4.12.3 established crosswind landing procedures, including the use of wing-low technique, rudder coordination, and immediate go-around criteria if directional control could not be maintained. The operator's wind limit policy, documented in FOM Section 4.15.1, specified a maximum demonstrated crosswind of 33 knots, with an internal operational limit of 20 knots for dry runways. The policy required a mandatory go-around if the calculated crosswind component exceeded the operational limit or if wind shear alerts were active during the final approach phase.

6.2 Previous Similar Incidents and Safety Data
A review of the operator's internal safety reporting system identified three previous hard landing events involving Boeing 737-800 aircraft between 2018 and 2020. All three events occurred during gusty crosswind conditions and resulted in NLG shock strut over-compression. In each case, the aircraft sustained minor structural damage and was returned to service following manufacturer-approved inspections. The National Transportation Safety Board's aviation accident database contains 14 similar hard landing events involving 737-800 aircraft between 2010 and 2020, with 6 resulting in NLG collapse. The operator's safety management system (SMS) had previously issued a fleet-wide safety bulletin in 2019 emphasizing stabilized approach criteria and crosswind landing technique reinforcement.

6.3 Applicable Regulations and Guidance
The aircraft was certified under 14 CFR Part 25, with structural compliance verified against Section 25.571, which mandates damage tolerance and fatigue evaluation of the primary structure. The operator's maintenance program adhered to 14 CFR 121.369 and 121.373, requiring continuous airworthiness inspections and structural integrity monitoring. Advisory Circular 120-29A, Criteria for Approval of Category III and Other Weather Minimums for Landing, provided guidance on wind shear recognition and crosswind landing procedures. The manufacturer's Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM) and Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) contained specific procedures for gusty wind approaches, including recommended airspeed adjustments and touchdown technique modifications.

6.4 Evacuation and Emergency Response
The emergency evacuation was initiated by the flight crew within 12 seconds of the aircraft coming to a complete stop. All four forward and overwing emergency slides deployed automatically. Ground emergency response units arrived on scene within 3 minutes and 45 seconds. Fire suppression equipment was deployed as a precautionary measure due to minor hydraulic fluid leakage near the collapsed NLG. No fire or smoke was observed. The evacuation was conducted in accordance with 14 CFR 121.310, and all occupants exited the aircraft without obstruction. Post-evacuation accountability confirmed all 168 occupants were accounted for and safely relocated to the terminal.

1. INTRODUCTION

This Specialist's Factual Report documents the examination and analysis of the nose landing gear (NLG) assembly, forward fuselage structure, and associated flight data recorder (FDR) parameters for the Boeing 737-800, registration N737XX, involved in a hard landing event on August 15, 2021. The scope of this examination encompasses the structural integrity of the NLG strut and drag brace, the deformation characteristics of the forward fuselage skin and stringer frames, the condition of the forward avionics access DOOR PLUG, and the correlation of recorded flight parameters with design limit loads. The investigation was initiated following the collapse of the NLG during a gusty crosswind approach, which resulted in substantial damage to the forward fuselage and lower lobe structure.

The physical examination of the recovered components was conducted between September 10 and September 18, 2021, at the NTSB Materials Laboratory in Washington, D.C., and the Boeing Field Salvage Facility in Seattle, Washington. The FDR and Quick Access Recorder (QAR) data were downloaded, decoded, and analyzed at the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory on September 20-22, 2021. All examinations were performed in accordance with NTSB Investigative Procedures Manual (IPM) guidelines, with documentation captured via high-resolution digital photography, three-dimensional laser scanning, and standardized metallurgical sampling protocols. This report presents factual observations, measured data, and analytical results derived from the examination. No conclusions regarding probable cause are presented herein.

2. BACKGROUND

The Boeing 737-800 is a twin-engine, narrow-body transport aircraft certified under 14 CFR Part 25, with the landing gear system designed to meet the requirements of FAR 25.473 (Landing Gear Loads) and FAR 25.561 (Emergency Landing Conditions). The NLG assembly, part number 65-43210-001, serial number 8842A, is a dual-wheel, oleo-pneumatic strut system designed to absorb vertical impact energy and transmit ground loads to the forward fuselage structure. The primary load-bearing components include a 300M steel outer cylinder, a 4340 steel inner piston, and a forged aluminum alloy drag brace assembly. The forward fuselage section 41, which houses the NLG attachment lugs and avionics bay, was manufactured by Spirit AeroSystems, Inc. (SAS) under Boeing drawing 65-12345-001, revision 14. Spirit AeroSystems (Spirit) supplied the section 41 assembly to Boeing's final assembly line in 2014, with all structural fasteners torqued and sealant applied per Boeing Process Specification BAC 5000.

The aircraft's operational history, as documented in the maintenance tracking system, indicates a total of 42,118 flight hours and 28,542 flight cycles at the time of the event. The NLG assembly underwent a scheduled overhaul at 20,000 cycles, including replacement of the main seal, nitrogen recharge, and non-destructive inspection (NDI) of the drag brace pivot points. No deferred maintenance items or structural service bulletins were open for the NLG or forward fuselage at the time of the accident.

The forward avionics bay is accessed via a removable DOOR PLUG, part number 65-43210-1, serial 8842A-03, secured by four quick-release latches and a continuous perimeter silicone seal. The DOOR PLUG is designed to maintain cabin pressurization integrity and provide environmental sealing for the forward electronics rack. During the post-accident recovery, the DOOR PLUG remained attached to the fuselage but exhibited visible deformation of the latch engagement surfaces.

Wiring harness routing within the forward fuselage, including fuel quantity indication system (FQIS) cabling, was evaluated for compliance with Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 (SFAR 88) requirements. SFAR-88 mandates rigorous ignition source prevention measures for fuel tank systems, including separation of high-energy wiring from fuel lines and implementation of arc-fault protection. The forward fuselage wiring bundles were inspected for chafing, insulation degradation, and proper standoff clearance per SFAR 88 compliance documentation. No pre-accident discrepancies were noted in the maintenance logs regarding fuel system wiring or DOOR PLUG sealing integrity.

3. EXAMINATION AND FINDINGS

The physical examination of the NLG assembly commenced with macroscopic documentation of the collapsed configuration. The outer cylinder exhibited a 14.2-inch lateral displacement relative to the forward fuselage attachment lugs, with the drag brace buckled at the mid-span pivot joint. The fracture surface of the drag brace was located at the lower clevis attachment, approximately 3.1 inches from the pivot centerline. The fracture exhibited a 45-degree shear lip morphology consistent with ductile overload, with no evidence of fatigue striations, corrosion pitting, or manufacturing defects. The fracture surface was preserved and sectioned for laboratory analysis.

Hardness testing was performed on the drag brace material using a calibrated Rockwell C scale indenter. Ten measurements were taken across the fracture face and adjacent parent material, yielding an average hardness of 48.2 HRC (range: 47.8–48.6 HRC). This value falls within the Boeing Material Specification (BMS) 7-222 requirement of 46–50 HRC for 7075-T7351 aluminum forgings. Chemical composition analysis via optical emission spectroscopy confirmed the alloy composition as 5.8% Zn, 2.3% Mg, 1.5% Cu, and 0.12% Cr, consistent with 7075-T7351 per SAE AMS 4079.

The NLG outer cylinder was sectioned longitudinally to evaluate the oleo-pneumatic seal condition and internal scoring. The main piston seal exhibited circumferential abrasion marks with a maximum depth of 0.008 inches, well within the 0.015-inch service limit. Nitrogen pressure at the time of recovery was measured at 1,850 PSI, consistent with the pre-accident maintenance record of 1,800 ± 50 PSI. The strut compression travel was measured at 11.4 inches, exceeding the design limit of 9.5 inches, indicating full bottoming of the oleo chamber.

The forward fuselage skin and stringer frames were examined for plastic deformation and fastener failure. The lower lobe skin, constructed of 2024-T3 aluminum clad sheet (0.063-inch thickness), exhibited permanent deformation with a maximum deflection of 2.8 inches at station 340.0. Stringer frame 342.5 showed localized buckling at the NLG attachment lug interface, with three of eight 1/4-inch titanium fasteners (NAS1398-4-12) sheared at the shank. Fastener torque verification on the remaining five fasteners yielded an average of 142 in-lbs, within the specified 135–150 in-lbs range per Boeing Standard Practices Manual (SPM) 20-10-01.

The DOOR PLUG was removed for detailed inspection. The four quick-release latches exhibited plastic deformation at the cam engagement surfaces, with latch 2 and latch 3 showing 0.045-inch and 0.052-inch permanent set, respectively. The perimeter silicone seal (part number 65-43210-2) was compressed to 68% of its original cross-sectional height, indicating exposure to elevated localized pressure during the impact sequence. No fastener pull-through or skin tearing was observed around the DOOR PLUG cutout. The latch mechanism was disassembled and tested for spring return force, yielding an average of 18.4 ft-lbs, below the design minimum of 22.0 ft-lbs, consistent with overload deformation.

Metallurgical analysis of the forward fuselage skin included tensile testing per ASTM E8 and fracture toughness evaluation per ASTM E399. Specimens extracted from the deformed region exhibited a yield strength of 42.1 ksi and ultimate tensile strength of 68.4 ksi, within the 2024-T3 specification limits of 40–45 ksi and 65–70 ksi, respectively. The fracture toughness (K_IC) was measured at 31.2 ksi√in, indicating no significant degradation of material properties. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the fracture surfaces confirmed microvoid coalescence, characteristic of ductile tearing under high-strain-rate loading.

Photographic documentation of the examination is referenced as follows: Photo 1-1 through 1-12 (NLG assembly overview), Photo 2-1 through 2-8 (drag brace fracture surface), Photo 3-1 through 3-6 (forward fuselage deformation), Photo 4-1 through 4-4 (DOOR PLUG latch deformation), and Photo 5-1 through 5-3 (fastener shear and torque verification). All measurements were recorded using calibrated digital calipers (±0.001 inch), laser displacement sensors (±0.0005 inch), and a coordinate measuring machine (CMM) for three-dimensional reconstruction of the collapsed geometry.

4. DATA ANALYSIS

The FDR and QAR data were decoded using the Boeing 737-800 standard parameter list, with a sampling rate of 1 Hz for vertical acceleration (Gz), pitch attitude, and radio altitude, and 4 Hz for control surface positions and engine parameters. The data was synchronized with the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) time base and cross-referenced with air traffic control (ATC) radar tracks.

The approach phase commenced at 15:42:10 UTC, with the aircraft established on a 280° heading at 3,200 ft MSL. The recorded indicated airspeed was 148 knots, with a calculated crosswind component of 24 knots, gusting to 31 knots. At 15:42:45 UTC, the aircraft descended through 1,500 ft MSL, with the autopilot disengaged and manual control inputs initiated. The pitch attitude stabilized at -2.1°, and the vertical speed increased to 1,850 ft/min.

At 15:43:02 UTC, the radio altitude indicated 50 ft, with a sink rate of 1,120 ft/min (18.7 ft/s). The FDR recorded a sudden increase in vertical acceleration to 1.8 Gz, followed by a rapid spike to 3.8 Gz at 15:43:05.5 UTC, coinciding with main gear touchdown. The NLG contacted the runway surface 0.8 seconds later, with the recorded vertical load factor peaking at 4.1 Gz. The design limit vertical load for the 737-800 NLG is 2.0 Gz, with a maximum certified sink rate of 10 ft/s. The recorded sink rate at NLG touchdown was 14.2 ft/s, exceeding the design envelope by 42%.

Control surface data indicated a 12° left aileron deflection and 8° right rudder input during the final 3 seconds of approach, consistent with crosswind correction techniques. The elevator trim was set at 4.2 units nose-up, within the normal approach range. No abnormal system warnings or fault codes were recorded in the aircraft condition monitoring system (ACMS) prior to touchdown.

The DOOR PLUG pressure differential sensor recorded a transient spike to 0.8 PSI at 15:43:06 UTC, followed by a rapid decay to 0.1 PSI. This transient is consistent with localized aerodynamic loading and structural flexure during the impact sequence, but does not indicate seal failure or pressurization loss. The DOOR PLUG remained latched throughout the event, as confirmed by post-accident latch engagement measurements.

Wiring harness continuity testing was performed on the forward fuselage fuel quantity indication system (FQIS) and associated grounding paths. All circuits exhibited resistance values within ±5% of baseline specifications, with no evidence of short circuits, open conductors, or insulation breakdown. The inspection confirmed compliance with Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 (SFAR 88) ignition source mitigation requirements, as all high-energy wiring was properly routed, shielded, and separated from fuel system components. No arc-fault detection system (AFDS) triggers were recorded in the FDR data.

The timeline reconstruction indicates that the NLG collapse occurred within 0.6 seconds of initial runway contact, with the drag brace buckling at approximately 112% of the certified limit load. The forward fuselage skin deformation initiated at 15:43:06.2 UTC, with the maximum deflection recorded at 15:43:07.1 UTC. The aircraft came to a complete stop at 15:43:12.4 UTC, with a total ground roll of 2,840 ft. The recorded deceleration profile was consistent with maximum manual braking and reverse thrust deployment, with no evidence of asymmetric braking or tire failure.

Comparison with normal operational parameters indicates that the vertical load factor, sink rate, and crosswind component exceeded the design envelope for the NLG assembly. The FDR data confirms that the aircraft was within certified weight and balance limits, with a calculated landing weight of 142,500 lbs (maximum certified landing weight: 146,300 lbs). The recorded wind shear and gust parameters were consistent with the reported meteorological conditions, with a peak gust of 35 knots recorded at 15:43:04 UTC.

5. SUMMARY

The following factual findings are derived from the physical examination, material testing, and flight data analysis:

- The nose landing gear (NLG) assembly collapsed during runway contact, with the drag brace exhibiting ductile overload fracture at the lower clevis attachment. No pre-existing fatigue cracks, corrosion, or manufacturing defects were identified.
- The NLG outer cylinder bottomed out at 11.4 inches of compression, exceeding the design limit of 9.5 inches. Nitrogen pressure and seal condition were within serviceable limits.
- The forward fuselage skin and stringer frames exhibited permanent plastic deformation, with a maximum deflection of 2.8 inches at station 340.0. Three of eight NLG attachment fasteners sheared at the shank; remaining fasteners were torqued within specification.
- The DOOR PLUG latches exhibited plastic deformation with permanent set measurements of 0.045 to 0.052 inches. The perimeter seal was compressed to 68% of original height, but the DOOR PLUG remained engaged throughout the event.
- Material testing of the drag brace and forward fuselage skin confirmed compliance with Boeing Material Specifications (BMS 7-222 and BMS 7-223). Hardness, chemical composition, tensile strength, and fracture toughness values were within certified ranges.
- FDR data recorded a peak vertical acceleration of 4.1 Gz and a sink rate of 14.2 ft/s at NLG touchdown, exceeding the design limit of 2.0 Gz and 10 ft/s. The crosswind component was 24 knots, gusting to 35 knots.
- No abnormal system warnings, fault codes, or wiring anomalies were recorded. Continuity testing of the forward fuselage fuel quantity indication system confirmed compliance with Special Federal Aviation Regulation 88 (SFAR 88) ignition source prevention requirements.
- The aircraft's weight and balance were within certified limits. The recorded deceleration profile and control surface inputs were consistent with manual crosswind landing techniques and maximum braking application.
- All measurements, test results, and data parameters are documented in the referenced photographs, laboratory reports, and decoded FDR/QAR files. No evidence of pre-impact structural degradation, maintenance discrepancies, or material non-conformance was identified.

INTERVIEW OF MARCUS THORNE, RAMP SUPERVISOR
Date: August 18, 2021
Time: 10:15 AM
Location: Conference Room B, Terminal 3 Operations Building
Interviewer: NTSB Investigator J. Davis

Q: Please state your full name and current position for the record.
A: Marcus Thorne. I’m the ramp supervisor for the ground handling division here at the airport. I’ve been in this role for about six years, and before that I worked line maintenance for roughly eight. So I’m familiar with both sides of the operation.

Q: And on August 15th, 2021, what were your specific duties and location?
A: I was on the day shift, covering the south ramp and taxiway Bravo. Mostly coordinating pushbacks, fueling, baggage transfers, and keeping the apron clear of FOD. Standard day, except for the weather. It had been blowing hard since early morning.

Q: Walk me through your first awareness of the incident.
A: Right. So, it was... I want to say around 14:22, maybe 14:25 local time. I was out near gate 14, checking a belt loader that had a hydraulic leak, when I heard the approach. You know how you can just tell when a jet’s coming in differently? The engine pitch changes, the spool-up sounds... strained. I looked up toward runway 27, and the 737 was just... it was low, but the descent rate was way too aggressive. I remember thinking, "That’s not right. They’re too fast on the glide path."

Q: What happened next?
A: Well, it touched down. Hard. I mean, *really* hard. There was this massive bang—like a freight train hitting a retaining wall, but sharper. Then a second impact, almost immediately after. The nose gear just... folded. It didn’t bounce or skip. It collapsed inward, straight down. The aircraft pitched forward, the nose scraped the pavement, and sparks flew everywhere. It slid for maybe... I don’t know, a hundred, hundred-fifty feet before it finally stopped. The engines were still running for a few seconds, then they spooled down. You could hear the wind whistling through the damaged cowling.

Q: Can you describe the sensory details more specifically? What did you see, hear, smell?
A: Yeah. The sound... it wasn’t just a thud. It was a metallic crunch, followed by this tearing noise. Like aluminum giving way under stress. And the smell—burnt rubber, hydraulic fluid, ozone. It hung in the air for a while. Visually, the nose was resting on the concrete, the forward fuselage was scuffed, and there was a trail of fluid leaking from the nose wheel well. The main gear held, though. The slides deployed on both sides within seconds. Passengers started coming out. I’d say it was chaotic but controlled. Flight attendants were doing their jobs, shouting directions, pointing people away from the wings. I ran over with a couple of ramp guys to help direct the evacuees to the muster point.

Q: Approximately how long from touchdown to full evacuation?
A: I’d say... maybe eight to ten minutes total. The slides deployed within thirty seconds of the aircraft stopping. Most passengers were off by minute four or five. The last few were elderly, needed a bit of help down the slides. By 14:40, everyone was accounted for. No serious injuries, just bumps, bruises, a couple of sprained ankles. The crew did a great job.

Q: What was your role after the evacuation was complete?
A: I stayed on scene to coordinate with maintenance, the airline’s safety rep, and the preliminary NTSB team. We had to secure the area, keep non-essential personnel back, and preserve the evidence. I also helped pull the maintenance logs and ground handling records. There was a lot of back-and-forth with the FAA inspectors. They were already talking about structural assessments, you know, damage tolerance requirements for the forward pressure bulkhead and the nose gear attachment points. I’m not a structural engineer, but I’ve been around long enough to know they were looking for overstress failures, checking if the airframe exceeded its certified load limits during that impact.

Q: During the post-incident inspection, did you overhear any technical discussions about the aircraft’s systems or components?
A: Yeah, a bit. The maintenance crew was going over the engine mounts and the pylon attachments. I remember one of the lead mechanics mentioning the LEAP-1B engine specs, though... wait, no, that’s the MAX, right? This was an 800. He was probably just comparing it to the newer fleet’s mounting brackets or referencing a service bulletin that covered both platforms. Anyway, they were checking for any secondary damage from the hard landing. The engines themselves looked intact, but the forward mounts took a hit. They were talking about torque values, shear pins, that kind of thing. I just nodded along, mostly. My background’s more on the airframe side.

Q: Were there any other aircraft or operators involved in the immediate response or perimeter management?
A: Not directly, but... uh, Island Express Helicopters actually had a couple of their birds parked at the FBO just north of the runway. Their chief pilot, Dave, he came over with a drone to get some overhead shots for the insurance adjusters and the safety team. It was helpful, honestly. Gave us a better angle on the gear collapse and the fuselage scrape. We coordinated with them to keep their airspace clear while the ARFF was working. They also ran a quick thermal sweep to make sure there were no hot spots in the wheel wells or near the fuel lines.

Q: Let’s go back to the weather. Can you describe the conditions more specifically?
A: Yeah, it was gusty. We had wind advisories all day. I think the tower was reporting something like 25 knots, gusting to 35, with a crosswind component of maybe 18 or 20. The wind was shifting, too. One minute it’s a quartering tailwind, next it’s a direct crosswind. You could see the trees bending, debris blowing across the taxiway. It wasn’t ideal for a 737, honestly. The pilots were probably fighting it all the way down. I saw the aircraft crabbing on final, then it just... didn’t quite align before touchdown.

Q: Is there anything else you observed that might be relevant to the investigation?
A: Just... the aftermath. The way the nose settled. It wasn’t a clean break. The gear doors were bent inward, the strut was compressed, and the forward fuselage skin was wrinkled. I also noticed the runway lights near the touchdown zone were intact, which tells me the main gear hit first, then the nose came down. The wind didn’t let up, either. Even after the plane stopped, the crosswind was still pushing against the fuselage. I was worried it might tip, but it settled. The nose was resting on the pavement, but the main gear held. I’ve seen hard landings before, but this one... it was different. The energy transfer was just too much for the nose structure.

Q: Thank you, Mr. Thorne. We’ll follow up if we need clarification or additional documentation.
A: Yeah, sure. Happy to help. Just... let me know if you need the radio logs, the ramp camera footage, or the maintenance sign-off sheets. I’ve got it all backed up. And if you need me to walk the site again, I’m available.
